Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 1:

(Verse) No. 1.

O you who believe, fulfil the bonds (fully observe the obligations). Life requires certain regulations. The relationship between a human being and his own self also has principles and rules. Then there are principles governing the relationship between one human being and another, and then the relationship between human beings and all other living creatures and non-living things. The ties with relatives, the ties with non-relatives and distant people, relations with the members of one's family and tribe, relations with the community (jamaʿah), the relationship of an individual with the whole Ummah, relations with enemies, relations with friends, relations with those living creatures of the world that Allah has placed under human control, and relations with those that are unrestrained and uncontrolled, and the principles governing the relationship of human beings with all the things of this vast and wide universe, are all present in their entirety within the Islamic system of life. Then the link of human life with its Lord, with its Master, is a relationship that is the fundamental value of life. All these matters are fixed and regulated within this system.

The Islamic system practically establishes all these regulations and relationships in human life. It establishes these relationships, sets limits and bounds for them, and explains them fully. All these ties are made in the name of the Lord, the Possessor of Majesty. He guarantees the respect of all these ties. He does not permit their dishonour or their being mocked. Regarding these ties, the Islamic system does not tolerate the situation in which they are handed over to changing carnal desires, or made subservient to aims and objectives related to the desire and thinking of a single individual, or in which a group is interested in these aims and desires, or some nation among the nations of the world has these aims, or some generation among the generations of human history is interested in them and, for these reasons, wishes to break them. The welfare of human beings lies in all these ties, provided that these ties have been laid down by Allah and His Messenger for people, even if some individual, some group, some nation or some generation considers that there is no benefit for human beings in them, because Allah knows best.

And the knowledge of people is limited. What Allah decides is better than what people decide for themselves. The first step in the respect and reverence due to Allah is that a person should not place his personal estimation against the decree of Allah, and should believe that what Allah has determined is best. And whatever Allah has determined, one should submit before it with complete willingness, complete certainty and full satisfaction.

Allah refers to all the regulations we have mentioned above by the word "al-'Uqud" (the bonds), and commands the believers to fully observe these bonds. Allah commanded the Muslims to observe the bonds and obligations, and after that began explaining what is lawful and unlawful. He explained the prohibited items in food and drink, explained the prohibited persons in marriage, and after them explained other Shariah rulings and the details of the methods of worship. Along with this, the correct beliefs and ideologies were also explained, the methods of servitude and worship were stated, and the details of the sovereignty of Allah were also given.

Then the nature of the relations between the Muslim Ummah and other nations was also mentioned, and rulings were also stated. It is the duty of the Muslim Ummah to bear witness to the truth, to establish justice in the world, and to watch over all of humanity, because its Book is also comprehensive of and a guardian over all the scriptures. Then there is the command that in an Islamic society decisions should be according to the law of Allah, and the command not to fall into strife, and not to abandon the bond of justice and equity on account of personal and individual reasons. All these matters explain the "al-'Uqud."

In short, the opening of this Surah with the word "al-'Uqud," and after it the explanation of all the rulings, beliefs and acts of worship, indicates that the meaning of the word "'uqud" and "'aqd" is far broader than the meaning that comes to mind upon hearing this word; rather, it refers to the entire code of life which Allah has prescribed for human beings. The foundation of the code of life that Allah has prescribed for human beings rests upon faith in Allah and the knowledge of what the divinity of Allah means, and what the requirements of Allah's divinity, sovereignty and worship are. This "'aqd" (covenant) springs from this faith and the concept of Allah's sovereignty, and all the regulations of life are built upon this faith, belief and the fulfilment of bonds.

The covenant of believing in Allah, the acknowledgment of Allah's sovereignty, lordship and His being the Sustainer and Overseer, and the requirements of complete worship of Allah and the promises of all-encompassing and profound obedience and submission that result from this covenant and acknowledgment, are the matters upon which the edifice of Islam is built. This covenant was first taken by Allah from Hadrat Adam at the time when Allah entrusted to him the keys of the office of khilafah (vicegerency) on earth. This pact and covenant has been stated by the Holy Qur'an in these words and conditions:

(Verse) "We said: Go down from it, all of you. Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve. And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide forever." (2:38-39)

(We said: all of you go down from here. Then when guidance from Me reaches you, those who follow My guidance will have no fear or sorrow. And those who refuse to accept it and deny Our signs, they are the people of the Fire, in which they will abide forever.) The station of khilafah on earth that was given to Hadrat Adam, and after him to humankind in general, is conditional upon the acceptance of the guidance that Allah's Messengers bring. If the Messengers of Allah and the guidance revealed upon them are not accepted, this will be a clear violation of the covenant, and then humankind will have no right to remain alive on this earth, nor will it be its owner. If this covenant is violated, then whatever acts are contrary to this covenant will be void and null, will have no legal standing, and those acts cannot be set right again. Therefore, whoever truly believes in Allah and wishes to fulfil his covenant with Allah has a duty to resist this falsehood, never to accept it, and not to enter into any transaction on the basis of this falsehood; if anyone does so, he will certainly not be fulfilling the covenant.

The covenant with Allah and this pact have been renewed with the offspring of Adam. With every generation of Adam's descendants that has come into existence, this has been renewed again. In another verse it is said:

(Verse) "And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves, saying: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes, we testify.' This, lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: 'Indeed we were unaware of this.' Or lest you should say: 'Only our fathers associated partners with Allah before, and we were offspring after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?'" (7:172-173)

(And, O Prophet, remind the people of the time when your Lord took out from the loins of the children of Adam their offspring and made them bear witness concerning themselves, asking them: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Certainly You are our Lord; we bear witness to it." We said this so that on the Day of Resurrection you would not say: "We were unaware of this," or say: "The beginning of shirk was made by our fathers before us, and we were their descendants after them. Will You then destroy us for what the wrongdoers did?")

In short, this was another explicit covenant which was concluded with every individual. This covenant is one which Allah says was concluded with all the children of Adam, and that it took place while they were in the loins of their fathers. We cannot question here how this covenant was concluded, because it is Allah alone who knows how it was concluded. How Allah addressed people, Allah alone knows, while they were in the loins of their forefathers. In any case, Allah addressed them and established the proof against them, and a covenant was taken from them that He is their Lord, and they acknowledged this, as Allah has described. Now, if people do not accept the divinity of Allah, this will be a violation of the covenant on their part.

Further on in this Surah it is stated that Allah took a similar covenant from the Children of Israel, at the time when He raised the mountain over them like a canopy, and it seemed that the mountain was about to fall upon them. It will be explained later how they violated this covenant and pact, and how the punishment of God then descended upon them.

Likewise, those people who believed in Hadrat Muhammad (ﷺ) in fact made a covenant with Allah by believing in him. They pledged hearing and obedience, in ease and in hardship, and that they would hold this covenant above everything else, and would not challenge the entitlement of a person who is deserving and fit for any task.

After this general covenant and bond, specific covenants also took place. At the occasion of the Second Pledge of 'Aqabah, as a result of which the process of Hijrah began and the Prophet (ﷺ) moved from Makkah to Madinah, a similar covenant was concluded with the representatives of the Ansar, and at Hudaybiyah also a covenant was concluded under the name of Bay'at al-Ridwan.

In short, all other bonds are built upon the covenant of faith in Allah and the pledge of worshipping Allah, whether they relate to Allah's commands or prohibitions, or to ordinary people, living things, or the other things of this universe, or to the limits about which Allah has given a legal ruling. All these are bonds, and Allah is commanding the believers, as believers, to carry them out fully, because upon coming to faith they have become bound by them, and it is the requirement of faith that they do so. This is why the address came in this manner: (Verse) "O you who believe, fulfil the bonds," and after this further details of these bonds come as follows.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

The limits and conditions of permitted and forbidden matters, whether concerning the animals that may be slaughtered, the various things that are lawful or unlawful, the places where something is lawful or unlawful, or the times when something is lawful or unlawful, are all ʿuqūd (binding covenants). All these ʿuqūd and covenants and pledges are founded upon faith. Therefore, the requirement of the faith of those who have believed is that they take all guidance concerning the lawful and the unlawful from Allah, and that in this matter they accept nothing from other than Allah. This is why, at the very beginning of the discourse, it was said that you must fully observe the ʿuqūd and bonds. After this, the explanation of the lawful and the unlawful begins.

﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you (later)﴾ (5:1).

That is: because Allah made it lawful for you, and because Allah has explained this lawfulness for you, and no other lawmaker has made it so, it became permissible for you to eat all those animals that are of the kind of livestock, that is, slaughtered animals and game animals, except those whose prohibition Allah Himself explains afterwards, and those whose prohibition is yet to be stated. Such a prohibition is either specific to a particular time, or specific to a particular place, or it is an absolute prohibition connected to every time and every place. The term bahīmat al-anʿām includes camels, cattle, sheep and goats, and wild animals of this kind are also included in it, such as wild cattle, deer and wild donkeys.

Now, from this general ruling of lawfulness, certain exceptional cases are presented. The first is that hunting is declared forbidden while in the state of iḥrām: ﴿not violating the sanctity of game while you are in iḥrām﴾ (5:1). This prohibition applies to the act of hunting. As soon as a person puts on iḥrām for Ḥajj or ʿUmrah, he gives up his ordinary life and turns towards Allah. He enters the House of Allah with a new manner of life. Allah has prescribed certain etiquettes for His House and has declared it a abode of security (dār al-amn and dār al-amān). Whoever enters its boundaries, it is forbidden for him to raise his hand against any living creature. This is a psychological pause, and such pauses are necessary for the human soul. In this way, the bond of all living things is established with the Giver of life, and during this period and within the boundaries of this place, no living creature can be harmed. Through this command, the scope of human needs is also limited, which is why the eating of game was permitted, and the eating of other animals was made lawful, so that during this period a person may rise a little above ordinary daily life, rise above earthly impurities in the House of Allah, and have his gaze directed towards a high and luminous horizon.

Before proceeding further into the details of the lawful and the unlawful, this covenant is connected with that great covenant which every believer and every human being made with Allah. The believers are reminded that the great covenant was made with Allah, and that Allah commands what He wills: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands what He wills﴾ (5:1). The will of Allah is free; His will is the true sovereign. He alone holds this right of rule, so He commands whatever He wills, and there is no one else who shares in His will. No one else has any right of command. No one can reject His commands, and here too He makes unlawful whom He wills and makes lawful whom He wills, for He is the lawgiver. After this, further explanation is given and emphasis is laid that it is not permissible for you to violate the sanctity of the things that are honoured in the sight of Allah.

﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the offerings or the garlands or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His approval. And when you have come out of iḥrām, then you may hunt﴾ (5:2).

What are the rites of Allah (shaʿāʾir Allāh)? What comes to mind here is that they refer to Ḥajj and ʿUmrah, and to the prohibitions (muḥarramāt) whose commission is forbidden during Ḥajj and ʿUmrah, and to the obligatory acts performed in them, until Ḥajj and ʿUmrah are completed, that is, after sacrifice. In the state of iḥrām, it is not permissible for the one in iḥrām to declare these rites of Allah lawful or to disregard their sanctity, because if he does so, he will not uphold the sanctity that Allah has attached to these things. These rites are attributed to Allah because they are most honoured in the sight of Allah, and to disregard them would be a very dangerous crime.

What are the sacred months? Rajab, Dhu al-Qaʿdah, Dhu al-Ḥijjah and Muḥarram are the four months. Allah has made warfare unlawful during these months. Before Islam, the Arabs also considered fighting in these months to be impermissible, but they would alter these sacred months as they pleased. In this they practised nasī’, that is, they postponed the sanctity of one month for a period, and they obtained a ruling for this postponement from soothsayers, or had it announced through some powerful desert tribes. This postponement would be carried from one year to the next. When Islam came, Islam declared the practice of nasī’ unlawful, and declared these months sacred in the same way that Allah had made them sacred, and in the way that Allah had fixed these months from the time He created the heavens and the earth. The mention of this in the verse of Surah al-Tawbah is as follows:

﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them, four are sacred. That is the correct religion, so do not wrong yourselves therein. And fight against the polytheists all together as they fight against you all together. And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ (9:36).

In the next verse it was decided that the practice of nasī’ is an additional act of disbelief, and the correct position is the command of Allah, which is that fighting in these months is forbidden, provided that no one attacks the Muslims in these months. If they are attacked, they may defend themselves. It is not permissible to allow attackers to use these months as a shield while themselves not observing the sanctity of these months. However, if their scheme is to use these months as a cover to escape the counter-action of the Muslims, this would not be permitted. The command regarding fighting in the sacred months has already passed earlier in Surah al-Baqarah.

The "hady" is the animal that a pilgrim or one performing ʿUmrah brings along, and which he slaughters after completing Ḥajj or ʿUmrah. This is called naḥr, and with it the rites of the pilgrim or ʿUmrah performer come to an end. It is either a camel, or some cattle, or a sheep or goat. And the statement "the hady is not lawful" means that it may not be used for any purpose other than the one for which it was bought or brought. It may not be slaughtered until the day of sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr) in Ḥajj arrives and the rites of ʿUmrah are completed. No person may benefit personally from the meat, skins, hair, wool and so on of these sacrificial animals (even in the form of their value), and it is necessary that he spend these things upon the poor.

Qalāʾid: this refers to the animals upon whose necks their owners would place a garland or collar. This collar was a sign that the animal was a hady. Pilgrims, after placing such a collar, would leave the animal free and slaughter it on the day of sacrifice. When collars were placed around the necks of animals, afterwards they would not be lawful for any other purpose, and they could not be slaughtered for any purpose other than that. Some scholars have said that the qalāʾid are those upon whose necks collars were placed, with the intention that these animals had been bought for Ḥajj and ʿUmrah. In this way they were protected from robbers and enemies. They would make such things from the trees of the Sanctuary and place them around the necks of these animals. These animals were generally let loose in the area, and no one would lay a hand on them. Those who have explained qalāʾid in this sense say that this verse has been abrogated, because the verse revealed after it:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are impure, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Ḥarām after this year of theirs. And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ (9:28)

and in another place: ﴿So seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾ (9:5). But the first opinion is stronger, and it is evident that the qalāʾid are the animals that have been dedicated for slaughter in the name of Allah, and whose necks have been fitted with collars, and it is also evidence for this that their mention came after hady. The meaning is that by them is meant the hady that is garlanded, and these are the garlanded animals of Ḥajj and ʿUmrah.

Allah has also forbidden those who are "āmmīn al-bayt", that is, those who have resolved to go to the House of Allah and whose aim is the seeking of Allah's bounty and His pleasure. These are those who intend Ḥajj or intend ʿUmrah. In this journey, two things may be before their minds: trade and the attainment of the pleasure of Allah. In this journey Allah has given such people a guarantee of security.

At the end, it has been made clear that hunting has not been permanently forbidden to you. When you come out of iḥrām, hunting is lawful for you, but outside the boundaries of the Sanctuary, because within the boundaries of the Sanctuary hunting is forbidden in every state. ﴿And when you have come out of iḥrām, then you may hunt﴾ (5:2), but outside the boundaries of the Sanctuary, because Allah has declared the boundaries of the Sanctuary a zone of security, just as He has declared the sacred months a period of security. This is the region in which people, animals, birds and trees all remain at peace, and they have no fear of being harmed by anyone. In short, there is a comprehensive security which, like a dense, shady tree, always flourishes over this House. This comprehensive "shade of security" is spread over the boundaries of the Sanctuary because Ibrahim (peace be upon him) made this supplication for this nation, that Allah make this House a place of security, and Allah accepted this supplication. For four months the atmosphere of peace covers the whole land of Arabia, and for those full four months this peace and safety displays its glory under the shade of the Islamic order. This safety is so comprehensive that every human heart feels its tranquillity and calm, and every person of taste feels its sweetness. Therefore it is our duty to be extremely active in creating this atmosphere of peace and safety, and after these four months, in the whole course of life, in the twelve months of the year and everywhere, to strive to create such an atmosphere.

Within this zone of security, in this atmosphere of sanctities, Allah now calls upon those who believe in Allah and who have made a covenant with Allah that they will fulfil their covenant, and will raise their station, their programme and their position to the height required by the great purpose and ideal that has been entrusted to them. What is that great ideal and purpose? It is that the Muslim ummah is a overseer over all the nations living on this earth, and it must discharge this mission of its life without being influenced by personal feelings, individual inclinations or temporary circumstances. It is commanded that you must not oppress even those who, on the occasion of Ḥudaybiyyah, prevented you from entering al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, and who, even before that when they were in Makkah, used to create such obstacles. Although the wounds they inflicted were still fresh in the hearts of the Muslims, and the hatred against those people for preventing them from the Masjid al-Ḥarām was still fresh in the hearts of the Muslims, nevertheless, although this situation existed, the duties and objectives of the Muslim ummah were above these things; the aims and duties of the ummah were from the standpoint of this great character of the ummah. He says:

﴿And let not the enmity of a people, because they hindered you from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, incite you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾ (5:2).

This is the highest station in the field of self-restraint, and the highest degree of magnanimity, and it is an obligation upon this ummah, which Allah has now appointed as the overseer and mentor of all humanity, which has been entrusted with the task of the refinement and progress of the common people, and which has been commanded to turn the whole of humanity towards this lofty and luminous horizon and ideal.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 5, verse 2 (part 2 of 2):

These are the duties that are indispensable to the office of leadership, oversight and guardianship. It is the obligation of the believers to put aside all the afflictions and hardships that they suffered at the hands of these enemies. This is so that they practically present to the world the model that Islam desires, so that the tolerance that Islam seeks to create is practically presented before mankind. Only in this way can the Muslim ummah bear witness to the truth on behalf of Islam, and people can turn towards Islam and come to like it.

The truth is that this is a great responsibility, but in this form it is not burdensome to the human soul, nor is it beyond the strength and capacity of a human being. Islam permits a person to become angry; it is a person's right to dislike what is bad. But people do not have the right, upon disliking something, to immediately react, or to become utterly helpless under the grip of enmity and rancour. Islam commands them that in good deeds and acts of piety they should rise up at once and react promptly, but in sin and the work of oppression they should not form factions. They should fear Allah, protect themselves from His punishment, and through piety and God-fearing keep their souls under control. They should hold its reins firmly and develop within themselves forbearance and tolerance. They should fear Allah, and His pleasure should always remain before their eyes.

It was the perfection of Islam that its training gave an uncouth and ignorant people such as the Arab nation self-restraint, and created in them a very strong consciousness in this regard, and they adopted a most compassionate and generous attitude, although it was a people from whom little could be expected of such a high level of moral conduct and good treatment, because the direction of their culture was opposed to that. The Arab way of knowledge and their attitude in this matter was: (Help your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed) (Support your brother, whether he is the wrongdoer or the wronged). This was ignorant zeal and the partisanship of the Age of Ignorance. In their view, cooperating in sin and oppression was more attractive than cooperating in matters of righteousness and piety. They always concluded pacts of mutual cooperation in falsehood and misguidance, and their gatherings upon truth and justice were very rare. Few oaths were sworn for truth in the history of the Age of Ignorance. And this is the natural characteristic of every society whose connection and relationship is not with the Being of Allah, and whose customs and traditions do not conform to the Islamic method and the standards set by Allah the Exalted. This principle was fully encapsulated in that famous maxim of the Age of Ignorance: help your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. And a pre-Islamic poet presented this principle thus:

Wa hal ana illa min Ghazyata in ghawat ghawaitu
Wa in tarshud Ghazyatu arshad
(I am but a member of the clan of Ghazyah; if it goes astray, I too shall go astray, and if it finds guidance, I too shall find guidance.)

When Islam came and the Islamic system of training came, Allah the Exalted revealed this command:

(Verse) "And let not the enmity of a people, because they hindered you from the Sacred Mosque, incite you to transgress. Cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment." (5:2)

"And let not the anger at a people who barred you from the Sacred Mosque drive you to commit excesses against them. Cooperate with one another in acts of righteousness and God-fearing, and do not cooperate in sin and transgression. Fear Allah; His punishment is severe."

Islam came and joined hearts to Allah. The standards of Allah for morality and the values of life came into the field. Islam brought the Arabs and the whole of humanity out of the zeal of ignorance. It forbade the slogan of partisanship, and it delivered people from personal inclinations, individual impressions, and the narrow thinking of family and tribe, and it made humanity alone the axis when dealing with friends and enemies alike.

After the victory of Islam, a new human being came into being within the Arabian Peninsula. This human being was adorned with divine morality. Thus the Arabs received a new birth, and when this light spread into the world, humanity received a fresh birth across the whole globe. Before Islam, the entire Arabian Peninsula was immersed in the darkness of ignorance, whose slogan was: "Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." Indeed, the whole world was drowned in the darkness of this ignorant slogan.

The distance and gulf between the deep pit of ignorance and the luminous horizon of Islam is very great, and how beautifully this distance becomes clear through these two statements: one, "Help your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed," and the other, the saying of Allah the Exalted:

"And let not the enmity of a people, because they hindered you from the Sacred Mosque, incite you to transgress. Cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment."

This is part 1 of 3 of the commentary, so it ends mid-argument, after the explanation of the verse "Today I have perfected your religion for you..." and its implications.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

The difference between these two statements is as wide as the difference between earth and sky.

Now, after the general permission to eat the lawful animals among the cattle, some forms are mentioned that are not lawful:

﴿Forbidden to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored to death, and that which has been eaten by a beast of prey, except what you slaughter while it is still alive, and that which is sacrificed on the altars (nusub). And that you seek decision through the arrows (azlam) is a transgression. Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion. But whoever is compelled by hunger, not inclining willfully to sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (5:3)

The prohibition of dead animals, blood and the flesh of swine has already been mentioned earlier (see Surah al-Baqarah, verse 172). There, the extent to which human knowledge can comprehend the wisdom of the Islamic law was also explained. Whether human knowledge is able to grasp the wisdom of the divine law or not, Allah has nevertheless decided that these things are not pure for food. For us, the command of Allah alone is sufficient, because Allah declares unlawful only those things that are impure, and these also carry some harm in some aspect of human life, even if people are not aware of that harm. The question is: have people discovered all the things that are harmful or beneficial to them?

Similarly:

﴿wa ma uhilla li-ghayrillah bihi﴾ (5:3), meaning those that have been dedicated to other than Allah, are unlawful because they are fundamentally opposed to the concept of faith. Their very basis contradicts the belief that Allah is One, without partner, that He alone is the Sovereign and the God, and that He alone holds the power of benefit and harm. The demands of this doctrine of Tawhid are that a person direct every intention, every will and every action solely to Allah. He should mention the name of Allah over everything and begin every deed and every movement in the name of Allah alone. Therefore, every movement or action over which Allah's name has not been mentioned, and everything over which the name of someone other than Allah has been pronounced, and likewise every slaughtered animal over which no name has been mentioned at all, neither of other than Allah nor of Allah, is also unlawful, because this act is in conflict with the foundations of faith. If there is true faith in someone's heart, such an act cannot proceed from him, because it is an impure act. And since this act is impure in belief, it has been included among those impure things that are impure physically, such as blood and the flesh of swine.

﴿wal-munkhaniqah﴾ (the one strangled to death, or that which died on its own), ﴿wal-mawqudhah﴾ (the one that falls from a high place, or dies by falling from a mountain or into a well), ﴿wal-nathiha﴾ (the one killed by being struck by another animal), ﴿wa ma akalas-sabu'﴾ (the one eaten by a beast of prey): all these are kinds of carrion and are unlawful. However, if they are still alive and are slaughtered, then eating them is lawful. The exception of slaughter is mentioned here so that it is not thought that the prohibition is due to falling, strangulation, or being mauled by an animal. Among the jurists there are differences of opinion as to when an animal is considered slaughtered and its meat becomes lawful. According to some opinions, an animal killed by all these means is unlawful if these means quickly take its life or render it completely dead. According to them, even if such an animal is slaughtered, it will still be unlawful, whereas according to some other opinions it is lawful provided that there is life in it and it is slaughtered, however it may be slaughtered. Details can be seen in the books of jurisprudence.

﴿wa ma dhubiha 'alan-nusub﴾ (the animals sacrificed at altars): idolaters used to slaughter animals on idols, and in the Jahiliyyah they used to smear their blood on the idols. Such rituals exist also among peoples other than the Arabs. These are unlawful because such animals were slaughtered for idols, even if the name of Allah was pronounced while slaughtering them, since slaughtering for an idol inevitably entails shirk.

It is also unlawful to divide by means of arrows. Azlam are the arrows through which the Arabs used to seek omens, deciding whether to do a thing or not. According to some opinions there were three such arrows, and according to others seven. They were also used in gambling. By means of them people also distributed the meat of slaughtered animals: each person had an arrow, and if the arrow that corresponded to a particular portion of the animal came out, that portion of meat became his. Allah declared this method of distributing meat unlawful, because it was also a form of gambling, which had already been prohibited. Accordingly, meat divided in this way was also declared unlawful.

﴿Fa man idturra fi makhmasatin ghayra mutajanifin li-ithm, fa innallaha Ghafurun Rahim﴾ (5:3)

Whoever is compelled by hunger, not inclining willfully to sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

A person who is in a state of necessity due to hunger (that is, in makhmasah), and whose life is in danger, may eat from these forbidden things, provided that he is not deliberately committing a sin. Jurists differ regarding how much he may eat: whether he should eat only enough to save his life, or eat until satisfied to the extent of need, or, if there is a fear of scarcity of food in the future, also store some. We do not go into these details here; it is only necessary to keep in mind that ease and facility have been placed in the religion of Islam. At the time of need, the rules of Islam are not applied harshly, nor are difficulties created for people. Matters are left to people's circumstances and entrusted to the fear of Allah and God-consciousness. If someone commits a prohibited act under compulsion, and his intention is not to disobey the commands and he does not do it deliberately, then he will not be held accountable. ﴿Fa innallaha Ghafurun Rahim﴾ (5:3) (Allah is Forgiving and Merciful).

Now here we stand at an important turning point. After the mention of the prohibitions, and before the list of lawful things begins, this verse suddenly comes in the middle:

﴿Al-yawma akmaltu lakum dinakum wa atmamtu 'alaykum ni'mati wa radītu lakumul-Islama dinan﴾ (5:3)

"Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion."

This verse is among those revealed last of all. Its purpose is that the mission of prophethood reached its final stages, and thus Allah's grace and favour upon people was completed. With the revelation of this verse, Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه), through his keen insight and God-given understanding, perceived that the days of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in this world were few, because he had delivered the trust to the people and conveyed the message of Allah; only the meeting with Allah remained. Therefore, after this verse was revealed, he began to weep, understanding that the time of separation from the Messenger (ﷺ) had now drawn very near.

It is worth reflecting that this verse has been placed right in the middle of the rulings on the lawful and unlawful, and that it has been placed in the surah whose aims and themes we have already discussed. What is its purpose? Its purpose is that the Shariah of Allah is a complete system, a whole, and its parts cannot be separated. Its parts are so interconnected that they cannot be detached from one another, whether they are doctrinal and ideological, or acts of worship, or collective rules for society, or relate to international affairs. All these matters are included in (al-din), whose completion is announced in this verse, and further, it is announced that by completing this religion Allah has also completed His favour upon you. In this religion there is no distinction between doctrinal matters, the rules and forms of worship, the rules of lawful and unlawful, and collective and international laws. All of them are parts of one whole, with which Allah has expressed His pleasure, and He has approved it for us. If believers deviate from any part of this religion and deny it, that will amount to a denial of the whole religion. It will be rebellion against the religion, and as a consequence the person will no longer remain a believer.

If someone denies even one part, the ruling will be the same as what we have explained earlier: abandoning any one part of this religion and putting in its place a code made by a human being is, in effect, a denial of Allah's sovereignty. In this way a person attributes to a human being a specific right of Allah in one matter, which is shirk, and it is an assault upon Allah's right to rule on this earth, and a claim of sovereignty and government for oneself, which Allah will never permit. Thus, a person openly rebels against the religion, and as a result of rebelling against the religion, a person goes out of the religion.

﴿Al-yawma yaisa alladhina kafaru min dinikum﴾ (5:3) (Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion): they have despaired that this religion could be nullified, made deficient, or distorted in any way. Allah has written that it will remain complete and perfect. Allah has recorded that this religion will remain forever. The people of disbelief may dominate the Muslims at some moment, and they may remain dominant for some period, but they cannot remain dominant over the religion of Islam. It is the only religion among all the religions that is preserved and will never be erased. It cannot be distorted, despite the fact that the enemies of this religion will always continue their efforts to distort it. They will continue to plot the harshest conspiracies against this religion, but they will not succeed. It may also happen that in some periods the people of Islam will be extremely heedless of their religion and will have very little knowledge of it. But Allah preserves it in this way: He always keeps in this world a group that carries this religion, which knows it well, and which constantly defends it; the religion remains in perfect form within that group, is preserved in their lives, and they continue to transmit this trust onward. Thus the promise of Allah remains true, that the people of disbelief remain hopeless concerning this religion in every age.

﴿Fa la takhshawhum wakhshawn﴾ (5:3) (So do not fear them but fear Me): because the people of disbelief do not have the power to harm this religion. They can only harm the people of Islam to the extent of turning them somewhat away from this religion, to the point that they appear to be a living picture of it while not fulfilling its obligations and requirements, and while not actually implementing the aims and duties of this religion in their lives.

Was the guidance given to the Muslims in Madinah Tayyibah only for the people of Madinah? Certainly not. Was it for that generation alone? Certainly not. Rather, it is a general address that is for the believers of every time and place. We humbly submit to the believers that the true believers are indeed those who are pleased with the religion that Allah has chosen for them, who implement the entire religion in their lives, and who make it their system of life.

﴿Al-yawma akmaltu lakum dinakum wa atmamtu 'alaykum ni'mati wa radītu lakumul-Islama dinan﴾ (5:3)

"Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion."

This verse was revealed on the occasion of the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada'). The meaning is that Allah has completed the religion, and now nothing can be added to it. The favour of the Lord has been completed upon the believers, and He has been pleased that Islam be accepted by them as their religion; and from today onward, whoever chooses any other religion than this is, in effect, rejecting the pleasure of Allah.

This is an extremely important verse, and a believer should pause and reflect upon its awe-inspiring words. If it is reflected upon carefully, the truths and realities hidden within it will never be exhausted. Profound guidance and the duties and demands of that era will come to mind from it.

The first truth that comes to mind from this reflection is that Allah has perfected the religion. Then a believer surveys all the messengers in the history of humanity, from the prophethood of Adam (peace be upon him) to the final prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and surveys the caravans of faith across all eras. He sees that this is a long and unbroken chain of messengers. It is a caravan of guidance and light, carrying a torch through this long journey. The signposts of this long journey are clearly visible. In this survey we clearly see that every messenger was sent for a particular people or a particular era. All the messengers before this final prophethood were sent for a particular period or a particular stage: a specific message, a specific stage, and a specific society. For this reason, the messengers bore the colour of their particular era and society. They were influenced by the circumstances and conditions in which they were sent. All these messengers were calling to the worship of one God alone. They were all calling to the servitude and sovereignty of one deity alone, because this is the religion of Islam: that we regard Allah alone as our sovereign and our object of worship, and obey Him alone. However, the law, the code, and the system given to those prophets was suitable for their people, their era, and their society, and was in accordance with their circumstances and conditions.

When Allah willed to bring the chain of messengers to an end, and to stop sending particular messengers to particular people, He sent a final messenger for all of humanity, and sent a Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets, for all mankind, whose message was not confined to a particular society, a particular people, or a particular era, and was not specific to the circumstances of any one age. This message was not bound by the confines of time and place, nor was it limited to the conditions of any one society. Allah raised this message upon the true innate nature of man, which does not undergo change or alteration, and human nature does not deviate from its course. Allah the Exalted says:

﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth. [Adhere to] the fitrah of Allah upon which He has created [all] people. No change should there be in the creation of Allah. That is the correct religion, but most of the people do not know.﴾ (30:30)

Then Allah granted this final message a law so detailed that it contains solutions to the problems of every aspect of life, and within it is the code for every human activity. For this law, Allah set out universal principles and foundations, in the light of which it resolves the problems of every age. In every time and place it appears, in the light of these principles, as though it has just been revealed. This law explicitly contains rules and commands that never change. Thus this law, with its foundations and principles, and with its detailed and enduring rulings, encompasses all the principles and requirements that any human being could ever need. This final message is for the period from the beginning of creation until the Day of Resurrection. Its rules, its guidance, its legislation, and its institutions of governance are for the Day of Resurrection, so that it may always remain alive and progress, and its renewal and development should take place in the light of these principles, but within the axis and the framework that was established for it from the very first day. Allah says:

﴿This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed upon you My favor and have approved for you Islam as religion.﴾ (5:3)

Through this verse, Allah has announced that your worldview is complete, your law is complete, and it is your religion. Therefore, for the believers there is no longer any opportunity to think that some deficiency remains in this religion which they would correct, nor is there any shortfall which they would complete. Nor is there any element of a particular time and place in it, such that they would add to it the colour of a new time and place. If they do so, they will neither be believers, nor will the religion they have fashioned be the religion of Islam, nor will it be acceptable to Allah, and true believers will not accept it.

The law of the era in which the Qur'an was revealed is for every era, because it is the law of the religion that has come into this world for all ages, and it is an eternal religion. It has not come for a particular group of people, nor for the people of a particular era, nor for a particular region, as was the case with the messages before Islam, which were confined to limited times and places.

The detailed rulings of Islam are such that they are enduring rulings, and the comprehensive principles of Islam are such that within their framework a detailed system for life can come into being in every era, and human life can develop in their light until the Day of Resurrection, without any difficulty. Except that life must be subject to the bounds of these principles, and then not step outside the sphere of faith.

Man was created by Allah, and Allah knows what He has created. Allah has chosen this religion for mankind, which rests upon His enduring law. Therefore, whoever says how can the legal system of yesterday be the law and the shariah for today, he in truth claims that he knows better than Allah about the needs of man, and that he has greater knowledge of human ways than Allah does.

In this pause for reflection, we see that Allah has completed His favor upon the believers, and this favor was completed in that Allah perfected their religion. Indeed, this is a complete, great, and weighty favor. Through this favor, man has been given a new birth, and through it the paths to his growth and his perfections have been opened. For man does not truly become a human being until he attains knowledge of Allah in the manner that this religion opens the doors of the knowledge of Allah. Until he understands the reality of this universe in the manner that this religion teaches it, and until he attains knowledge of his own self in the manner that this religion teaches him, that he is, in the sight of Allah, a noble creature. Man does not truly exist until he rejects all servitudes other than servitude to Allah and emerges from them, and until he attains the true equality which the law established by Allah grants to man, which is neither given by any human being nor involves any human intervention.

For man, comprehending these great truths is in truth a new birth for him, provided that he comprehends these truths in the manner that this religion has commanded him to comprehend them. Apart from this knowledge, it is possible that man may be an animal, or that he may be a plan for a human being still under construction and in formation, but he cannot be called a complete human being. He will be a complete human being only when he comprehends these truths according to the standard whose image the Qur'an has drawn. There is a great difference between this Qur'anic concept of man and all those concepts that people have fabricated on their own. (See the first part and the book Khasais al-Tasawwur al-Islami.)

Impressing the features of this image upon human life is in truth the guarantee that man has attained complete humanity. This image becomes complete when a person holds complete faith in Allah and believes in the angels, the books, the messengers, and the Day of Judgment. Then the human being will leave the sphere of the animal, perceptible world and enter the human world of the seen and the unseen. He will know the perceptible and also the world beyond the perceptible. He will be aware of matter and also of that which is beyond matter, and thus he will step out of the limited sensory sphere of the animal. He will attain this perfection through the belief in the Oneness of Allah. In this way he will also step out of the sphere of servitude to other human beings, and will worship Allah alone. Thus he will attain true equality, true freedom, and true exaltation in the face of everything other than Allah. Now he will worship Allah alone, and will take his law and system of life from Allah alone. He will rely upon Allah alone and fear Allah alone. This station will be attained by him when a person raises the level of his preferences according to the Islamic system of life, dedicates his refined inclinations and his powers to building and progress, and expends his powers in opposition to animal desires, and does not chase after the mere pursuit of pleasure like the animals and beasts. (See the book Hadha al-Din.)

Whoever has not spent time in the life of jahiliyyah (ignorance) and has not witnessed the ravages of jahiliyyah cannot comprehend the blessing of the religion of Islam, nor can he truly appreciate this blessing. Jahiliyyah is, in every era and every place, the system that Allah has not sent. Therefore, the one who has seen jahiliyyah and tasted it, in its concepts and ideas and in the conditions of practical life, can truly sense jahiliyyah and be aware of it. He can know it well, and it is truly he who can comprehend the great blessing of this religion.

Whoever has been afflicted by the calamities of blindness and misguidance, whoever has been subject to disintegration and bewilderment and confusion, whoever has been seized by the calamity of ruin and mental emptiness, and whoever has been harmed by jahili concepts in any era and any place, only that person can appreciate the taste of faith. (See the chapter Tih wa Irkam in Khasais al-Tasawwur al-Islami.)

Whoever has been crushed under the millstone of arrogance and oppression, whoever has suffered restraint and turmoil, whoever has passed his life in excess and deficiency, and whoever has lived by the ways of jahiliyyah, only that person can appreciate the Islamic and faith-based system of life. (See the chapter on restraint and turmoil in al-Islam wa Mushkilat al-Hadarah.)

The Qur'an first addressed the Arabs. They knew its words and expressions well, and the meanings and implications of its words had been practically established in their lives. All these qualities existed in the generation that the Qur'an addressed.

They themselves were cogs in the machinery of jahiliyyah. For a long time they had kept jahili concepts in their minds. They had practised the collective ties of jahiliyyah, they had repeatedly displayed the collective and individual morals of jahiliyyah, and they had also tested in their own lives what they had gained through this religion and the grace and favour that had been bestowed upon them through it.

They had seen the depths of jahiliyyah and had also experienced the heights of Islam. Islam had carried them along for a long time, and this religion had raised them, in a short span, to heights. (See the introduction to Surah al-Nisa.) They had already looked down upon the nations of the world from very lofty heights and with great joy, and in glancing back they were also viewing the past.

Consider the ways in which Islam elevated them. In beliefs and concepts, when they had been taking stone idols as lords, and angels, jinn, stars, and their own idols as lords, and even more foolish and erroneous notions were clung to in their hearts, Islam removed them from these ideas and brought them into the doctrine of Tawhid. It granted them certainty in one, unique God, who is Merciful and Loving, Powerful and Dominant, All-Hearing and All-Seeing, All-Knowing and All-Aware, Just and Perfect, Near and Responsive, and the God and object of worship without intermediary. All became His servants. They came out from the rule of soothsayers, they came out from the dominion of human states, and they emerged from the rule of illusions and superstitions, as though they had come out of darkness into light.

Then Islam also brought them out of jahiliyyah in their collective practices. It abolished class distinctions, removed detestable habits, and they desisted from oppression and tyranny, because in jahiliyyah they would commit every evil that was within their power. (It is a widely held but mistaken belief that Arab life before Islam was a democratic life.) I give here some excerpts from the book of Ustadh al-Aqqad.

"From the north to the south of the Arabian Peninsula, the ability to oppress was regarded among all their chiefs and leaders as a sign of honour and status. The famous poet Nabigha, while satirizing his opponent, exaggerates in a sarcastic manner in order to show that they are weak:

Qabilah la yaghdarun bi dhimmah
wa la yazlimun an-nasa habbata khardal

(His tribe never betrays a covenant, and its people do not oppress anyone even to the extent of a mustard seed.)

When Hujr ibn al-Harith, the Arab king, decided to enslave the Banu Asad, the poets of the Banu Asad came to intercede for them. They said:

Anta al-malik fihim
wa hum al-abid ila al-qiyamah
dhallu lisawtika mithlama
dhalla al-ashaiqu dhu al-khizamah

(You are their king, and they are slaves until the Day of Resurrection. They are as submissive to your whip as the deep yellow-red camel is submissive to the one who holds its nose-rope.)

And Amr ibn Hind was also a king who had accustomed people to address him from behind a screen. And the mothers of all the chiefs of Arabia would serve in his house.

Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir was also an Arab king. He was so cruel and foolish that he had set for himself two days: a day of joy, on which whoever came to him was given livestock, and a day of sorrow, on which whoever came to him he would kill, and this routine continued from morning until evening."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 3 of 3):

It is said regarding Kulayb ibn Wa'il that he was called Kulayb because wherever he liked the hunting, he would release a pack of dogs there. Now, whoever heard the barking of those dogs would not dare to approach that area. It is said that within the valley of Awf no one is free, because he would not allow any free person to live in the valley of Awf, so that no other free person would remain with him like himself. They were free, but they were like slaves.

(Haqa'iq al-Islam, al-Aqqad, pp. 150-151)

Islam raised these Arabs from Jahiliyyah in the fields of their customs, traditions, morals and social relations. It purified them from the Jahili weaknesses of burying daughters alive, oppressing women, drinking wine and gambling, sexual anarchy, obscenity and nakedness, considering women contemptible and insulting them, seeking revenge, raiding, plundering and ravaging, and showing cowardice before every invader, and the like. As far as cowardice and disunity in the face of external invaders is concerned, the attack of the Abyssinians before Islam is perhaps a witness to this. All the Arab tribes, which held the most severe positions against one another, were unable to resist that army. (See the commentary on Surat al-Fil.)

Then, having purified them of these filths, Islam made the Arabs into one ummah (community), a community so exalted that it looked down upon all humanity from a very lofty station, while this humanity was at that time in the lowest of the low depths of degradation. In every sphere of life, the humanity of that time was fallen. At that time there was either the exaltation of Islam or the abasement of Jahiliyyah. That generation knew what Jahiliyyah is and what Islam is. This is why these people understood well the meaning of God's command:

﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favour upon you, and I have approved Islam as your religion.﴾ (5:3)

And once again, let us reflect as a matter for serious thought: what a religion Allah has chosen for us. What favours and mercies Allah has bestowed upon this ummah. He Himself prescribes a religion for them and then also accepts it. This is a mode of expression which shows that Allah loves this ummah very much and is very pleased with this ummah, that He prescribes for them a system of life.

This great Furqan places a very heavy burden upon the shoulders of this ummah, equal to this responsibility. God forbid... what does this ummah have to present before Allah in return for His immense favour and mercy? Rather, neither this ummah nor all its past and future generations have anything to offer that could equal this blessing. Yes, upon the ummah it is obligatory, as thanks for this blessing, to strive to the extent of its ability. Recognition of Allah's bounties is obligatory upon it, that is, awareness of its duty is necessary. After that, striving according to its capacity is essential, and seeking forgiveness for its shortcomings and failings is required.

From Allah's side, the first demand upon this ummah, in His acceptance of Islam as a religion for them, is that it understand the worth of this choice of Allah. After that, it should hold firmly to this religion according to its strength and capacity. If it does not do so, then it is very short-sighted and very foolish, for it has rejected Allah's choice and selection and has chosen for itself some other religion and system. This would be an extremely dangerous crime on the part of this ummah, and for it there will surely be a punishment. It is never possible that such a person would be saved, since he has rejected Allah's selection. Allah sometimes leaves alone those who have not accepted Islam as a religion, so that they may do what they wish, and grants them respite for a time. But those who have recognised and known this religion well, and then abandoned it, and have themselves chosen for their lives some system other than this system, such people Allah will by no means leave alone, nor grant them respite, until they taste the consequences of their evil deeds, which they deserve.

Enough: it is not appropriate here to say more about the perfection of the religion and these great words; the discussion has become very long. We will rest content with this. These are but reflections of the Quran; now we take a separate portion from the context of this surah.

(Verses 4–5)

This question comes from those who believed, and it concerns what has been made lawful for them. From this we can see the psychological state of the chosen community at the time of the Qur'an's revelation. This community, which was receiving the honour of Divine address for the first time, through this question shows that within those pure souls there were constantly feelings of caution and God-fearing, and they felt scruple regarding all those practices that were customary in the Age of Ignorance. Their hearts were fearful that Islam might have declared those things unlawful, and so this community was compelled at all times to ask whether a matter at hand was lawful or unlawful.

The student of Islamic history today perceives how great a revolution Islam had brought about within the Muslim community. Islam shook this community so forcefully that it shook off all the dust of the Age of Ignorance from it. The Muslims whom Islam had raised from the depths of ignorance had a fresh sense that through Islam they had been given an entirely new birth. They were growing afresh, and these people had a deep feeling and awareness that a great revolution had come about within them; they had made a tremendous leap, had reached very exalted heights, and had been blessed with a sublime favour. This deep and firm awareness and this powerful jolt had produced in them an intense alertness and caution, and they had begun to look upon everything of the Age of Ignorance with suspicion. When they heard those verses in which certain things were declared unlawful, they began to ask the Messenger ﷺ also about lawful things.

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them.﴾ And the answer is given: ﴿Say: Lawful for you are all good things.﴾ This is an answer worthy of reflection. It was instilled in their consciousness that no good thing has been made unlawful for you, nor have you been forbidden from using good things; all pure things are lawful for you. Only the impure and filthy things have been made unlawful. The truth is that the things which Allah has declared unlawful, a person's natural sense also does not like them, such as carrion, blood and swine; or the heart of the believer does not like them, such as those things over which a name other than Allah's has been invoked, or which have been slaughtered at shrines or idols, or whose meat has been divided by arrows (al-azlam), because this too is a kind of gambling.

Now, after the general permission for good things, one tangible thing from among them is mentioned; this is specification after generalization. That is, the game caught by trained dogs or beasts of prey, such as dogs, falcons and hawks, or trained cheetahs and lions, which their owners have trained, so that the prey is caught in this manner and is kept captive in this way.

﴿And those trained hunting animals which you have trained, teaching them of what Allah has taught you, eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it; and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (5:4)

The permissibility is conditioned on these hunting animals being so well trained that they hold the prey captive and do not eat it until the owner arrives; they keep it safe for the owner. The exception is if these animals were hungry and the owner had gone far from that place... If these hunting animals begin to eat the prey after catching it, such an animal cannot be called trained, for it has hunted for itself, and therefore it is not lawful, even if only a small part of the prey has been eaten and a large part remains; even if the animals brought it alive, but they ate some of it, then it is still not pure.

Allah here also reminds the believers that the training and teaching you give to the animals you train is not your own knowledge, but this knowledge has been taught to you by Allah. It is Allah who made them subservient to you, and then gave you the ability to train them; it is Allah who gave you the wisdom of training. This is one of the methods of the Qur'an's education: at every stage it turns the believers' attention to Allah and does not let any opportunity pass. It continually draws their attention to this foundational and basic truth, that it is Allah who has given you all this. He is the Creator, He is the Teacher, He is the One who has subjected the universe to man. The source of all perfections and virtues is He. All creatures, in every movement, every effort and every possibility, turn to Him. Therefore a believer does not forget for a single moment that whatever is in his body and in his personality returns to Allah. Whatever events and incidents occur around him are from Allah. A believer constantly beholds Allah's perfections and sees Allah's grace and bounty in every matter. In every breath he sees how much of Allah's kindness there is; in short, in every movement and every part of the body he perceives wisdom. He is wholly devoted to his Lord and never heedless for an instant.

Allah commands that over the trained animals which hold the prey for you, you should mention the name of Allah, and this name is to be pronounced at the time an animal is released, because it may kill the prey with its teeth and claws. This will be in place of slaughter, because at the time of slaughter the name of Allah is mentioned. Thus it was commanded that on releasing the animal the name of Allah be invoked.

Finally, they are told to keep God-consciousness in view at all times and to fear Allah's reckoning and accounting. In this way the rulings of lawful and unlawful are connected with the consciousness of God-fearing and piety, which is the axis of every intention and every action in a believer's life, and because of this consciousness the whole of life becomes linked to a sense of Allah's greatness and to fear of Him, both in open and in hidden circumstances. ﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (5:4) The discussion of lawful things continues, and at the same time it is also explained from which women marriage is permissible for you.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 5:

"Today all good things have been made lawful for you. The food of the People of the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And chaste women from among the believers, and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, are lawful for you, when you have given them their due dowries, taking them in lawful wedlock and not in fornication, nor taking them as secret lovers."

Now again the things that are made lawful are enumerated... ("Today all good things have been made lawful for you"). This is an emphatic indication toward the meaning to which we drew the reader's attention above. Now some further things are added to the list of good things, because they too are good.

Here a sample of Islam's tolerance appears. In the Islamic society a particular manner of dealing with non-Muslims is described. These are people who live in the Abode of Islam, who are ahl al-dhimmah, who are citizens of the Islamic state, and who belong to the People of the Book.

Islam does not, by merely granting religious freedom to the non-Muslim People of the Book, isolate them within society, nor does it cast them away to a degree of hatred within the Islamic society. It gives them a sense of collective participation and love, and it also provides them opportunities to merge into the Islamic society. Islam declares their food lawful for the people of Islam. It also permits the people of Islam to offer their food to the People of the Book, so that they may meet one another, be guests of one another, and eat and drink together, and so that an atmosphere of love and tolerance may come into being within society. Similarly, Islam permits the people of Islam to marry chaste women from among the People of the Book, on condition that they are muhsanat, that is, chaste. This is permitted for Muslims, and here the mention of chaste Muslim women is joined with the mention of chaste women of the People of the Book. This is a tolerance which would be rarely found in any religion other than Islam, because among the Christians, the Catholic sect does not consider it proper to marry Orthodox women. Likewise, they do not consider marriage with Protestants and Maronites permissible, and if a Christian in Christian society contracts such a marriage, the Christian Orthodox consider it not valid but rather an evil act.

It becomes clear that it is Islam alone which permits the establishment of a universal society. Islam has not established complete separation between the people of Islam and the People of the Book, nor has it placed permanent screens between those holding different beliefs. Those people of belief who are citizens of the Islamic state may, from the viewpoint of good social conduct, maintain relations with Muslims, and Muslims with them. (As for the matter of establishing secret friendships with these people being permissible or not, if not, its ruling is coming ahead.) As for the condition that the women of the People of the Book be muhsanat, this condition applies to the believing women as well, that they be muhsanat.

"...when you have given them their due dowries, taking them in lawful wedlock and not in fornication, nor taking them as secret lovers" (5:5)

That is: give them their dowries, contract a lawful marriage with them, in which the man brings the woman into the fortress of marriage and protects her. Let it not be that you pay a price and then engage in lust with them, or make secret friendships. Al-sifah means that a woman makes an agreement with any man; and al-mukhadanah means that a woman takes one person as a lover without a lawful marriage. Both these forms were well known and recognized in pre-Islamic Arabia, and the jahili society accepted both kinds of relations. Islam came and purified society of these filths, and lifted it from these pits and raised it to eminence.

"And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deeds will certainly be lost, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter" (5:5) (And if anyone refuses to walk the path of faith, all his achievements in life will be wasted, and he will be bankrupt in the Hereafter.)

All this legislation is linked with faith. Implementing it is as important as believing; it is a proof of faith. Therefore whoever turns away from the implementation of these rulings is in effect denying faith, concealing faith, and covering faith. Thus whoever denies faith, his deeds become void and are rejected; otherwise that person would keep acting upon that deed forever. Al-hubut in Arabic refers to the swelling of livestock when it eats some poisonous grass and dies from it. This is a fine depiction of false deeds: outwardly they swell, but in reality the body has become poisoned and it dies. Likewise false deeds appear abundant but have no effect, and after becoming futile and useless in this world, in the Hereafter they will be unprofitable and a bitter loss.

This severe, intense and frightening concluding warning comes after a legal ruling. This ruling, concerning food and marriage in terms of lawful and unlawful, shows that every part of the Islamic system of life must be practised, and that every detail of the Islamic system is also religion, and therefore its violation is not permitted. In opposition to the Sharia, whether a little or a lot, no permission can be given.

In the course of describing pure foods and pure wives, the command concerning prayer comes in, and the rules of preparation and purity for prayer are being stated:

"O you who believe, when you rise up for prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of major impurity, purify yourselves by bathing. If you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from relieving himself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then take clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. God does not wish to put any hardship upon you, but He wishes to purify you and to complete His blessing upon you, so that you may be grateful." 

Immediately after the rules of lawful sustenance and pure women comes the statement of prayer and purity for prayer. The mention of the rules of purity for prayer alongside the rules concerning dealing with those who prevent Muslims from the Sacred Mosque, and the rules of hunting, is not merely by chance, as if one statement ended and another began, nor is it inappropriate to the context and purposes of the discourse; rather this mention too is in its proper place and in exact accordance with the wisdom of the Holy Quran's expression.

First of all, this is a new kind of purity among the pure things: spiritual purity. Along with pure food and drink and pure wives, a pure thing, the provision and arrangement for the purity of the soul, is also mentioned here. This is the colour in which the believing heart finds what it does not find in any other equipment; this is the equipment which is the means of meeting the Beloved. In an atmosphere of purity, cleanliness and humility, when the discussion of the worldly provisions of food and drink ended and the mention of pure spouses also occurred, then the spiritual purity and cleanliness which is attained through ablution and prayer was mentioned. All the colours of purity gathered in human life, with which the picture of a human being is completed.

Also intended here is to show that the rules of purity and prayer are part of religion in the same way as the rules of eating, the rules of marriage, the rules of hunting, the rules of lawful and unlawful, and as the rules concerning how to deal with people in peace and war, or the other rules mentioned in this whole surah. All these rules are the worship, obedience and servitude of God. All are part of religion. In Islam there is no difference among these rules of the kind that jurists later established within their own terminology, namely, "these are the rules of worship and these are the rules of transactions."

These terminologies which the jurists established merely under the requirements of classification, and to determine the chapters and sections of books, have no real connection with the actual system of life, and the original Sharia offers no justification for this division. In the Islamic system both worship and transactions exist, and the ruling on both is the same; that is, both matters are part of the Islamic system of life, the Sharia and religion. Regarding obedience and following, the Sharia has made no distinction or differentiation between the two. Rather, the establishment of the Sharia itself is not possible unless both parts are implemented, and the religion of Islam cannot be correctly established unless both aspects are enforced equally in the life of the Muslim community.

These are all covenants, concerning which God's command is that they be fulfilled. These are all acts of worship which a Muslim will carry out for the pleasure of God; all these matters are part of Islam, and a Muslim will act upon each one so that he may affirm his servitude.

In Islam, worship and transactions do not have separate standing. Their description has been separated only in juristic works. Both transactions and worship are in reality acts of worship. All of these are obligations from God, and we have made a covenant (uqud) with God that we will act upon them; violation of any one of them means that we have violated the covenant of faith made with God.

This is the important perspective toward which the Quran is pointing here. It is presenting, one after another, various kinds of rulings in this surah, all of which are part of religion.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 5, verse 6:

In Islam, prayer (salah) is a meeting with Allah. A person stands before Allah with folded hands, supplicates to Allah, and engages in intimate conversation with Him. Therefore, to stand at this station, proper preparation is necessary.

Before spiritual purification, there was a need for physical purity as well. For this reason, ablution (wudu') was commanded. As far as we have understood, the real wisdom lies in the knowledge of Allah. Nevertheless, wudu' includes the following obligatory acts: washing the face, washing the hands up to the elbows, wiping the head, and washing the feet up to the ankles. There are minor juristic (fiqhi) differences regarding these obligations. The important difference is whether these obligatory acts must be performed in the same order in which they are mentioned in the Qur'an, or whether wudu' is valid without that order. There are two opinions on this matter.

This wudu' pertains to the impurity which makes wudu' obligatory. As for major impurity (janabah), whether it arises from sexual intercourse with a woman or from wet dream (ihtilam), ghusl (the full bath) is obligatory for it. After mentioning the obligatory acts of ghusl and the obligatory acts of wudu', the mention of tayammum (dry ablution) is also made here. The permission for tayammum is conditioned upon the following circumstances:

For example, when water is entirely unavailable; or when a person is ill and is unable to perform wudu'; or when a person is required to perform ghusl but water would cause him harm. Also, a traveler who needs wudu' or is required to perform ghusl and does not find water.

Here Allah has expressed the impurity which necessitates wudu' by the words: ﴿or if any of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾ (5:6). The word ghait (غائط) means a low-lying place where most people go to relieve themselves, even if one only urinates and does not go to a low-lying place.

And the impurity which necessitates ghusl is expressed by the words ﴿or you have touched women﴾ (5:6). This is a euphemistic manner of expression for sexual intercourse. In such circumstances, in which one needs wudu' or needs ghusl, one is not permitted to approach prayer unless one performs tayammum and intends to use clean earth. That is, one strikes something that is from the earth and is pure. Whether this dust is on the back of a mount, or whether one strikes one's palms upon dust or the like, then one shakes off both hands, wipes the face, and then wipes the hands up to the elbows. One strike is sufficient for the whole tayammum, or one may strike twice. According to two juristic opinions, there is also a difference regarding the meaning of the phrase ﴿or you have touched women﴾ (5:6). Does it refer only to mere touching, or to sexual intercourse, or does it refer to touching in general, whether accompanied by desire and pleasure or without them? There are also juristic differences on this point. ...... Likewise, there is a difference as to whether tayammum is permissible in any illness, or only in an illness in which there is pain or fear of increased pain.

Furthermore, it is also disputed whether, when there is no illness but the water is extremely cold and there is a risk of falling ill from using it, tayammum is permissible. The preferred view is that it is permissible. At the conclusion of this verse there follows this addition:

﴿Allah does not desire to put upon you any difficulty, but He desires to purify you and to complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful.﴾ (5:6)

As we have explained, cleanliness in the state of meeting Allah has been made obligatory in the Shariah. Through wudu' and ghusl, both physical and spiritual cleanliness are attained.
