As for tayammum, at least spiritual cleanliness is attained through it, and for cleanliness it stands in place of wudu' and ghusl when water is not found or there is a risk of harm in using water. This has been permitted because Allah does not want people to face needless hardship and severity, nor does He want to place people in toil and difficulties. Rather, Allah's purpose is to purify people. This purity comes to them as a blessing, and after that they should give thanks for this favor, and in return for this thanks Allah will increase His grace, generosity and bounty. This is the gentleness, mercy, and the practical realism and continual facilitation of the Islamic system. The wisdom of wudu', ghusl and tayammum is that Allah explains thus:

﴿Allah does not desire to put upon you any difficulty, but He desires to purify you and to complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful.﴾ (5:6)

The Islamic system of life grants Muslims a beautiful harmony between the rites of worship and the system of law. Wudu' and ghusl do not merely provide the benefit of physical purification, so that today's so-called modern thinkers of Islam could not raise the objection that in this modern age we do not need such arrangements merely for cleanliness, as the backward Arabs needed, because now there are good arrangements for health and cleanliness in bathhouses, and we, being civilized, take great care of cleanliness. ...... They cannot raise this objection, because through wudu' and ghusl Islam has established for us a system of purification from both physical and spiritual aspects. Then, by connecting this system with worship, it has made it regular so that all people are pure and clean when they turn towards their Lord. Since wudu' and ghusl give greater consideration to spiritual cleanliness than to physical cleanliness, tayammum has been placed in their stead, because when the use of water is not possible, tayammum has been placed in their place, and it is evident that tayammum does not in fact achieve outward cleanliness. Moreover, the Islamic system of life is a general system, and it is for every kind of circumstance. There is one system and one method for every family and every manner of life, so its benefit is realized in every kind of circumstance, every kind of environment, and every kind of society. In every form and in every meaning its wisdom and benefit exist, and in no form does it deviate.

It is our duty first to try to understand the Islamic ideology of life well, and only afterwards to express opinions about it; otherwise our verdict will be without knowledge and without the guidance of the Book which gives clear light. Then our endeavor should be to conduct ourselves towards Allah with utmost courtesy and reverence, and to treat with respect both what we know and what we do not know. (An example of this is the difference between zakat and tax. Therefore, because of tax we cannot abolish zakat. This discussion will also come soon.)

These issues—that when wudu' is not possible, or ghusl is not possible due to excuse or harm, tayammum is permissible at that time—contain a matter for our reflection, namely how great the importance of prayer is within the Islamic system of life, and how the Islamic system wisely resolves the obstacles and difficulties that stand in its way. If one keeps in view this ruling of tayammum, and then the other rulings concerning prayer, such as the rulings of prayer in fear (salat al-khawf) and prayer of the sick, it will become evident that performing prayer is obligatory in whatever manner is possible: sitting, lying down, or on one's side. Islam emphasizes this very strongly. From all these rulings it is known how much importance the Islamic system of life gives to prayer in the moral and psychological training of Muslims, because standing before Allah and meeting Him has an extraordinary effect upon a person. Islam does not permit abandoning it even in the hardest conditions and in the most difficult times, and it does not allow any difficulty to stand in its way. Five times a day it is obligatory for the servant to meet his Lord, and he must not give up this meeting for any reason. It is the refreshment of the heart, the delight of the eyes, and the shade of Allah, a pleasant shade.

After the rulings of purification and the rulings given before them, there now comes this concluding passage, which contains a reminder of the blessing of faith and a recollection of the covenant that they made with Allah, in which they affirmed hearing and obedience. This was the same covenant through which they entered Islam, as we have explained earlier. Also, Muslims are directed towards the fear of Allah, and it is told that Allah has knowledge of all those things which are hidden in their hearts.

(Verse 7)

The people first addressed by the Qur'an knew well the worth of this religion, as we have said earlier, because they were seeing the reality of this religion alive in their own selves and personalities. The religion was before their eyes in their lives, in their society, and in its position among all of humanity around them. For this reason, a mere allusion to this blessing was sufficient for them, by which they could easily turn their attention to the great reality that existed in their lives and their environment.

Similarly, it contains a reference to the covenant that Allah took from them. It is mentioned here because it too was a clear reality that they knew, and they took great pride in it. The first party to this agreement was Allah, and the second party was them. This matter was extremely valuable and honourable for them, and it was extremely great, and they were well aware of its significance and reality.

For this reason, Allah entrusts them to God-consciousness, and they are awakened to feel the fear of Allah in their hearts and to be alert against hidden dangers.

﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (Fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do.)

The expression ﴿بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ﴾ (5:7) is, in its imagery and rapid conveying of meaning, a beautiful one. It is appropriate to point out the beauty, depth of meaning and profundity that it contains. The meaning of Dhat al-Sudur in Arabic is "the owner of hearts," which is attached to hearts; metaphorically it refers to the hidden emotions that lie concealed in hearts: hidden inclinations, the agitations of hearts, and secret matters, secrets that are attached to the hearts. These hidden secrets are also completely open before Allah, because He is the One who knows even what is hidden in hearts.

The covenant that Allah has taken from the Muslim Ummah also includes this: that this Ummah will be the guardian of justice and equity for all of humanity. Such justice that the scale of its balance does not tilt because of friendship or enmity, nor be influenced by kinship or base desires, nor be swayed by any expediency. This justice should be solely for the pleasure of the Divine Being, and the one who dispenses justice should not be affected by any influence of the world; and this justice should be under the awareness that Allah is the Watchful and the Guardian, and is aware of the most hidden corners. For this reason, the call of Allah is this.

(Verse) "Number 8."

Earlier, Allah had forbidden the believers from letting enmity toward a people, who had barred them from the Sacred Mosque, lead them to abandon justice and to commit injustice against anyone. Such restraint of the self and such tolerance was the extreme limit to which Allah wished to bring them, and this was Allah's exceedingly firm method of training. Here too, Allah forbids the believers from refraining from justice out of enmity. This is an extremely lofty summit, and so difficult and arduous a path that walking upon it is extremely burdensome for the soul. In the first verse it was said that you should not commit injustice out of enmity, and this stage goes further: that you should act justly despite enmity, that is, even though your feelings are inflamed against them and you feel aversion, you should still act justly. The first command was very easy, because it was a negative act; a person could refrain from committing injustice. The second command, that you should act with justice toward those unjust ones and enemies, is a positive and burdensome task, that is, compelling the human soul to act justly toward people who are hateful and detestable.

The wise system of training in Islam could demand such a difficult task from those it has trained, so Islam commands:

"O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses to justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness" (Qur'an 5:8).

O people who have believed, be upholders of truth for the sake of Allah and bearers of witness to justice. Let not the enmity of a group move you so much that you turn away from justice. Act justly; this is more suited to God-fearing piety. Then what is necessary for this difficult task is told:

"And fear Allah; indeed Allah is Acquainted with what you do" (Qur'an 5:8). Keep doing your deeds fearing Allah; Allah is fully aware of what you do. The human soul can never reach such heights unless the matter is solely between the person and Allah directly, when a person stands up purely for Allah and leaves aside everything other than Allah. When a person has consciousness of God-fear and the assurance that nothing hidden can escape Allah's sight.

There is no system in the world that can give human beings such justice in which friend and foe are equal. It is only the task of the religion of Islam that invites believers to stand up purely for Allah in matters of justice, and to abandon every consideration other than justice for the sake of justice.

These are the fundamental elements because of which this religion has been declared the religion of humanity and a universal religion. Its system is entirely sufficient for all people, whether they are adherents of this religion or not. All people can live a life of justice under its shade. Establishing justice is an obligation upon those who adhere to this religion, and in this establishment of justice their matter is with their Lord, even though they may have been victims of the oppression and aggression of those who seek justice, and even though enmity toward them may be in their hearts. This is the duty of the community which has been made the overseer of all humanity, even though difficulties may come their way in establishing this justice.

The truth is that this community performed this duty very well in history. It bore great hardships in its path while Islam was established, and this was not merely a matter of preaching and advice in the life of this community, nor a few examples of lofty models, but the reality of its daily life. It was a situation that humanity had neither seen before nor after. On this standard, humanity saw such justice only in the Islamic system of life. Its examples, and the highest examples, are countless in Islamic history and are part of history. From them it becomes known that Allah's guidance and the duties He has prescribed were seen in the life of the Muslim community as a real and practical system, which were fulfilled in a very simple manner, and in the daily life of this community they were vividly embodied. These were not merely matters of imaginary lofty standards, nor some individual lofty examples, but a captivating picture of practical life, beyond which no lofty standard has been seen by humans to this day.

When one looks upon the jahiliyyah of the world from this lofty station and highest summit, whatever the time and whatever the place, including the polished jahiliyyah of the modern era, the observer feels that Allah created him for humanity, and that this is the system Allah has made for all humans. From this lofty height it appears that there are such long distances between the Islamic system of life and all those jahili systems of life that cannot be crossed, both in practical life and in terms of human conscience and beliefs.

Sometimes people recognize principles and also raise slogans of principle-keeping, but putting principles into practice is the real thing. It is natural that people speak of principles and say these things for others, but these principles do not exist in the realm of action. The real point is that people should be invited to principles, but one should look at where the invitation comes from, what the purpose of the invitation is, and what the inviter is like. The invitation should rule over the inviter's conscience and inner self. The real matter is the source from which the invitation flows, and the inviter's struggle and effort that he spends in giving practical form to the invitation and principles.

The real worth of the Islamic invitation is that it calls to a few religious principles. Their worth comes from the authority of the religion of Islam. The worth of the religion of Islam is that it is Allah's religion, so the one who calls to religion seeks support and authority from no one other than Allah. And if by someone's help this ever happens, what effect does such authority have on the faith and conscience of people? And what concern do people have to struggle to enforce someone else's principles, and what does that other person have to give people as reward?

Thousands of people raise slogans in favour of justice, raise slogans of purity, raise slogans for freedom, and raise slogans of tolerance, magnanimity, love, sacrifice and selflessness, but as a result of these slogans people's conscience does not stir from its place, and their hearts are not affected, because they are giving a call that has no authority from Allah behind it. In short, the real matter is not mere verbal talk, but the real reality is what lies behind the words.

People keep hearing principles, lofty examples and lofty signs from the mouths of people like themselves, but behind them there is no authority from Allah. So what effect do their words have? Their nature says that this is merely a statement from people like themselves, and the speaker has all the same flaws, defects and shortcomings that other people have. People accept such words only on that basis, so their nature is not ruled by these words, nor can these words shake their personalities. The effects of these words do not reach those people; if there is any effect at all, it is as weak as a spider's web.

Furthermore, the guidance of religious principles is not complete until they are given practical form in life. Islam does not scatter these guidances into the air, but implements them in practical life. Therefore, when religion becomes merely advice and remains only the name of a few rituals of worship, then its advice does not take on the form of reality. This situation is visible to us everywhere today: religious people give only advice, but they do not have executive power.

Therefore, the real point is that religion needs a system of life that conforms to the method of religion, and that Islamic guidance be acted upon in the light of that system. This system should implement these guidances in all the ways of life, with complete balance between practical measures and practical steps. From the Islamic perspective, religion also has this meaning: religion means that system of life which rules over all aspects of life, and behind which is executive power.

When religion, in this meaning, takes the form of reality in the life of the Muslim community, only then can it reach heights in this world, and from there survey all of humanity. Over that humanity which is still fallen into the pits of modern jahiliyyah, just as at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an people had fallen face-down into the pits of the ancient jahiliyyah of the Arabs. But when religion is confined to the pulpit as sermons and to a few rituals of worship inside mosques, and is removed from the wide practical field of life, then in such a case religion will have no reality in human practical life. It will neither be enforced, nor will it appear in practical form.

For the believers, a reward from Allah is necessary: those believers who deal with Allah alone, so that they may perform their duty of overseeing humanity with greater zeal and full strength, and fulfil the firm covenant they have made with Allah. Then it is also necessary that there be a difference between the end of those who work in the way of Islam and do righteous deeds, and the end of those who reject Islam.

(Verses 9–10)

This is the reward for those chosen servants from whom worldly pleasures and material gains are lost. They do not get the opportunity to indulge in luxury in this world. They keep carrying out the duties of the Islamic revolution in the world, and despite this great reward, the duties of guarding humanity in the world are seen very rarely, and a person does not heed human inclinations, human envy and enmity, and the greed of this world. Then through this the attribute of Allah's justice is manifested, that Allah does not place the righteous and the wicked on the same level.

There is a need for the eyes of the revolutionary believers to be fixed upon this reward of Allah, and their dealings with Allah should be such that no obstacle among the obstacles in their path can come between them, in the circumstances of life and in various conditions as well. Some hearts are such that the mere desire to attain the pleasure of Allah is sufficient for them, and they savour it greatly, just as they take great delight in fulfilling the promise made with Allah. However, the Islamic system keeps in view the common people besides those people of resolute determination. The temperament of ordinary humans is also kept in view by Allah. Allah knows that for ordinary people the hope of forgiveness is also necessary, and the common people are also kept in view. The temperament of ordinary humans is also kept in view by Allah. Allah knows that for ordinary people the hope of forgiveness is also necessary, and the promise of a great reward is also necessary for the common people. Likewise, the common people also need to know what the end and punishment of those who deny will be, because the common people are satisfied with this and this is their temperament. Therefore, the common people become content on hearing the command of their reward and the punishment of the disbelievers. In this way, the anger and wrath that arises in their hearts at the deeds of the wicked is cooled. Especially on occasions when the believers are commanded to act with justice and fairness even towards their enemies. Especially in circumstances in which the believers have endured deceit, harm and stinging malice at their hands. The Islamic system of life takes humanity in the manner in which human nature is, and Allah knows it well. Islam gives people a slogan and a call such that through it the windows of their consciousness are opened, and to which their life and soul respond with "Labbaik." Then this reward, namely forgiveness and a great reward, is a proof of Allah's pleasure.

Moving further along the context, you will find the spirit of justice, fairness and tolerance now very strong within the Muslim community. Within it, the sense of oppression, spite and one-sidedness is eliminated. Allah reminds the believers how great a favour of Allah this is upon them, that Allah stopped all the hostile actions of the polytheists against them, when at Hudaybiyyah and on other occasions they could not take any aggressive step against the Muslims.
