One of these is that the Children of Israel were among those who first opposed the Islamic call in Madinah, plotted against it, remained at war with it in Madinah, and continued to fight against it throughout the Arabian Peninsula. From the very first day they were at war with the Muslim community. They created hypocrisy in Madinah and continued to nurture the hypocrites. They kept supporting these hypocrites, and this support was against the Islamic way of life and also against the Muslims. They incited the polytheists to war against the Muslims, made grand promises to them, and plotted together with them against the Muslims. It was these very people who spread rumours against the Muslims, carried out secret intrigues, kept resorting to cunning, and kept creating unrest in the ranks of Islam. They also tried to spread doubts, both regarding Islamic beliefs and against Islamic leadership. And after some time these people came out fully in the open against the Muslims. Therefore there was a need to lay bare before the Muslim community their complete reality, so that it would know what kind of people its enemies are, what their temperament is, what their history is, what their means of hostility are, and what the nature of the struggle is that they have launched against the Muslims.

Allah knew that these people would remain enemies of the Islamic nation throughout the whole future history of Islam, exactly as they had always been enemies of truth in their own history. Therefore Allah placed their history before the Islamic nation, clearly and thoroughly, and He also laid before it the means that these people used against the Islamic nation.

Another aspect of this wisdom is that the Children of Israel were the bearers of the religion which, before the final religion of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ), was the true religion, and before Islam the Children of Israel were a nation with a long history. Deviation had occurred in their beliefs, and they repeatedly broke the covenant that they had made with Allah, which they had made with Allah. Because of this ideological deviation and violation of the covenant, their lives were adversely affected. All these matters required that the Muslim nation be made aware of their entire history, because it is the trustee and heir of all the earlier messages and the guardian of the divine way of life and correct beliefs. For these reasons Allah wished that the Muslim nation should know of all these historical upheavals, and that it should know where these people stumbled and what consequences followed. What effect their history and conduct had on the life and morals of the Children of Israel, so that through this experience the Islamic movement would proceed cautiously at those points where people stumble, where Satan attacks, and where deviation begins, so that by means of these historical experiences it would remain on the right path.

And another aspect of this wisdom was that the experiences of the Children of Israel had many dimensions. These were very long experiences, and Allah knew well that when a long period passes over nations and communities, they become hard-hearted, their later generations深 drift away from the true path, and that the history of the Muslim nation will remain long until the Day of Resurrection, and that periods will come upon it in which it will be afflicted with circumstances exactly like those of the Children of Israel. Therefore there was a need that, before the leaders and the renewers and revivers of religion (mujaddids) who arise in Islamic history, there should also be examples of such experiences, showing how deviation and misguidance seep into nations and communities. These renewers should know that once the disease has been diagnosed, how its cure will be effected. For those who deliberately turn far from guidance and the straight path are very hard-hearted. Heedless, unrefined and less-informed people accept guidance very quickly, because a new call comes before them which pleases them, and they accept it. They shake off the dust from themselves, because it is a new thing for them. Since this new call is something new for their nature, life blossoms in them. But for those people before whom a call has already come, that call is no longer attractive to them. It neither stirs movement in them, nor does it create in them the sense that this is a great call which should be taken seriously. For this reason, to influence such people much more effort, and a long and patience-testing struggle, is required.

These were among the very important aspects of the wisdom in the details of the story of the Children of Israel. Therefore Allah has always given these narratives with details, because the Muslim nation was the heir of beliefs, and it now had to discharge the duties of leading humanity. There may be several other aspects, but it is not possible to give more than these indications here. So in this lesson we return to that assembly.

(Verses) "And [recall] when Moses said to his people, 'O my people, remember the blessing of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds. O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has assigned to you, and do not turn back [in retreat] on your heels, for you will turn back as losers.'"

Here, in the words of Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him), there is an indication that he had perceived that his people were hesitant regarding this struggle, and he feared that they would turn back on their heels. He had thoroughly tested them during the long journey of the Children of Israel's return from Egypt, and had found that these people repeatedly disobeyed. Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) had brought them out of Egypt and freed them from that life of humiliation and misfortune in which they had been afflicted during their long period of slavery in Egypt. This freedom was granted to them in the name of Allah, and by the overwhelming power of Allah the sea was split for them, and in it Pharaoh and his army were drowned. Then, when they passed by a people who worshipped idols, they immediately demanded, "O Musa, make for us also a god just as they have gods." (Verse: "Yā Mūsā ijʿal lanā ilāhan kamā lahum ālihah.") And when Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) went to Mount Sinai at the appointed time for conversation with Allah, Samiri, from the ornaments which their women had taken from the women of the Egyptians when they came out, made a calf for them. This calf would make a sound just as a calf makes a sound. These people fell upon this calf and said that this is indeed the god whom Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) went to Mount Sinai to meet. Again, a clear miracle of Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) was that he brought forth for them twelve springs from a rock within the scorching desert. Manna and quail, very delicious foods, were sent down upon them, but they rejected these delicious and nourishing foods and demanded the foods they used to eat in Egypt, though there they had lived a life of great humiliation. There they demanded greens, vegetables, wheat, garlic and onions, and they did not show patience with the food that was being sent down upon them, although they were working for honour, sincerity and lofty aims. Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) was drawing them toward those lofty aims, while they were running backwards. Then Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) also tested them in the matter of the cow, when Allah commanded them to slaughter a cow, and they hesitated, made excuses, and for a long time groped in darkness. Finally, compelled, they acted upon the command, but they were hardly willing to do it. (Verse: "Fa-dhabahūhā wa-mā kādū yafʿalūn.")

Then they were also tested when they returned from Mount Sinai, and they had the tablets containing the covenant which Allah had taken from them. They rejected this covenant and remained steadfast in breaking it. Despite these blessings, and their disobedience in return, and after that Allah's forgiveness of them, they still did not accept that covenant, and Allah had to hold the mountain over their heads as though it were a piece of cloud, and they came to such a state that they were certain it was about to fall upon them. (Verse: "Wa-ẓannū annahu wāqiʿum bihim.") Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) had thoroughly tested them during that long journey to freedom. He brought them up to the threshold of the Holy Land, the promise of which Allah Himself had made to them, and it was for that land that they had left Egypt. It was the land concerning which Allah had covenanted that these people would establish a kingdom in it, and that Allah would again send prophets among them, so that they might spend the best days of life under Allah's supervision and guidance.

Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) had tested them well, so it was his right to fear once more their breach of faith. That is why, in this final call, Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) placed before them all the matters worth mentioning from their past history, and placed before them all the good tidings that were to be attained by them in the future. He set before them all the matters by which their courage could be increased, and he also set before them the sternest warning:

(Verses) "And [recall] when Moses said to his people, 'O my people, remember the blessing of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds. O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has assigned to you, and do not turn back [in retreat] on your heels, for you will turn back as losers.'"

The blessing of Allah and those promises were fulfilled. Allah sent prophets among them and raised up kings. In this regard Allah gave them what He had not given any other nation of the world up to that point in history, and the Holy Land which they were about to conquer, which had been written for them. And this writing was Allah's, so its fulfilment was certain as the truth of certainty. Every promise that Allah had made to them before had been fulfilled one by one, and this was a promise towards which they were moving. To turn back from it would be for them a loss in this world and the Hereafter... But the Children of Israel were, after all, the Children of Israel: cowardly, lazy, those who turn back on their heels, and who break their word again and again.

"They replied, 'O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of great might, and we will never enter it until they leave it. And if they should leave it, then we will enter.'"

Here the true character of the Children of Israel comes into view: they are laid completely bare, and not even a thin veil remains over them. This is because they now stood before a real danger. They could no longer make any show of pretence; they could neither display a false bravery nor bluster, nor could they practise hypocrisy. The danger stood before their eyes, embodied and near. Therefore even the fact that this land had been given to them, and that Allah had written it as their destiny, could not save them, for they wanted a very cheap victory, one for which they would have to pay no price and in whose path they would have to make no struggle. They wanted a comfortable conquest that would descend upon them like manna and salwa.

Their words were: "...a people of great might, and we will never enter it until they leave it. And if they should leave it, then we will enter."

But the responsibilities of victory and help are not what the minds of the Children of Israel conceived. Their hearts were empty of faith. Their believing men said to them:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 23:

"Among those who feared, two men upon whom Allah had bestowed His favour said: 'Enter upon them through the gate, for when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious. And put your trust in Allah, if you are believers.'" (23)

Here it becomes clear what the worth of trust in Allah and of God-fearing is. These two men were those who feared Allah, and their God-fearing produced in them such courage that they paid no heed to the tyrants. Within them was matchless bravery in the face of an imaginary danger. Both of them bore witness to the importance that faith and certainty hold in times of severity and peril. Their stance shows what the position of those who fear Allah is when faced with the fear of tyrants, for Allah does not place two fears in one heart, such that a person fears Allah and also fears people. Whoever fears Allah fears none but Allah. With what boldness they speak!

"Enter upon them through the gate, for when you have entered it, you will be victorious" (5:23). It is the established principle of the world of hearts, and then of the world of confrontation, that you take the initiative and advance. When you have reached a people within their very gate, their hearts will break, and to the same degree your resolve will grow. In this way defeat enters the psychology of those people, and victory is decreed for you.

As for the believers, their trust is placed in Allah alone: "And upon Allah put your trust, if you are believers" (5:23). This is the characteristic of faith and the sign of faith, and this is the logic of faith and the demand of faith.

But the question is: to whom are these two believers saying this? Regrettably, their addressees are the Children of Israel.

(Verse 24) "They said: O Musa, we shall never enter it so long as they are in it. So go you and your Lord and fight, we are sitting here."

But they said again: "O Musa, we will never go there as long as they remain in it. So you and your Lord go and fight; we are sitting right here." Thus the cowards withdraw from the ranks and become ashamed. Out of fear of dangers they become immobile, just as the feet of donkeys are tied, and then they take no initiative. Cowardice and shamelessness are not contradictory to each other, nor are they far apart from one another. These qualities often come together. A coward, when he moves forward towards his duties, shows cowardice and draws back. He withdraws in the very manner in which he has abandoned his duty. Then he speaks ill of that very goal, and speaks ill of the call that makes demands of him that he does not wish to fulfil.

﴿Go you and your Lord, then fight, we are sitting here﴾ (5:24). (We are sitting here.) This was the helplessness of a weak and cowardly person. His tongue is very sharp, but for advancing towards the goal his feet are heavy, and he feels the sting of arrows. ﴿Go you and your Lord﴾ (5:24). (Go you and your Lord.) If he now compels us to war, we do not accept his divinity; he is your Lord. ﴿We are sitting here﴾ (5:24). (We are sitting right here.) We have no need of a kingdom, nor of honour, nor of the Promised Land. At that time there was a tyrannical people in it... This was the end of the great struggle of Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him): a long journey, in it humiliation and disgrace, and repeated deviation from the Children of Israel, evasion and disobedience at every step... Surely this is their end: they turn back from the conquest of the Holy Land, although Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) is with them and they are on the threshold of that land. They are on the threshold of that land. They turn away from the covenant made with Allah, although that ancient covenant was closely linked with this covenant, namely the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis. Now what could Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) do in this state of despair?

(Verse 25) ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have control over none but myself and my brother; so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ (5:25)

This is a call full of grief and sorrow. In it there is, on one side, supplication, and on the other, complete submission and acceptance, and after that decisive firmness. Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) knew well and was certain that Allah the Exalted knows that, for Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him), no supporter remained except his brother. Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) stands between the weakness of a remorseful human being and a prophet who is Kalimullah (the one who spoke with Allah), and he holds the resolute determination of a truthful believer. Before him there is no path except to turn only to Allah and to express his pain and sorrow in the form of a whisper before Him, and to make the demand: O Allah, grant me permission to separate myself from this defiantly disobedient people forever. For when they turned away from their firm covenant with Allah, what connection remained between them and the prophet who spoke with Allah? They were not bound to him by lineage, nor by the fact that their history was one, nor was their relationship with him based on having struggled together in one place as companions. Their bond was based only on the call to the Truth. Their bond was this ancient covenant, and they had broken this covenant. Therefore complete severance occurred between them, and it went to the very depths. Now there is no connection left between Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) and them. He is bound by his covenant and promise, and the people have disobeyed him. He is firmly fixed upon the covenant, and the people have turned away from it.

This is the manner of respect and reverence from Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him). This is his sunnah, and this is the plan of a true believer. And this is the foundation and bond upon which people gather and separate from one another. In this path, nation, lineage, descent and shared history count for nothing; no relation of this earth is of any use. On the path, when the bond of ideas is broken, all relationships are broken; and when beliefs separate, the ways and methods also separate. At this point Allah answers the call of His Prophet, and the wicked are given their full punishment.

(Verse 26) ﴿He said: "Then it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ (5:26)

Allah handed these wretched people over to the deserts, although they were on the threshold of the Holy Land. Allah made forbidden to them that land which had been written for them. The preponderant view is that Allah made that land forbidden to their generation then present, and as long as a new generation was not produced from their loins, they kept wandering in this manner. Thus entry into the Promised Land remained prohibited for them until a new generation was prepared, a generation that accepts admonition. This generation was formed in the pure condition of the desert, and it was entirely free-spirited and freedom-loving. It was not the generation that humiliation, slavery and the oppressions of the Egyptians had made accustomed to weakness. Therefore that generation was not suited to the task that belongs to people of resolute determination. Humiliation, slavery and oppression corrupt the nature of a human being; in the same way, through these things the nature of nations also becomes corrupted, because in slavery the consciences of nations change.

Here the matter ends, and those people are handed over to the desert. Nothing further is said about them here. This is a manner in which psychological lessons and artistic beauty both come together in one place; this is the distinctive style of expression of the Holy Qur'an.

The Muslims had understood this lesson well; Allah had placed this entire story before them in the very manner in which it occurred. So they said to their Prophet: O Muhammad! Today we will not say what the Children of Israel said to their prophet: "Go you and your Lord and fight, we are sitting here" (5:24). (These are some examples of the Qur'an's manner of instruction. The Qur'an instructs in the manner of general narratives; these were some aspects of the wisdom in relating the story of the Children of Israel.)

Lesson No. 48 at a glance:

In this section, some very fundamental laws for human life are laid down, the commandments that are for the protection of life. These commandments are for the society in which Islamic life is practised. The purpose of these laws is to block the paths of rebellion against the Islamic system of life and support of that system, and to preserve the government that is established according to Allah's command and functions under the shelter of the Shari'ah. Furthermore, the protection of the society which functions under the shelter of Islamic Shari'ah and under the shelter of an Islamic government is intended. Through these commandments, the protection of both the property and the lives of the subjects of an Islamic government is intended, provided that this society, this government and this system are operating in accordance with the Islamic Shari'ah.

Throughout this whole section, very fundamental commandments have been given concerning the preservation of the collective life of society, but the beginning of this section is made with the story of the two sons of Hazrat Adam (peace be upon him). Through this it is intended to show what the psychology of criminals is at the time of committing this crime of murder and bloodshed: what causes and factors are there because of which a criminal commits the crime. Further, in this section it is shown that this crime is extremely heinous, and that its prevention and prohibition are extremely necessary. Punishing the criminal for this crime is also very necessary, and controlling the causes and influences because of which a person commits this crime is also necessary.

It appears that all the allusions of this story are fully connected with the commandments that come after this story. A reader who reads with reflection can easily perceive what the purpose of bringing this story into this context is, and what a profound and satisfying allusion it is, which this story pours into the human self and embeds in it. This story prepares the human heart and mind to accept these commandments, so that it accepts the severe punishments which Islam will enforce through the Islamic courts that work according to Islamic Shari'ah, for offences of hirabah (armed robbery), crimes against life, crimes against property, and crimes against the system of the state.

It is the duty of an Islamic society to run its entire life according to the Islamic system, under the Shari'ah of Muhammad. It should organise its affairs, its connections and relationships in accordance with the Islamic system and the Islamic law of the Shari'ah. This is the method by which this society will be a guardian of the individual as well as of the group, and will be able to give justice, security, contentment and peace to both the individual and society. It will be able to close the doors of corruption to all those elements which produce disorder, unrest, pressure and suffocation, and all the causes through which oppression and injustice arise within society will be eliminated. Likewise, the needs and requirements of people will also be fulfilled with great ease. In the same way, within such a mutually supportive, balanced, just and virtuous society, committing crimes of this kind against someone's life and property, against an individual's ownership, or against the system of the state, is regarded as an extremely vile act and a grave crime. There is no justification, excuse or circumstance for it that would mitigate (Milderung) this crime. From this it becomes clear that this severity of Islam against crime and criminal is applied when every opportunity has been provided to the individual to walk on the right path, that is, when conditions exist for moderate people to live correctly, and when conditions exist such that an individual and a group, if they wish, can live a pure life. Despite all these matters, the Islamic system of government and the Islamic system of justice grant the accused the full rights of legal investigation and legal judgment. If even the slightest doubt arises, the hudud are set aside because of doubts. Furthermore, the door of repentance is also left open, by which, in certain circumstances, his crime may be forgiven even in this world, while in the Hereafter Allah will in any case forgive all his crimes and sins... In this lesson we shall find all its aspects and examples, and many commandments and laws will be mentioned.

But before commenting on the verses and speaking directly about the commandments, it is necessary to note here one general and important matter: what kind of society will these severe laws be enforced in, and what are the limits and conditions of the enforcing power?

Whether the commandments and laws stated in this lesson relate to crimes against the person, or to commandments concerning offences against the system of the state, or to commandments concerning offences against someone's property, their status is similar to the other Shari'ah rulings found concerning the crimes of hudud, qisas and ta'zir. That is, all these commandments will be enforced only when their enforcing power exists in the form of an Islamic society, in Dar al-Islam. Therefore it is necessary that the definition of Dar al-Islam according to the Shari'ah also be given.

According to Islam and Muslims, the whole world is divided into two blocs, and we do not recognise a third bloc.

The first bloc is Dar al-Islam, and by this is meant the state within which Islamic commandments are enforced, whose legal system is based on the Shari'ah, whether its inhabitants are all Muslims, or consist of Muslims and dhimmis, or whose people are all non-Muslims while the ruler is a Muslim and the law of the Islamic state applies and decisions are made according to the Shari'ah. (Although not all the Shari'ah rulings are binding on the dhimmis; only the civil and criminal rulings of Islam are binding on them.) Or the situation may be that the entire population is Muslim, or there is a mixed population of Muslims and non-Muslims, but the country has come under the control of hostile non-Muslims, while the legal system of the country has not been changed and the inhabitants continue to decide matters according to Islamic law. Therefore the complete basis for a country being Dar al-Islam rests solely on whether its legal system conforms to the Shari'ah or not, and whether disputes within it are decided by the Shari'ah or by some other law.

Second, the Abode of War (dar al-harb) is every country in which Islamic Shari'ah is not enforced and in which judgments are not made according to Shari'ah. As for its inhabitants, whatever religion or community they follow, whether they call themselves Muslims or call themselves People of the Book, or whether they are other disbelievers, they will be inhabitants of the Abode of War. Therefore, whether a country is an Abode of War depends entirely on this alone: that Islamic laws are not enforced within it and that judgments in its courts are not according to Islamic Shari'ah. Such a country will be called an Abode of War from the point of view of a Muslim and of an Islamic community.

A Muslim society is one that is established in the Abode of Islam (dar al-Islam), according to the meaning stated above... And this Islamic society, which follows the Islamic methodology and over which the rule of Islamic Shari'ah prevails, has the right that the lives of its people be protected, that the properties of its people be protected, that its system of governance be preserved, and that in it, and only in it, the prescribed punishments mentioned in these verses be carried out against those criminals who are against the people's lives, property and the state's order. From this lesson and from the other Qur'anic teachings it becomes clear that this will be an extremely elevated and virtuous society. In it there will be justice and freedoms. In this society there will be a guarantee of employment and the necessities of life, whether a person is able to work or is disabled. It will be a society in which the factors that encourage goodness will be many and the factors that encourage evil will be very few. Therefore such a society has a right over all those who live within it and benefit from it, that they protect it wholeheartedly, and that they observe and protect the financial, personal, honour and moral rights of the other citizens of the country. All these inhabitants should protect the Abode of Islam in which they live safely and securely and in peace, in which they have complete security, in which they have all fundamental rights, and in which they hold all the ranks of human distinction, in which they have all social and collective rights; rather, it is the duty of all inhabitants to protect all these rights. After this, if anyone rises in rebellion against the system of the Abode of Islam, then he is a wrongdoer, a sinner, a mischief-maker and a saboteur, and he deserves to be given the severest punishment. Yet even in this, he has been given these rights: that no one should be seized merely on conjecture and suspicion, and this principle will also apply to this law, because prescribed punishments (hudud) are dropped due to doubts.

As for the Abode of War, whose definition has been given above, it and its inhabitants do not deserve to be given the benefit of the punishments enforced under Islamic Shari'ah, because there the Shari'ah is not implemented at all.

Nor does this society acknowledge the sovereignty of Islam. Moreover, this Abode of War does not provide protection even to Muslims who live in the Abode of Islam and who enforce Islamic Shari'ah in their own land. In the view of those of the Abode of Disbelief and the Abode of War, the lives and property of Muslims are permissible. Therefore, in Islam, such people have no sanctity, except where someone has a covenant with the Muslims, and treaties are concluded between them and the people of the Abode of Islam. Islamic Shari'ah also provides to those individuals who migrate or travel from the Abode of War to the Abode of Islam all the facilities that Muslims enjoy in the Abode of Islam. When they enter the Abode of Islam under a peace treaty, with a fixed term of covenant, and they come within the boundaries of the Abode of Islam, whose ruler is a Muslim, and a Muslim ruler is one who enforces the true Shari'ah in the Abode of Islam.

Today we will not say what the Children of Israel said to their prophet: "Go you and your Lord and fight, we are sitting here" (5:24). (These are some examples of the Qur'an's manner of instruction. In this section, some very fundamental laws for human life are laid down, the commandments that are for the protection of life. These commandments are for the society in which Islamic life is practised. The purpose of these laws is to block the paths of rebellion against the Islamic system of life and support of that system, and to preserve the government that is established according to Allah's command and functions under the shelter of the Shari'ah. Furthermore, the protection of the society which functions under the shelter of Islamic Shari'ah and under the shelter of an Islamic government is intended. Through these commandments, the protection of both the property and the lives of the subjects of an Islamic government is intended, provided that this society, this government and this system are operating in accordance with the Islamic Shari'ah.

Throughout this whole section, very fundamental commandments have been given concerning the preservation of the collective life of society, but the beginning of this section is made with the story of the two sons of Hazrat Adam (peace be upon him). Through this it is intended to show what the psychology of criminals is at the time of committing this crime of murder and bloodshed: what causes and factors are there because of which a criminal commits the crime. Further, in this section it is shown that this crime is extremely heinous, and that its prevention and prohibition are extremely necessary. Punishing the criminal for this crime is also very necessary, and controlling the causes and influences because of which a person commits this crime is also necessary.

It appears that all the allusions of this story are fully connected with the commandments that come after this story. A reader who reads with reflection can easily perceive what the purpose of bringing this story into this context is, and what a profound and satisfying allusion it is, which this story pours into the human self and embeds in it. This story prepares the human heart and mind to accept these commandments, so that it accepts the severe punishments which Islam will enforce through the Islamic courts that work according to Islamic Shari'ah, for offences of hirabah (armed robbery), crimes against life, crimes against property, and crimes against the system of the state.

It is the duty of an Islamic society to run its entire life according to the Islamic system, under the Shari'ah of Muhammad. It should organise its affairs, its connections and relationships in accordance with the Islamic system and the Islamic law of the Shari'ah. This is the method by which this society will be a guardian of the individual as well as of the group, and will be able to give justice, security, contentment and peace to both the individual and society. It will be able to close the doors of corruption to all those elements which produce disorder, unrest, pressure and suffocation, and all the causes through which oppression and injustice arise within society will be eliminated. Likewise, the needs and requirements of people will also be fulfilled with great ease. In the same way, within such a mutually supportive, balanced, just and virtuous society, committing crimes of this kind against someone's life and property, against an individual's ownership, or against the system of the state, is regarded as an extremely vile act and a grave crime. There is no justification, excuse or circumstance for it that would mitigate (Milderung) this crime. From this it becomes clear that this severity of Islam against crime and criminal is applied when every opportunity has been provided to the individual to walk on the right path, that is, when conditions exist for moderate people to live correctly, and when conditions exist such that an individual and a group, if they wish, can live a pure life. Despite all these matters, the Islamic system of government and the Islamic system of justice grant the accused the full rights of legal investigation and legal judgment. If even the slightest doubt arises, the hudud are set aside because of doubts. Furthermore, the door of repentance is also left open, by which, in certain circumstances, his crime may be forgiven even in this world, while in the Hereafter Allah will in any case forgive all his crimes and sins... In this lesson we shall find all its aspects and examples, and many commandments and laws will be mentioned.

But before commenting on the verses and speaking directly about the commandments, it is necessary to note here one general and important matter: what kind of society will these severe laws be enforced in, and what are the limits and conditions of the enforcing power?

Whether the commandments and laws stated in this lesson relate to crimes against the person, or to commandments concerning offences against the system of the state, or to commandments concerning offences against someone's property, their status is similar to the other Shari'ah rulings found concerning the crimes of hudud, qisas and ta'zir. That is, all these commandments will be enforced only when their enforcing power exists in the form of an Islamic society, in Dar al-Islam. Therefore it is necessary that the definition of Dar al-Islam according to the Shari'ah also be given.

According to Islam and Muslims, the whole world is divided into two blocs, and we do not recognise a third bloc.

The first bloc is Dar al-Islam, and by this is meant the state within which Islamic commandments are enforced, whose legal system is based on the Shari'ah, whether its inhabitants are all Muslims, or consist of Muslims and dhimmis, or whose people are all non-Muslims while the ruler is a Muslim and the law of the Islamic state applies and decisions are made according to the Shari'ah. (Although not all the Shari'ah rulings are binding on the dhimmis; only the civil and criminal rulings of Islam are binding on them.) Or the situation may be that the entire population is Muslim, or there is a mixed population of Muslims and non-Muslims, but the country has come under the control of hostile non-Muslims, while the legal system of the country has not been changed and the inhabitants continue to decide matters according to Islamic law. Therefore the complete basis for a country being Dar al-Islam rests solely on whether its legal system conforms to the Shari'ah or not, and whether disputes within it are decided by the Shari'ah or by some other law.

Second, the Abode of War (dar al-harb) is every country in which Islamic Shari'ah is not enforced and in which judgments are not made according to Shari'ah. As for its inhabitants, whatever religion or community they follow, whether they call themselves Muslims or call themselves People of the Book, or whether they are other disbelievers, they will be inhabitants of the Abode of War. Therefore, whether a country is an Abode of War depends entirely on this alone: that Islamic laws are not enforced within it and that judgments in its courts are not according to Islamic Shari'ah. Such a country will be called an Abode of War from the point of view of a Muslim and of an Islamic community.

A Muslim society is one that is established in the Abode of Islam (dar al-Islam), according to the meaning stated above... And this Islamic society, which follows the Islamic methodology and over which the rule of Islamic Shari'ah prevails, has the right that the lives of its people be protected, that the properties of its people be protected, that its system of governance be preserved, and that in it, and only in it, the prescribed punishments mentioned in these verses be carried out against those criminals who are against the people's lives, property and the state's order. From this lesson and from the other Qur'anic teachings it becomes clear that this will be an extremely elevated and virtuous society. In it there will be justice and freedoms. In this society there will be a guarantee of employment and the necessities of life, whether a person is able to work or is disabled. It will be a society in which the factors that encourage goodness will be many and the factors that encourage evil will be very few. Therefore such a society has a right over all those who live within it and benefit from it, that they protect it wholeheartedly, and that they observe and protect the financial, personal, honour and moral rights of the other citizens of the country. All these inhabitants should protect the Abode of Islam in which they live safely and securely and in peace, in which they have complete security, in which they have all fundamental rights, and in which they hold all the ranks of human distinction, in which they have all social and collective rights; rather, it is the duty of all inhabitants to protect all these rights. After this, if anyone rises in rebellion against the system of the Abode of Islam, then he is a wrongdoer, a sinner, a mischief-maker and a saboteur, and he deserves to be given the severest punishment. Yet even in this, he has been given these rights: that no one should be seized merely on conjecture and suspicion, and this principle will also apply to this law, because prescribed punishments (hudud) are dropped due to doubts.

As for the Abode of War, whose definition has been given above, it and its inhabitants do not deserve to be given the benefit of the punishments enforced under Islamic Shari'ah, because there the Shari'ah is not implemented at all.

Nor does this society acknowledge the sovereignty of Islam. Moreover, this Abode of War does not provide protection even to Muslims who live in the Abode of Islam and who enforce Islamic Shari'ah in their own land. In the view of those of the Abode of Disbelief and the Abode of War, the lives and property of Muslims are permissible. Therefore, in Islam, such people have no sanctity, except where someone has a covenant with the Muslims, and treaties are concluded between them and the people of the Abode of Islam. Islamic Shari'ah also provides to those individuals who migrate or travel from the Abode of War to the Abode of Islam all the facilities that Muslims enjoy in the Abode of Islam. When they enter the Abode of Islam under a peace treaty, with a fixed term of covenant, and they come within the boundaries of the Abode of Islam, whose ruler is a Muslim, and a Muslim ruler is one who enforces the true Shari'ah in the Abode of Islam.

(Verse 24) "They said: O Musa, we shall never enter it so long as they are in it. So go you and your Lord and fight, we are sitting here."

But they said again: "O Musa, we will never go there as long as they remain in it. So you and your Lord go and fight; we are sitting right here." Thus the cowards withdraw from the ranks and become ashamed. Out of fear of dangers they become immobile, just as the feet of donkeys are tied, and then they take no initiative. Cowardice and shamelessness are not contradictory to each other, nor are they far apart from one another. These qualities often come together. A coward, when he moves forward towards his duties, shows cowardice and draws back. He withdraws in the very manner in which he has abandoned his duty. Then he speaks ill of that very goal, and speaks ill of the call that makes demands of him that he does not wish to fulfil.

﴿Go you and your Lord, then fight, we are sitting here﴾ (5:24). (We are sitting here.) This was the helplessness of a weak and cowardly person. His tongue is very sharp, but for advancing towards the goal his feet are heavy, and he feels the sting of arrows. ﴿Go you and your Lord﴾ (5:24). (Go you and your Lord.) If he now compels us to war, we do not accept his divinity; he is your Lord. ﴿We are sitting here﴾ (5:24). (We are sitting right here.) We have no need of a kingdom, nor of honour, nor of the Promised Land. At that time there was a tyrannical people in it... This was the end of the great struggle of Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him): a long journey, in it humiliation and disgrace, and repeated deviation from the Children of Israel, evasion and disobedience at every step... Surely this is their end: they turn back from the conquest of the Holy Land, although Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) is with them and they are on the threshold of that land. They are on the threshold of that land. They turn away from the covenant made with Allah, although that ancient covenant was closely linked with this covenant, namely the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis. Now what could Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) do in this state of despair?

(Verse 25) ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have control over none but myself and my brother; so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ (5:25)

This is a call full of grief and sorrow. In it there is, on one side, supplication, and on the other, complete submission and acceptance, and after that decisive firmness. Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) knew well and was certain that Allah the Exalted knows that, for Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him), no supporter remained except his brother. Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) stands between the weakness of a remorseful human being and a prophet who is Kalimullah (the one who spoke with Allah), and he holds the resolute determination of a truthful believer. Before him there is no path except to turn only to Allah and to express his pain and sorrow in the form of a whisper before Him, and to make the demand: O Allah, grant me permission to separate myself from this defiantly disobedient people forever. For when they turned away from their firm covenant with Allah, what connection remained between them and the prophet who spoke with Allah? They were not bound to him by lineage, nor by the fact that their history was one, nor was their relationship with him based on having struggled together in one place as companions. Their bond was based only on the call to the Truth. Their bond was this ancient covenant, and they had broken this covenant. Therefore complete severance occurred between them, and it went to the very depths. Now there is no connection left between Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) and them. He is bound by his covenant and promise, and the people have disobeyed him. He is firmly fixed upon the covenant, and the people have turned away from it.

This is the manner of respect and reverence from Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him). This is his sunnah, and this is the plan of a true believer. And this is the foundation and bond upon which people gather and separate from one another. In this path, nation, lineage, descent and shared history count for nothing; no relation of this earth is of any use. On the path, when the bond of ideas is broken, all relationships are broken; and when beliefs separate, the ways and methods also separate. At this point Allah answers the call of His Prophet, and the wicked are given their full punishment.

(Verse 26) ﴿He said: "Then it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ (5:26)

Allah handed these wretched people over to the deserts, although they were on the threshold of the Holy Land. Allah made forbidden to them that land which had been written for them. The preponderant view is that Allah made that land forbidden to their generation then present, and as long as a new generation was not produced from their loins, they kept wandering in this manner. Thus entry into the Promised Land remained prohibited for them until a new generation was prepared, a generation that accepts admonition. This generation was formed in the pure condition of the desert, and it was entirely free-spirited and freedom-loving. It was not the generation that humiliation, slavery and the oppressions of the Egyptians had made accustomed to weakness. Therefore that generation was not suited to the task that belongs to people of resolute determination.
