(Verses 27–31)

This is a story given as an example of evil and oppression. It presents a model of plain injustice for which there is no justification, and the same story also presents a model of goodness of soul and tolerance, the highest example of a pure-natured, peace-loving person. In this story both models are placed opposite each other. Each acts according to his own temperament and his own nature. The story depicts a crime which is a manifestation of evil and open oppression, and on reading it the human conscience is stirred and feels that the law of retribution (qisas) is necessary against such open oppression. Only a just legal system can prevent the commission of this evident evil, so that after this evil is stopped from committing oppression, it can be restrained from committing crime by being made fearful. If, even after this deterrence, evil commits a crime, it will have to face a just punishment, precisely the punishment that is proportionate to the crime of this evil, so that the good-natured people of society may be protected, and the lives and property of good-natured people remain secure. The kind of good-natured people presented as an example in this story deserve to be given protection: they should be able to live, to remain in peace, and to live under a just legal and administrative system.

The Qur'an has not given details about the names, time and place of these two brothers, although some narrations mention Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain) in this connection. They were sons of Adam (ʿalayhi al-salam), and the narrations also give details of the dispute between them, that their dispute concerned two sisters. However, we prefer to leave this story in its concise form, because all these narrations are not of certain authenticity. They have been taken from the People of the Book. This story appears in the Old Testament, where both names are mentioned and the time and place of the event are also given, as is found in the narrations. A sound hadith related about this story also does not give details. This narration is related from Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one is killed unjustly except that a share of the responsibility for that blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish the practice of killing a human being." (Narrated by Imam Ahmad.) Its chain of narration is: al-Aʿmash, ʿAbd Allah ibn Murrah, Masruq, ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him). It has also been narrated by other muhaddithin besides Abu Dawud. Regarding it we can only say that this event occurred in the early days of human life, that it was the first incident of killing, and that the killer did not even know how to bury the corpse.

Leaving this story vague as it appears in the Qur'an does not affect its purpose. The purpose for which it has been brought is fully achieved, and its indications and guidance are fully understood. The basic aims of the story are not increased by the details of the narrations, so we too leave them here. There is no need for details, nor for brevity.

﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth, when they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but was not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Allah accepts only from the righteous."﴾

That is, present to these people an example of both of these two models, that is, after the events of Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) and the Children of Israel, place before them these two truthful models. This story is entirely true in its narration, and it is true also in the sense that these two models are found within human nature in every time and place. Then it is true also in the sense that it demands a just system of justice by which wrongdoers are restrained from committing crime.

The circumstances of these two sons of Adam (ʿalayhi al-salam) were such that the readiness of one of them to kill had no justification within it. Both were obedient to Allah. Both offered a sacrifice: ﴿when they both offered a sacrifice﴾ (5:27). But what happened was that one was accepted and the other was not: ﴿and it was accepted from one of them but was not accepted from the other﴾ (5:27).

Here the passive form "fa-tuqubbila" is used. The meaning is that the acceptance or non-acceptance of a sacrifice is a matter connected with an unseen power, and its manner is also unseen. Using the third-person passive form has two benefits. One is that we have no need to go into the details of the manner of acceptance and non-acceptance. Many stories have been related in the exegeses in explanation of these verses, and these stories have been taken from the Old Testament. The second point is that the one whose sacrifice was accepted had committed no offence that would justify hostility toward him or a plot to kill him, since he had no part in the acceptance of the sacrifice; rather, that acceptance came from an unseen power according to an unseen manner from a human perspective. This power lies beyond the perception of both of them, and its will is also beyond human will. Therefore the other brother had no justification for strangling his brother on account of that act, nor any justification for anyone to be moved to anger at the brother's killing. In this matter, readiness to kill is inconceivable from any sound-natured human being, because the matter concerns worship, and acceptance and non-acceptance come from an unseen power in which no human has any part.

﴿He said, "I will surely kill you."﴾ (5:27) It appears that the killer was set on committing this act, which is why he used an extremely emphatic form. Here the killer expresses fury without any reasonable cause; that is, his anger is entirely without reason. If it has any cause, it is his wicked intention and evil feeling, a consciousness filled with envy and hatred, which does not grow in any pure soul. In this scene of the story, at the first stage, we find ourselves faced with oppression, even though the verse is not complete; yet from this very word, indications of the commission of a crime are found.

Now the matter moves forward and this oppression is given a yet more horrific form. It is stated that the second model is acceptable, pure-natured and peace-loving.

﴿He said, "Allah accepts only from the righteous."﴾ (5:27)

Here the matter is openly returned to its reality and truth. Trust is placed in faith, and what is accepted is accepted on that basis; and in a most gentle manner the wrongdoer is addressed, that he should fear Allah, and he is called to the path that leads to acceptance. A subtle allusion is also made to the situation that is gnawing in his heart, which stirs him and incites him toward evil.

After this, the believing brother, who is a God-fearing, peace-loving and non-violent personality, shows how he wishes to reduce the fury of violent wickedness present in his wicked brother's heart.

(Qur'an 5:28) "If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds."

Thus is presented here, in vivid form, the model of peace, piety and forbearance toward all. This model is set forth at a time when even an ordinary human conscience becomes greatly agitated, though it may be very calm. In such circumstances every impartial person, every person of conscience, stands up against the oppressor and in support of the oppressed. Even in these circumstances, this oppressed one is serious and deeply composed, although he faces the danger of open aggression; yet his heart is filled with the fear of the Lord of the worlds, and therefore he is at peace.

This gentle and affectionate statement was sufficient to turn that enmity into friendship, to cool envy, to lessen the fervour of evil, to calm the agitated nerves, to bring that person into the love of brotherhood, and to create in his heart a sense of God-consciousness (taqwa). Indeed, this conduct was entirely sufficient for him; but this person did not desist. Therefore the righteous brother warns him and frightens him with the evil consequence in the Hereafter.

"I intend that you should bear my sin as well as your own, and thus you will be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers." (Qur'an 5:29)

If you raise your hand against me to kill me, my disposition is not to do the same to you. Nor is it my nature, for I cannot even imagine killing my brother; my mind does not turn in that direction. I refrain from this act because I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds. It is not that I cannot answer a brick with a stone. Rather, I leave you alone so that you may add the sin of my murder to the store of your earlier sins, because of which your offering was rejected. In this way your sin will increase, and then your punishment will also keep growing. "That is the recompense of the wrongdoers."

In this way, that righteous brother, by depicting his fear through the act of murder before the wrongdoer, sought to make this wrongdoing brother refrain from the act of injustice to which his own self repeatedly urged him, and to make him ashamed of how badly he thought about a brother who was peaceful, a brother who feared God.

That God-fearing brother set forth the dreadful consequences of the crime of murder before the wrongdoer, so that he would be repelled by this sin, would see it as better to escape from a sin that is multiplied many times over, and would keep the fear of Allah, the Lord of the worlds, within his heart. In this matter, this God-fearing brother goes as far as no human being can go, and beyond that there remains no other means of preventing shirk.

However, until we know what the outcome was, the picture of this wicked and corrupting brother cannot be complete. How did he respond to this most positive conduct?

"So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him, and he killed him, and thus he became among the losers." (Qur'an 5:30)

Despite all these efforts, despite this admonition, advice and warning, this wicked personality is inclined towards crime, and the crime is committed. His soul made every consequence easy for him. It removed every obstacle. He was readily brought to the act of murder. He did kill, but whom? His own brother. And now he deserves a dreadful end: "Thus he became among the losers" (5:30).

He caused loss to his own self; he cast it into destruction. He caused loss to his brother, who was his helper and companion. He caused loss in this world, in that his life became bitter in this world; and his loss in the Hereafter will be that he will bear the punishment for this very murder, and will also share in the sin of all the murderers who come after him.

Now his crime is presented to him in a new form. His brother's corpse lies there; the soul has departed. It is a heap of flesh, and it is rotting. This is something unbearable: a corpse. His sin now takes the form of a corpse.

Now it is Allah's will that this wicked being should stand helpless before what it has done, unable to understand what to do with this corpse. Until now he was a killer, bloodthirsty and harsh; and now he is powerless. He cannot figure out how to dispose of this corpse; now he is helpless even before a bird.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 31:

﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching the earth, to show him how to conceal the body of his brother. He said, "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the body of my brother?" Then he became one of the regretful.﴾ (5:31)

It is related in the narrations that one crow killed another, or that it found the body of another crow. This crow began to scratch the earth. Then it placed the dead crow in the pit and began to cover it with earth. At this moment, the murderer expressed his remorse in a sorrowful manner, and then he buried his brother's body.

This shows that the murderer had never seen anyone being buried before. Had he seen it, he would certainly have buried the body himself. It is possible that this was the first corpse on this earth, that is, among the children of Adam (peace be upon him). Or it may be that this murderer was young and had never seen anyone burying the dead before. Both matters are correct in their own place. Furthermore, it is also apparent that the murderer's remorse was not genuine, for otherwise Allah would have accepted his repentance. Rather, he regretted because his act brought him no benefit, and after this deed his difficulties increased, his life became bitter, and he fell victim to psychological breakdown.

Just as the crow buried the body of the other crow, so did he bury his brother. Some people say that crows do such things, and it is also possible that Allah sent a crow to teach this murderer, and that this was an extraordinary act which Allah caused a crow to perform. Both of these possibilities are equal for Allah, for the Being who bestows abilities upon a living human being is also able to cause those abilities to be manifested through any other living creature. Both matters are within His power.

After reading and observing this continuous story, the Qur'an here records the effects that it leaves upon the human mind, so as to make them a conscious way of thinking, and on the basis of this thinking, if any person does commit murder, then just retribution (qisas) should be taken from him fairly, and the criminal should know that if he commits a crime, the law of qisas awaits him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 32:

(Verse) "Number: 32."

For this reason, that is, because of the presence within humanity of such people, and because of the commission of such crimes against peaceful, reconciliation-loving, good-natured and pure-hearted people, who flee far from evil and oppression, and because some extremely wicked persons are not affected by admonition, advice and warning, and because, if evil has spread into a person's veins and sinews, then peace and amity are of no benefit with such people, for this reason Allah the Exalted has declared the killing of a soul to be a major sin and a grave crime. He has declared it so grave a crime that it is as if the perpetrator has killed the entire present human race. Then, by whatever act a person's life is saved, it is as if that act and that person have given life to all people. This is the principle which We laid down when We wrote the Shariah for the Children of Israel. (The details of the laws of retribution (qisas) will come later.)

Killing someone other than in qisas (retribution for murder), or killing someone other than to remove corruption on earth, is a crime as grave as if someone were to kill all of mankind. Every soul is equal to every other soul. The right to life belongs to every soul. Therefore, to kill one soul is equivalent to snatching the right to life from all souls, and so all souls share in the right to life. Likewise, all souls have the right to protection from being killed, and preserving life is obligatory for all. Whether defence of life is carried out while the person is alive, or after death by enforcing qisas so that the criminal does not lay hands on other souls, in either case the law of qisas holds, in effect, the meaning of giving life to all living people. For the law of qisas provides the right to remain alive, in which all people share.

From the explanation we have given regarding these rulings, it becomes clear that this ruling applies only to the inhabitants of the Abode of Islam, whether they are Muslims, dhimmis or musta'mins. As for the people of war (those with whom the Islamic state is at war), their blood is permissible, unless a treaty comes into being between them and the inhabitants of the Abode of Islam. Likewise, their property and possessions will also not have protection. Therefore we must always keep this principle of law in mind. We should also keep in mind that the Abode of Islam is a state in which Islamic Shariah is enforced and all institutions of government function in accordance with it, while the Abode of War is a territory in which Shariah is not enforced and the Shariah rulings are not followed in the conduct of state affairs.

Allah the Exalted had imposed this principle upon the Children of Israel, and therefore those people were then People of the Book. As long as they conducted the affairs of government in accordance with the Torah, their territory was considered the Abode of Islam, provided that the rulings of the Shariah had not been altered. But the Children of Israel always transgressed the limits of the Shariah, although their messengers had come to them with clear rulings of the Shariah. Even during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and in the periods after him up to today, there have been many among them who transgressed the limits of their Shariah, the Torah. The Qur'an is recording here their excess, transgression and aggression, which was without cause, and it is also being placed on record that before Allah they now have no argument, because Allah's messengers came to them and those messengers had explained the rulings of the Shariah to them.

(Verse) "And indeed Our messengers came to them with clear proofs; then, even after that, many of them are indeed transgressors in the land." (32)

(Translation of the verse's meaning in brackets: Our messengers came to them one after another with clear guidance, yet many of them remain, after that, transgressors in the land.)

And what greater excess and transgression could there be than for someone to exceed the limits set by Allah and to lay hands on the Shariah of Allah, either by altering and changing it or by leaving it aimless and unused?

In the previous verse it was said that taking a life falls under corruption in the land, and the life of both the murderer and the corrupter was excluded from protection. It was also said that taking an innocent life unjustly is an extremely abominable crime. This is because, in the Abode of Islam, the peace and security of a Muslim society, and the carrying out of good works by it with peace, tranquillity and contentment, is just as necessary as the peaceful living of individuals within an Islamic state. Indeed, the need for collective peace is greater than the need for individual peace, because individuals attain peace and tranquillity only when society attains peace and tranquillity. Moreover, it is even more important that the peace of such a lofty and virtuous society not be affected, and that such a society be guaranteed every kind of peace and stability. For through this guarantee, individuals in such a society find peace and tranquillity, and they can remain active in freedom, and under the shade of peace human life grows with tranquillity. It is only in the tranquil atmosphere of peace that every kind of goodness, noble morality, production and progress can continue without interruption. Such a society can also guarantee its members the necessities of life, and it is peace alone that provides the environment and atmosphere in which the seeds of goodness are sown and grow, and in which the seeds of evil are eliminated. The policy of such a society is that it acts in accordance with the principles of hygiene even before treating diseases, and where the principles of hygiene cannot work, it then applies treatment. Such a society leaves no opportunity for a sound-natured person to be inclined toward evil and aggression. If, in such conditions and within such a society, someone is still inclined to destroy public order, then understand that he is a corrupt element, and it is necessary to remove him from the body of society by surgical means, provided all other methods of treatment have failed. ... These are the very elements about whom rulings are given in this verse:

(Verses 33-34)

Who are these rebels whom this verse addresses, and what are the limits of this crime? That is, rising in revolt against the head of an Islamic state that is ruling in accordance with the Shariah. This rebellion takes the form of an organised group that rises up against the state and adopts a course of action that spreads terror among the people of the Dar al-Islam, and through which the residents of the Dar al-Islam face the danger of loss of property, life and honour. Some jurists have also stipulated that this kind of act occurs away from urban areas, where the administration of the state does not reach. Some jurists have also stipulated that this kind of act occurs away from urban areas, where the administration of the state does not reach. Some jurists have also stipulated that the gathering of a group of such rebels, and their beginning acts of aggression, and even if not in practice, the adoption of this position in potential, is enough for the application of this verse, whether this group is inside the cities or outside them, and this last opinion is practically closer to understanding, so that the rebels may be brought to their deserved punishment.

These rebels will be considered those who oppose a ruler who is governing in accordance with the Shariah, and who are in a position to commit aggression against those residents of the Dar al-Islam under whom the Shariah is in force (whether they are dhimmis, Muslims or musta'min). These people are not merely rebels against an authority, nor merely a rebellion against people, but a rebellion against Allah and His Messenger as well. They wage war against the Shariah of Allah and wage war against a society established on the foundation of that Shariah. Moreover, if their activities have endangered the Dar al-Islam, their war will be considered a war against Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This war will be considered a war against the Shariah, because there is no greater corruption in this world than suspending the Shariah of Allah. And there can be no greater corruption than the existence of the Dar al-Islam being endangered.

Since these people wage war against Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), although apparently they fight against the Muslim community, the Islamic society and its head, they cannot raise the sword against Allah Almighty, nor can they raise the sword against the person of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he has departed from this world. But if a war is against the Shariah of Allah, then it is as though that war is being waged against Allah and His Messenger. This war will be considered a war against the society that has adopted the Shariah of Allah and His Messenger, and against the region in which this Shariah is being enforced.

Another meaning of this verse is also determined here in accordance with the above meaning. It is that the head of state who has the authority, in accordance with the command of Allah, to impose the punishments mentioned in the verse upon the rebels, is the head of state who has been appointed in accordance with Islamic Shariah and who enforces the Shariah. No king or head of state other than such a ruler shall have such powers.

We make this decisive clarification because some lackeys of governments, who are available to every government, establish the authority for such punishments for certain governments which do not enforce the Shariah, even though those governments do not establish the Dar al-Islam in their territories, although they think they are Muslims. These lackeys have always advised those governments to impose these Qur'anic punishments on those who rise against them, and to enforce them in the name of the Shariah of Allah, although the members of these irreligious governments are rebels against Allah and His Messenger; rather, they are members of governments that are rebels against Allah and His Messenger.

In short, if a government is not established on the foundation of Islamic Shariah in the Dar al-Islam, it has no Shariah authority to impose those punishments upon its rebels. What connection do such irreligious governments have with the Shariah? Such governments are those that have committed aggression upon Allah's right of divinity and right of sovereignty. What connection does their law have with the Shariah?

These punishments shall apply to such rebel groups when they rebel against an Islamic caliph, and that caliph is an enforcer and supporter of Islamic Shariah. If these people are a danger to the residents of the Dar al-Islam, and their lives, property and honour are not safe from them, then killing them becomes lawful and obligatory, and they may be executed. Some jurists have said that after killing, the bodies shall be hung as a lesson for others, and that their hands and feet shall be cut off, namely the right hand with the left foot and the left hand with the right foot. (Min khilaf) means this.

Among jurists there has arisen a very wide difference of opinion regarding this verse. Does the imam have the discretion to impose on the rebels whichever of these punishments he chooses, or is there a separate punishment for each of these crimes?

From Imam Abu Hanifah, Imam al-Shafi'i and Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them) it is reported that these punishments are to be imposed according to the crimes committed by these rebels. If a person did not commit murder, he shall be given the punishment of amputation (qat' al-yad). Whoever took part in both murder and plunder shall be given the punishment of execution and crucifixion. And whoever merely spread terror, without killing and without taking part in plunder, shall be given the punishment of banishment.

From Imam Malik it is reported that if a rebel committed murder, he shall necessarily be given the death penalty, and the ruler of the time shall not have the discretion to impose amputation or banishment upon him; however, he has the discretion to have him killed or crucified. Similarly, if he did not commit murder, he shall not be liable to banishment. The imam has the discretion to kill or crucify, or, if he decides on amputation of limbs, to choose whichever of the opposite limbs he prefers. If the criminals are feared to have made the roads dangerous, the imam has the discretion to kill them, crucify them, cut off their hands, or banish them; and the meaning of discretion (ikhtiyar tamizi) according to Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) is that the matter depends on the imam's ijtihad. If the rebel is a man of judgement and capable of devising rebellious plans, then ijtihad requires that he be killed or crucified, because mere amputation will not remove his harm; if the rebel is not a man of judgement but merely a strong and brave person, then he shall be given only the punishment of amputation of opposite limbs; and if both these qualities are found in him to some degree, he shall be given banishment and a discretionary punishment (ta'zir). (Al-Tashri' al-Jina'i al-Islami, Abd al-Qadir Awdah)

In our opinion, the view of Imam Malik is more suitable, namely that the punishment is sometimes imposed merely for rebellion and waging war, or for the threat of highway robbery and making the roads dangerous, and this punishment is purely preventive. The aim is that crimes should not be committed, and the purpose is to deter those who destroy the peace and security of the Dar al-Islam and who terrify the society which is established on the foundation of Islamic Shariah in the Dar al-Islam. Yet this society and the territory of the Dar al-Islam are the most deserving that peace and tranquillity be established within them.

Likewise, among jurists there has also arisen a difference regarding the meaning of banishment. Will banishment be only from the region in which the crime was committed, or will he be banished from the region in which he is permitted to move about, and this aim can be fulfilled by imprisonment, or shall he be removed from the whole earth, which is possible only through the death penalty...? I think the closer meaning is that this criminal shall be expelled from the land in which he committed the crime. He shall be thrown so far away that he considers himself a stranger there. He shall be rejected and weak, and this is the full penalty for his crime: that he disturbed people, terrified them, and by the strength of his power committed aggression against people. This banishment is such that wherever he goes he should give up crime, and his gang should not be there, or he should be separated from his gang.

(Verse 33) "That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment."

The punishment they receive in this world does not thereby cancel their punishment in the Hereafter, and in the Hereafter they will not be purified from the filth of sin, unlike other hudud offences, where a person who is punished becomes purified for the Hereafter. This is also one aspect of the severity of the punishment, and by it the intention is to show this crime to be even more abominable. This is because the Islamic society in the Dar al-Islam deserves to live a peaceful life, and secondly because a government established in accordance with Islamic Shariah has the right over the people that they accept its commands.

The atmosphere of an Islamic system of government is an atmosphere of goodness, and it deserves to be given opportunities to flourish; moreover, the Islamic system of life is a just and complete system whose protection is obligatory upon Muslims.

Now, if these rebels abandon their misguidance and give up corruption, and refrain from their crime, considering it evil and abhorrent, and sincerely repent and return to the right path — even though they may still be in a position to continue their campaign and the Islamic state could lay hands on them — then their crime and its punishment are both considered forgiven. It is then not lawful for the government to lay hands on those who repent. Since Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, He will also forgive them on the Day of Reckoning in the Hereafter.

(Verse 34 of Surah al-Ma'idah:) "Except for those who repent before you gain power over them; so know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

The wisdom behind pardoning those who repent, and the reason for their punishment being lifted, is quite clear, and it has two aspects. The first is that their repentance is to be encouraged, even though they were powerful and could have continued their rebellion; and this is strong evidence of their readiness to reform and of their coming onto the path of guidance. The second aspect is that, seeing them, other people of the same kind will also be moved to repent and to come onto the right path. In this way, instead of subduing them through war and conflict, it becomes possible to bring them onto the right path by easier means.

The Islamic system of life employs for the reform of the human being all his emotions, inclinations, and every means and possibility, and this is a system that was devised by the Creator of human nature and temperament Himself. That Being knows the ups and downs of the human soul well. He knows how a person can be reformed and by what means. Does not He who created the human being know? He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware. (Verse: "Should not He know who created? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted.")

The Islamic system of life does not merely enforce Islamic law upon people. It does not impose by raising the sword of law in such a way that people refrain from committing crime out of fear. Punishment is given only to those who will not come onto the path of reform in any way without the stick. Islam first lays emphasis on the inner moral training of people. People's temperament is corrected, and their souls are brought onto the path of reform. But alongside this, the establishment of a society and a social order in which the seeds of reform, goodness and virtue can bear fruit is also essential. These seeds can bear fruit only in that soil from which weedy plants and wild growth have been removed. That is why the Islamic system of life, as soon as it takes action, turns towards the reform of the soul and the piety of the heart, and efforts are made to create spirituality and tender-heartedness in people's hearts. They are commanded to adopt other means too in order to reach God and to take up the path of reform, and striving in the way of Allah is the greatest means of reform. The Islamic society is warned of the consequences of disbelief, and a picture of the punishment of the Hereafter is drawn that is extremely frightening, so that every person can take a lesson from seeing it.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 5, verse 35:

(Verses) No. 35 to 37.

The Islamic system employs every means to reform the human soul and encompasses it from every side. The Islamic system also considers it essential to reform the inner being of the human personality. By employing all means, it brings the soul to obedience to Allah and restrains it from disobedience to the Creator. The primary aim of the Islamic system of life is the reform of the individual, and it is desired to protect an individual from every kind of deviation. And the system of punishment is also only one means of reforming a human being. Punishment is not the real objective at all.

Reflect on this lesson: it begins with the story of the two sons of Prophet Adam (peace be upon him). Throughout this lesson there are allusions. After that, a punishment is announced, so that hearts are prevented from moving toward that (deed). Then the fear of God is called for, and people are warned of the punishment of God in the Hereafter, and alongside this frightening depiction of punishment, it is said:

﴿O you who believe, fear Allah﴾ (5:35)

That is, the proper thing is that the real fear is the fear of Allah, and it is also befitting for man, who is the most honoured of creatures, that he fear God. Fearing the whip, the sword and the stick is a lowly station, and reform through the stick is needed only for those people who are fallen. God-fearing is a better, purer and more noble station. Moreover, God-fearing is a guardian who sits in the hearts, who sits over a person both openly and secretly. In circumstances where a person is hidden from the eyes of people, at that time too taqwa (God-consciousness) is his overseer. In such matters, only taqwa restrains from evil and wickedness, in those matters in which a person is far from the grip of law. It is worth remembering well that without taqwa the grip of law is loose, because the number of criminals who escape the grip of law is many times greater than those who fall into the grip of law. A society that rests only on law has neither the reform of any individual nor the reform of that society. Behind the law there must be a hidden guardian, and this guardian is only the guardian of God-fearing, which sits in every heart by virtue of God-fearing and taqwa.

﴿And seek the means of access to Him﴾ (5:35)

Fear Allah and seek the means to reach Him, and seek the causes that join you to Allah. A report from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding ﴿and seek the means of access to Him﴾ (5:35) (meaning: ask Him for your needs) means that when people feel the need to turn to Allah and then ask Allah for their needs, they are then in the correct position of servitude. At that time they become fully certain of Allah's lordship, and in such circumstances they come closer to both reform and success. Both interpretations agree with the words of this verse. Through both, the reform of the inner world of the heart, the life of conscience and spirit, and that eternal success which is our goal are attained.

﴿Strive in His way that you may be successful﴾ (5:35)

In contrast to this comes the scene of the disbelievers, who do not fear Allah, who do not seek a means to reach Allah, and who do not succeed in the Hereafter. This is a living and moving scene, right before the eyes. In its explanation of this verse, the Qur'an does not adopt the style of narration and legal rulings, but rather presents movements and impressions concerning them. Perhaps this is a particular style of the Holy Qur'an in describing the Resurrection, and through it all the aims and purposes of the discourse are achieved.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 36–37:

(Verse) "Indeed, those who have disbelieved—if they had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and they will have a painful punishment. They will wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it, and theirs is a punishment that endures."

(Khoob jan lo ki jin logon ne kufr ka rawaiya ikhtiyar kiya hai agar un ke qabze mein sari zameen ki daulat ho aur utni hi aur is ke sath aur woh chahein ki use fidyah mein de kar roz-e-qiyamat ke azab se bach jayen, tab bhi woh un se qabool na ki jayegi aur unhen dardnak saza mil kar rahegi. Woh chahein ge ki dozakh ki aag se nikal bhaagen magar na nikal saken ge aur unhen qaim rehne wala azab diya jayega.)

As a hypothetical, what a human can imagine is that the disbelievers possess all the treasures of the earth, and that the same amount again could be supposed for them. The Qur'an further supposes that they have another world like this one. Then the Qur'an supposes that on the Day of Resurrection these people wish to give all this supposed wealth as ransom and expiation for their disbelief, so that they may be saved from the punishment of the Hereafter. The Qur'an brings before the eyes a scene of how they wish to escape from the Fire, but they cannot escape. They fail in this aim and purpose, and remain forever in the Fire of Jahannam.

This is a scene containing several scenes and a succession of movements. In one scene the disbelievers have the wealth of this entire world, then suddenly this wealth is doubled. Then they take this wealth and offer it as ransom. Then comes the scene in which they return failing to achieve this aim, and now they have no hope of achieving it. Then suddenly they enter the Fire, and they want to flee from it but cannot flee. Then they are compelled to remain there forever. Now the curtain falls, and they settle there permanently. (See the book Al-Tasweer al-Fanni, chapter "Tariqat al-Quran.")

And now, at the end of this lesson, the rules concerning thieves:
