And now, at the end of this lesson, the rules concerning thieves:

(Verse) No. 38 to 40.

An Islamic society provides an environment for the inhabitants of the Abode of Islam in which no moderate person would even think of theft, whatever their beliefs and ideologies may be. The Islamic society guarantees its inhabitants economic sustenance, moral training and the adoption of correct conduct. It also makes arrangements for justice and the equitable distribution of wealth, and it arranges that the form of individual ownership within it be such that it is beneficial for the whole society and is not a source of harm to society. For this reason, even after creating such conditions, if someone commits theft, Islam gives him the severest punishment. Likewise, it gives a deterrent punishment to one who lays hands on individual ownership and disturbs the peace and security of society. Alongside the prescription of these severest punishments, Islam also suspends the hudud on the basis of doubts, and grants the accused the right and authority of a complete legal defence, so that no person may be punished without complete proof. Now it is appropriate that, after this summary, a somewhat detailed discussion be presented.

The truth is that the Islamic system is an interconnected whole. A part of this system cannot be understood unless one has in view all the fundamental discussions and the guarantees that this system provides to Islamic society, and the principles and rules upon which its particulars are based. Then, a single part of the Islamic system cannot be enforced unless it is enforced completely and put into practice as a whole. As for the case that implementing one part of this system, or one principle of its principles, within a society and a system which as a whole is not an Islamic system, would be of no benefit.

This part, cut off from Islam, will also not be considered the implementation of Islam, because Islam is not the name of parts and fragments of Islam. Islam is a system that encompasses all spheres of life, and its injunctions are interconnected... This was a general point.

As for the matter of the law of theft in Islam, the situation is somewhat different. The truth is that in the Abode of Islam, Islam gives every individual the right to live, and to use all means for the preservation and sustenance of his life. Every person may eat and drink; every person has a right to a dwelling and clothing in which he may spend the night in comfort and tranquility. An individual has a right upon Islamic society to provide him these basic necessities, and it is evident that a government is the representative of the whole society. This right is fulfilled in such a way that the government provides employment to all those who are capable of working. This right belongs to the individual upon society, and then upon the government. This society and government will also train people to work, and will provide them with opportunities for work and the tools of work. If someone becomes unemployed, in the sense that he does not find work, or does not get tools of work, or he is no longer able to labour, and this unemployment is partial or total, temporary or permanent, or the situation is that he does work but this work is not sufficient for his needs, then this individual has a right that the collective system or society provide these necessities to him from the treasury, or have them provided through those people upon whom the maintenance of such individuals is obligatory. The residents of the neighbourhood should provide the needs of such people; otherwise, as has been said, they should be provided from the Bayt al-Mal (public treasury) and the exchequer. One head of the Bayt al-Mal is zakat itself, for this purpose. If even the zakat fund is not sufficient, then a tax may be imposed upon the entire Abode of Islam for this purpose, through which the poor are given enough to meet their needs. But this tax too should be imposed only in accordance with the needs of the poor, and not beyond their need, and should not be an oppression upon individual property that was earned by entirely lawful means.

Furthermore, Islam imposes strict restrictions on the accumulation of wealth. In the Islamic system, individual wealth may be accumulated only through lawful means. For this reason, in an Islamic society individual ownership does not face envy and resentment, that is to say, from those who are needy. Likewise, in an Islamic society no one thinks of seizing another's property, especially when the Islamic system makes adequate arrangements for them and does not leave them completely deprived.

Islam also emphasises the training of people's consciences and their morals. Therefore Islam motivates people towards earning and work, and it wants this earning and work to be in accordance with the Islamic manner. If work and employment are not available, the Islamic system arranges for the supply of people's needs, and sustains them through pure and clean means.

The question is: in such a society and under such conditions, if a person commits theft, why does he do so? This person does not steal for needs; rather he steals to accumulate wealth. He does not wish to accumulate this wealth through earning and labour, but steals in order to accumulate wealth through theft. He does not wish to accumulate this wealth through earning and labour, but desires to accumulate wealth through theft, which endangers the security, peace and tranquility of the whole Abode of Islam. The Islamic society has the right to continue in peace and security, but this act of theft deprives the owner of lawful property of his right to tranquility, and then society too.

In an Islamic society, the person who earns lawful wealth, does not practise usury, does not commit fraud, does not hoard, does not withhold the wages of labourers, pays zakat, and also pays whatever tax the society may need, has a right upon the Islamic society and the Abode of Islam that his property be protected and that his wealth be safe from theft and robbery.

Even after all these conditions and facilities, if someone commits theft, he commits it while his needs are being met, he knows that theft is a grave crime, he has no need or necessity to plunder the property of others, and those wealthy persons have not accumulated this wealth through plunder nor through unlawful means. If someone commits theft under such circumstances, this theft is without justification. In such circumstances it is not permissible for anyone to show mercy to such a person, provided that the offence is established.

If the circumstances of the case are such that it is established that the thief was needy, or that there was some other excuse, then the general principle of Islamic law is that the hudud are dropped because of doubts. For this reason, in a year of famine, Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) suspended the punishment of amputation of the hand. On that occasion the conditions were such that people were generally hungry. Similarly, Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) did not impose the punishment of amputation in a particular incident as well. The slaves of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah stole a she-camel belonging to a man of Muzaynah. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) ordered their hands to be cut off, but when Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) learned that the master of these slaves kept them hungry, he suspended the hadd punishment and imposed upon the master of the slaves a fine of twice the value of the she-camel as compensation.

It is appropriate that we try to understand the Islamic hudud in this manner, and understand them in the form and shape of the complete and interconnected system of Islam, which provides the guarantees of life to the members of society. These guarantees do not provide for one class against another class; rather, Islam provides the means of averting punishment before it provides the causes of punishment. Islam punishes only those who commit crime without justification.

After expressing this general truth, we now consider it appropriate to present the details of the hadd of theft (hadd al-sariqah). The definition of theft is that another's property is taken secretly, which property is within a protected place (hirz). It is also necessary that the property be mutaqawwam, that is, that it have value. Regarding the amount (nisab) of property, the point agreed upon among the jurists is that the property taken, and taken secretly from within a protected place, should be equal in quantity to 41 dinars, that is, equal to 25 Egyptian qirsh of our time. It is absolutely essential that the property be within a protected place and that the thief take it from within the protected place and, having taken it, exit the protected place. Now, if someone holds another's property as a trust and then steals it, the hadd of theft does not apply to him. Likewise, a person who is an employee and comes and goes in a house, shop or warehouse, the hadd of theft does not apply to him either. Similarly, if someone takes something from another by asking for it, and then denies it and it is found in his possession, the hadd of theft does not apply to him either. Also, the hadd of theft does not apply to fruits until they have been gathered into the threshing ground (kaliyan). Nor does it apply to property which is outside the house or outside the chest made for its protection. It is also necessary that this protected property belong to another person; therefore, if a partner steals, the hadd of theft does not apply to him, because he is himself a partner in it and it is not purely another's. Likewise, if someone steals public property, that is, from the treasury of the Abode of Islam, he too will not receive the punishment of amputation, because he has a share in that property and it is not purely the property of another. In such circumstances the punishment is not amputation but a discretionary punishment (ta'zir). (It should be remembered that ta'zir punishment is less than the hadd punishment, such as whipping, imprisonment, reprimand, and also admonition and advice, and this punishment will be according to the circumstances, at the judicial discretion of the qadi.)

The amputation (qat' yad) is of the right hand, that is, up to the wrist. If he steals again, the left foot is cut off up to the ankle. Up to this point there is agreement among all people. Regarding the case of theft for the third and fourth time, there is disagreement among the jurists.

The hudud are waived because of doubts. The doubts that may arise in the hadd of theft are, for example, that the hadd is dropped on account of hunger and severe need. Similarly, if there is doubt about a share in the property, the hadd is also dropped. If someone has confessed, and there is no other evidence, then the hadd is considered dropped as soon as he retracts his confession. Likewise, if someone gave testimony but afterwards retracts his testimony, this too is a kind of doubt.

On the question of what is to be regarded as a doubt, the jurists differ. Imam Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) says that for an item which is originally permissible (mubah), there is no punishment of amputation even if it is within a protected place and under guard. For example, a person takes water from another's reservoir, or a person hunts and secures his game, and another steals it. These are two things which, by their original nature, are permissible for all.

It may be argued that the permissibility continues even after it comes into a protected place and under guard. Likewise, the common wealth of the public, even if it comes into the protected place and custody of a particular person, may still give rise to doubt that it is still a thing of public benefit. Whereas Imam al-Shafi'i, Imam Malik and Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them) do not accept doubt in such circumstances, and do not waive the hadd. Imam Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) waives the hadd in the theft of all those things which decay quickly, for example food, fruit, vegetables, meat, bread and other such items. However, Imam Abu Yusuf (may Allah have mercy on him) differs from Imam Abu Hanifah, and he, like the three imams, holds that amputation applies to them.

It is not possible for us here to discuss the differences of the jurists in detail; these details may be seen in the books of fiqh. These few examples are sufficient to show that the policy of Islamic law is not to enforce punishment needlessly; rather, Islam is interested in waiving the hudud because of doubts. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ward off the hudud by means of doubts" (Idra'u al-hudud bil-shubuhat), and Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I prefer to suspend the hudud because of doubts rather than to enforce the hudud in such circumstances."

But regarding the amputation, it is appropriate that there be a somewhat more detailed discussion. We have already stated why, in the Abode of Islam, harshness has been applied to the thief after providing the accused with protection and with full judicial safeguards. Here it is appropriate that we give some extracts from the well-known book of Mr. Abd al-Qadir Awdah.

"The punishment of amputation has been prescribed for the thief because when a thief commits theft, his intention is to acquire another's earnings and increase his own earnings. He considers what he earns lawfully to be insufficient, and thus he wishes to increase his earnings unlawfully. He is not content with the results of his own effort and earning, and covets seizing another's earnings. Behind this act he has the desire that thereby he may spend more or display greater wealth, or the motive is that he may escape from working and toiling, or his aim is that his future may be secured. In short, the factor that inclines him to theft is only what we have described above, namely greater earnings and wealth. Islamic law, in relation to their psychology, began treating this disease in such a way that it prescribed the punishment of amputation for the offence. Through this amputation of the hand or the foot, the earnings of this person will be affected, because the hands and the feet are both instruments of earning. Now, if his earnings decrease, his wealth will decrease, and if his wealth decreases, the display of greater spending and greater wealth will also decrease. As a result, such a person will need to work harder, and he will work for longer periods, and he will face the danger of losing his entire future."

Thus, by prescribing the punishment of amputation of the hand, the Shariah removed the psychological factors that incite a person to this crime, and placed within the criminal's psyche opposing psychological factors that deter him from committing it. Yet if, despite this, the factors inciting a person to theft in his psyche still prevail and he commits the crime, then the bitter punishment he receives in that case will overcome the influences that drive him to theft. In this way he will certainly not be willing to commit this crime again."

"This is the foundation upon which the punishment of amputation has been placed in the Islamic legal system. By God, from the beginning of humanity until today, this is the best punishment for this crime."

"The laws of the modern world impose imprisonment on the thief. This is a punishment that has been completely unsuccessful in eliminating every kind of crime, and especially it has not been able to eliminate the punishment for theft. The real reason is that imprisonment cannot place within the thief's psyche those factors that restrain him from this crime, because this punishment can only keep the thief from crime for the period during which he is in prison. When he is imprisoned, he has no need to earn, because all his needs and requirements are provided for inside the jail; and when he is released from jail, he has the capacity to earn and labour. He is given a fresh opportunity to increase his earnings, to grow his wealth, and to use both lawful and unlawful means in it. He can again deceive people, present himself as respectable, and gain people's confidence and cooperation. If he adopts good conduct, as he should, he will do so. And if he cannot achieve his aims, he has suffered no loss, and he can very easily return to the wrong path."

"As for the situation where he is given the punishment of amputation, he will either be completely unable to earn and work again, or his capacity for earning and working will be greatly reduced, and thus his opportunities for greater earnings will in any case be fewer. Sometimes these opportunities become very limited, and sometimes they disappear entirely. Now he will not be able to deceive people, and he will not be able to persuade them to place any trust or confidence in him, because the marks of the crime will be present on his body. His past conduct will be evident from his severed hand. If the punishment of amputation is enforced, then for the thief the loss will be certain and final. If he is given imprisonment, he will gain more and lose less. And it is the principle not only of thieves but of all people that they incline towards that in which the probability of profit is greater, and they never do a thing in which the loss is certain."

"After this discussion, the statements of those who say that the punishment of amputation does not suit the modern, advanced age and the civilized world are extremely strange. As if civilization and culture were the name for rejecting modern knowledge and profound wisdom, forgetting human temperament, and denying the experiences of all earlier and later nations. We would suddenly paralyse our reason and abandon the conclusions our thought has clearly reached, and adopt ideas whose proponents have no proof for them other than deviation and misguidance."

"If the requirement of civilization and culture is that whatever punishment there is should accord with civilization and culture, then imprisonment deserves to be abolished altogether and the punishment of amputation should be enforced. For the punishment of amputation is precisely in accordance with psychological motivations and the established principles of psychology. It is perfectly suited to human temperament and, in the light of the experiences of all the nations of the world, is also extremely beneficial. That is, the perception of all things and their wisdom. Civilization and culture too are based upon this principle of perception and principle of wisdom. As for imprisonment as a punishment, it is by no means founded upon psychology, wisdom and experience, nor does it agree with rational logic or the temperament of the created beings of the world."

"The foundation of the punishment of amputation rests upon human psychology and its soundness. This punishment is more suitable for individuals. It is also beneficial for society. Because of it, crime immediately decreases, and peace is established in society. When a punishment is suitable for the individual and beneficial for a society, it is better than all other punishments."

"But these arguments too cannot satisfy some people that the punishment of amputation is beneficial. Their opinion, for which they have only this proof, is that it is a merciless punishment. This is their first and last argument, and this argument is refutable in the following way: the word 'uqubat (punishment) is derived from 'iqab. And a punishment ceases to be a punishment if it is gentle and merely a diversion; rather, it would be merely a spectacle or something similar. Therefore, a punishment must be such that the criminal is subjected to severity, so that it may be called a punishment."

God, the Most Merciful of the merciful, is merciful indeed. God's command is this, and it is a very severe command:

﴿So cut off the hands of both of them as a recompense for what they committed, and as an exemplary punishment from God﴾ (5:38)

This is an exemplary and deterrent punishment from God. Whoever has the impulse to commit a crime in his heart and refrains from it, this becomes a mercy from God upon him. This divine mercy restrains him, and then it is a kind of divine mercy upon the whole society, because through it crime decreases and society lives a settled life. No one claims that he is more merciful towards people than their Creator, unless someone is spiritually blind, and his soul has been distorted. And it is a fact that in the first era of Islam, even after a century had passed, only a few people had their hands cut off. The reason was that, owing to the blessings of the Islamic system of life and the provision for people's needs in Islamic society, the punishment was enforced on only a few individuals.

Then God also leaves the door open for those who repent: if they repent, feel remorse, and refrain from committing crime, God is also forgiving, provided that they do not merely repent but also bring about a positive change within themselves and begin doing righteous deeds.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 39–40 (part 1 of 2):

(Verse) "But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." (5:39)

"And He is All-Knowing and All-Seeing. So whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms himself, Allah will turn His gracious regard back to him. Allah is Most Forgiving and Most Merciful."

Sovereignty belongs to Allah alone. He is the Owner of the kingdom. It is He who lays down the law for this world and then, in the Hereafter, fixes reward and punishment according to that same law. In these matters there is no plurality, no division, and these matters are not separate from one another. The affairs of people cannot be set right until the right of legislation and the system of reward and punishment, in both this world and the next, is concentrated in the one Divine Being. For if there were not only one God in this universe, but many gods, it would have been destroyed long ago. Thus He is the God in the heavens and the God on the earth.

Lesson No. 49 at a glance:

This lesson takes up a most important issue of the Islamic worldview and the Islamic system of life. The Islamic system of government and Islamic life depend upon it. The matter has been mentioned repeatedly in Surah Al 'Imran and Surah An-Nisa, but here in this lesson it has been presented in a very clear and definitive form. Here the issue is not taken as an implication of the text (ishara al-nass), nor as an indication of the meaning of the verse (mafhum al-ayah), nor as a necessary implication (iqtida' al-nass). Here it is stated as the explicit expression of the text (ibarat al-nass) and in its definitive meaning (qat'i al-dalalah).

This issue concerns the system of government, the legal system and the judicial system, and upon its foundation depend the question of Tawhid, the question of divine sovereignty (hakimiyyah ilahiyyah), and whether a person's faith exists or not.

The question is: will our system of government, our legal system and our judicial system be in accordance with the commands of Allah, in accordance with the Shari'ah, and in accordance with the laws that have been preserved in the revealed religions, namely the Shari'ah of the earlier messengers and of this Messenger of the Last Age? Or will they be in accordance with our desires, our changing desires, or our interests and changing interests, which are not in accordance with the Shari'ah of Allah, or will they keep changing and being altered merely according to the customs of a particular era or a particular generation? Will sovereignty, lordship and governance over the lives of people and over this earth belong to Allah, or will some matters belong to Allah and some to other people?

The command of Allah is that there is no other god besides Him. He has sent down one Shari'ah for mankind, and this Shari'ah and law is in accordance with His sovereignty. He has taken a covenant from people that they will remain upon the Shari'ah of Allah, and that this Shari'ah will remain dominant on this earth. It is the obligation of people to run their courts in accordance with this same Shari'ah, and it is also the obligation of the prophets to act in accordance with it. After the prophets, it is likewise the obligation of rulers to give their judgments in accordance with it.

The command of Allah is that in this matter there is no falsehood and no self-rule. In this matter, deviation even in the smallest of the affairs of life is intolerable. If any whole generation in any era should frame a law against it, that law has no standing. Nor does any principle of a tribe or a nation have any standing against it, unless Allah has granted permission for something.

Allah says: here the question is either one of faith and disbelief, or of Islam and jahiliyyah, or it will be Shari'ah or base desire. In this matter there is no middle position, no leniency, and no compromise. The believers are those who judge in accordance with the law of Allah, and do not deviate from it even by a mustard seed, nor alter it by a single letter. The wrongdoers (zalimun), the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun) and the disbelievers (kafirun) are those who, in this matter, deviate and do not give judgments in accordance with the law of Allah, the Shari'ah. If rulers rule in accordance with the Shari'ah of Allah, they enter the circle of faith; but if they follow some other constitution, code or law for which Allah has given no permission, then they are disbelievers, defiantly disobedient and wrongdoers. People have only two paths: either they accept the judgments issued by rulers and judges in accordance with the law of Allah, and do so in all the affairs of their lives, in which case they are believers; or if they do not adopt this path, they are not believers. There is no third path between these two. In this matter no argumentation will avail, no excuse will be accepted, and no expediency will be accepted. Allah, in any case, is the Lord of mankind, and He alone knows where the true interest of people lies. Allah legislates for the genuine welfare of people, and therefore no law or order can be better than the Shari'ah and commands of Allah. None of the servants of Allah may say, "I do not accept the Shari'ah of Allah," or that he knows the interests of people better than Allah does. If anyone says or does such a thing with his tongue or his actions, he will be considered outside the circle of faith.

This is the great issue which has been stated in this lesson in a decisive manner. Besides this, this lesson also describes the conditions of the Jews who lived around Madinah, who together with the hypocrites were plotting against Islam and devising schemes.

(Verse) "Among those who say, 'We believe,' with their mouths, while their hearts have not believed" (5:41). It also describes the circumstances in which the Noble Messenger (ﷺ) was confronting these conspiracies, and which the Jews have not ceased from since the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) until today.

Several points emerge from the wording of the Qur'an in this lesson. The first conclusion is that all the revealed religions that Allah sent down had all their judgments made in accordance with the law of Allah. Within them the entire system of life was founded upon the Shari'ah of Allah. This fact was the dividing line between Islam and disbelief, the basis of distinction between Islam and jahiliyyah, and the foundation of separation between Shari'ah and the desires of the self, in that it determines who judges by the Shari'ah and who does not. The Torah too was sent down by Allah because in it there was guidance and light.

(Verse) "By it the prophets who submitted judged for those who followed Judaism, and so did the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah, and they were witnesses to it" (5:44).

Elsewhere: "And with them is the Torah, in which is the command of Allah" (5:43). And elsewhere it is said: "And We prescribed for them in it: a life for a life" (5:45). And to Jesus, son of Mary (peace be upon him), the Gospel was given:

"Confirming what was before it of the Torah, and as guidance and instruction for the God-fearing (46). And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein" (47) (5:46–47). Then Allah sent down the Qur'an to His final Prophet:

"In truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a overseer over it" (5:48). And the Prophet of the Last Age was commanded:

"So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, turning away from the truth that has come to you" (5:48). And then it was said: "Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, they are the defiantly disobedient" (5:47). And it was commanded: "Do they then seek the judgment of jahiliyyah? And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain?" (5:50).

From these verses it is clear that there has been complete agreement among all religions on this point. Thus the boundaries of Islam are defined, and the conditions of Islam are determined, for departments and courts as well as for rulers. The essential matter is that all judgments be made in accordance with the commands of Allah, and that the common people accept these judgments, and do not run after other laws and commands abandoning the Islamic law.

Within this framework this issue acquires great importance, and the reasons for emphasising it from this angle must necessarily also be of great importance. The question is: what are these reasons? Whether we seek these reasons within these texts or throughout the verses and passages of the whole Qur'an, these reasons are entirely clear to us.

The first of these reasons is that this is in essence the question of acknowledging Allah's divinity (uluhiyyah), His lordship (rububiyyah) and His sovereignty, and that no one shares with Him in these matters. If this is not so, then the issue becomes one of denying this. This is precisely why this matter becomes a matter of faith and disbelief. It is a matter of Islam and jahiliyyah: either there will be jahiliyyah or there will be Islam.

Look at the whole Qur'an. It is a showcase, yet wherever you look it presents for observation this one truth: that Allah alone is the Creator. He alone created this entire universe, He alone created this human being, and He alone subjected to this human being the heavens and the earth and all things found between them. Creation belongs to Allah alone and He has no partner in it, whether this creation be small or great, little or much. ... That Allah is the Owner, and He is the Owner because He is the Creator. He is the Owner of the earths, the heavens, and whatever is between them and the heavens and between the two. He is the Owner of the earths and the heavens and whatever is between them: He is the sole Owner and He has no partner in it. ... Then, Allah is the Provider. No other being can provide sustenance to human beings or other living creatures, neither less nor more.

And further, Allah is the Sovereign of this universe and has authority over it, and He has authority over people as well. Because He alone is the Creator, the Owner and the Provider, and He possesses such powers that without His perfect power there can be no creation, no provision, and no benefit or harm can come. His sovereignty is over this entire universe.

Now, what is faith? Acknowledgement of the matters mentioned above is faith: that in sovereignty, ownership and lordship Allah has no partner. These attributes belong to the Divine Being alone. Islam is in reality the name of submitting oneself, and Islam is obedience to Allah within the requirements of these attributes: that the right of divinity, lordship, governance and sovereignty belongs to the Divine Being alone over this entire universe, of which man is a part. Acknowledgement of Allah's decrees of qada and qadar and acknowledgement of the laws of His Shari'ah are included in this. Indeed, acknowledgement of the Shari'ah of Allah is in fact acknowledgement of Allah's divinity, lordship, and His sovereignty and guardianship. To not submit before this Shari'ah means first of all that we are denying Allah's divinity, lordship, and His sovereignty and governance, in the sense that someone judges all the minor matters of his life according to some other Shari'ah and law. Submitting to Islam or rejecting it, whether by tongue or by action, there is no difference between the two cases. This is why this matter is one of disbelief and faith, a matter of jahiliyyah and Islam, and for this reason this verse has come:

"Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, they are the disbelievers" (5:44). And in other verses the words defiantly disobedient and wrongdoers have come.

The second aspect is that the Islamic Shari'ah is definitively superior and more excellent than other laws and codes, and the last verse of this lesson points to this:

"And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who have certainty?" (5:50)

This acknowledgment of the superiority of the Islamic Shari'ah is also part of the matter of faith. For a true believer, in every aspect and mode of life, the law and Shari'ah of God must be considered superior. Therefore, no believing person can claim that human laws could be superior to or equal to the Shari'ah of God, in any standard, any condition, or any custom and tradition. If someone makes such a claim, he will be neither a believer nor a Muslim. Rather, the meaning of his claim will be that he knows the circumstances of people better than God and makes better decisions regarding their circumstances than God does; or the meaning of his claim will be that people faced certain circumstances but God did not know these circumstances, and people had certain needs which were hidden from God's sight (God forbid), and yet God legislated for them; or that God knew of them but nevertheless did not make a law for them. Clearly, faith and Islam cannot be combined with such claims, even if someone outwardly claims faith and Islam with his tongue.

Now, as for how this excellence is practically manifested: the fact is that we cannot fully reach its reality, because God has never fully revealed the complete wisdom of His laws at any time. The wisdoms that have been mentioned, we cannot fully discuss here in Fi Zilal al-Quran, so here we can only give a few glimpses.

The reality is that God's Shari'ah is a complete and interconnected system of life. Within it is guidance for man, the organization of his life, and the means of his development and progress in every direction. This system presents a solution to the problems of human life in every kind of circumstance and in every time and place.

It is a system based on very profound knowledge of human personality and his self, and within it is the solution to all his needs. This system has been designed keeping in view the nature of this entire universe, and in its formation the natural disposition of human beings and the physical laws operating in this entire universe have also been taken into consideration. Therefore, in this system there is no excess or deficiency in the affairs of human life, and in it there is no conflict with the human nature. It neither disrupts natural inclinations nor imposes restrictions on natural human activities. There is also no conflict within this system and the laws of nature; rather, by acting upon this system, the most excellent balance, moderation and harmony are created within it and within the laws of nature. This is something that has never come into existence within any other human system. Man knows only outward matters, and a man lives in a specific era; he can only understand certain outward matters according to the circumstances of his era. Whatever system a human being creates, traces of human ignorance are nonetheless found within it, and some destructive effects of his created system also become apparent in certain aspects of human life. As a result of the destructive collision between human nature and these man-made laws, humanity keeps suffering destructive shocks.

Firstly, the Islamic system is founded on absolute justice, because only God truly knows by what means justice can be established and how it can be brought to fruition. Secondly, God alone is the Lord of all, so judging between all is also His right alone. God's system is as free from personal desire, particular inclination, and every kind of defect as it is free from ignorance, deficiency and excess and deficiency. These are qualities that cannot be combined in any system of life made by man, because man has personal desires, he has individual inclinations, and within man there are personal desires and individual inclinations, and within man there is ignorance and other defects, whether this law is made by an individual, or by a class, or by an entire nation, or by the whole of human race of a particular age, or by the generations of all periods of humanity, because all these lawmakers have their own tendencies and inclinations, and the personal desires and interests of each of them influence them. Above all, in all the aforementioned situations, lawmakers are not free from ignorance, deficiency and incapacity, and they cannot encompass all aspects of a matter even within a single time and place.

Furthermore, the Islamic system is a system that is in harmony with the order of this entire universe, because the Islamic system is God's system, and the order of the universe is also established by God. The Divine Being is the Creator of this universe and He is also the Creator of this human being. Therefore, when God has laid down a code for man, it is just as He has laid down a code for a part of the universe. The Divine Being dominates all the elements of this entire universe and watches over them. All these elements move according to God's guidance, and all these elements know the laws that govern them. These laws govern them by the command of their Creator. This is why within the Islamic system there is a kind of harmony found between a human being and the universe surrounding him. Thus the code of Shari'ah, which organizes human life, possesses a cosmic character, and this code does not deal only with the human self, nor only with the human race, but it deals with living and non-living things and with the entire universe in which this living being lives, from which he cannot escape, and with which he must live joined in peace and harmony.

Moreover, it is the only system of life in which a person is completely freed from the servitude of all other human beings. In all systems of life other than Islam, humans are slaves of humans, and only in the Islamic system do all people emerge from servitude to all other people, and in it they are only servants of God, all of them.

As we have repeatedly stated before, one of the most important attributes of God is His sovereignty. And whoever makes laws for human beings himself takes this attribute exclusively for himself and becomes a claimant to a kind of divinity over those humans. Those people who accept him as the lawgiver become the servants of that man. They come out of the worship of God. These people are on that religion, not on the religion of God. When Islam entrusts the right of legislation exclusively to God, it excludes people from the servitude of all humans and brings them into the servitude of God alone. It proclaims human freedom; rather, Islam proclaims a new birth for humanity, such that a person's neck is not considered free as long as it is free from the rights of another human being, and as long as all these people do not stand on an equal level before the Lord of mankind.

The issue taken up in these verses is a very important and dangerous matter in Islamic belief and the Islamic view of life. It is a matter of divinity and servitude. It is a matter of justice and reform. It is a matter of freedom and equality. It is a matter of the freedom and new birth of all humanity. This is why it has been declared a matter of disbelief and faith, and it has been declared a matter of distinguishing between Islam and jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance).

Jahiliyyah is not the name of any one era. It is the name of a state which has certain basic constituent elements. Wherever its elements and essentials are found, jahiliyyah comes into existence there. The system and circumstances in which these elements are found will be a jahili system, and that condition will be called a state of jahiliyyah. Its backbone is that someone in legislation and governance becomes subservient to human desires and not subservient to the Islamic system and the Shari'ah of God. Whether these desires are the desires of an individual, or of a class, or of a single nation, or of the whole human race, because all these desires and all these people, as long as they are not subservient to the Shari'ah of God, will remain only carnal desires.

If an individual legislates for a society, this is jahiliyyah, because in that case his desire becomes the law. His opinion becomes the law, and if there is any difference in this regard, it is only in words. The reality is what we are saying.

Or if one class is legislating for all classes, this situation is also jahiliyyah. In this case, the interests of that class take the form of law, or the majority opinion of that class's parliament becomes law. In this case, if there is any difference, it is only in words.

Or again, if the right of legislation is granted to representatives of all classes and to all groups of the Ummah, this too is a jahili situation, because people's opinions are never free from personal desires. Then ignorance will also be included in this legislation, because people are never free from ignorance. Or if it is in the form of a referendum, the opinion of the majority of the whole nation becomes law. Even then, if there is any difference, it will only be in words.

On a still wider scale, if a collection of all nations legislates, that too will be jahiliyyah, because the national aims of those nations will take legal form, or the opinion formed by international assemblies will become law, and this system too will be jahili. If there is any difference, it will only be in words.

Now, if the Creator of all individuals, all societies, all nations and all generations legislates a law, this law will be for all people, and it will be the Shari'ah of God. In it, no one is harmed to benefit another. In it, specific matters concerning any individual, any society, any international body, or any entire human race are not taken into consideration, because God is Lord of all the worlds for everyone, and before Him everyone has equal standing. Furthermore, He knows well the welfare and interest of everyone, and all these matters are also free from excess and deficiency.

Now, if anyone else legislates, then certainly people will be slaves of that other, whoever that other may be, whether it is an individual, a society, a class, a nation, or an association of nations... But in God's legislation, all people become free and come to an equal level. Their foreheads do not bow before anyone except God. They do not worship anyone except God.

This is why this issue holds extreme importance in human life, and it also has importance within this very order of the universe.

Therefore, to judge according to other than God means corruption and mischief, and ultimately, because of it, a person goes out of the sphere of faith. Read the Quranic verses carefully. This is what the text demands.

"And He is All-Knowing and All-Seeing. So whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms himself, Allah will turn His gracious regard back to him. Allah is Most Forgiving and Most Merciful."

In these matters there is no plurality, no division, and these matters are not separate from one another. The affairs of people cannot be set right until the right of legislation and the system of reward and punishment, in both this world and the next, is concentrated in the one Divine Being. Lesson No. 49 at a glance:

This lesson takes up a most important issue of the Islamic worldview and the Islamic system of life. The Islamic system of government and Islamic life depend upon it. The matter has been mentioned repeatedly in Surah Al 'Imran and Surah An-Nisa, but here in this lesson it has been presented in a very clear and definitive form. Here the issue is not taken as an implication of the text (ishara al-nass), nor as an indication of the meaning of the verse (mafhum al-ayah), nor as a necessary implication (iqtida' al-nass). Here it is stated as the explicit expression of the text (ibarat al-nass) and in its definitive meaning (qat'i al-dalalah).

This issue concerns the system of government, the legal system and the judicial system, and upon its foundation depend the question of Tawhid, the question of divine sovereignty (hakimiyyah ilahiyyah), and whether a person's faith exists or not.

The question is: will our system of government, our legal system and our judicial system be in accordance with the commands of Allah, in accordance with the Shari'ah, and in accordance with the laws that have been preserved in the revealed religions, namely the Shari'ah of the earlier messengers and of this Messenger of the Last Age? Or will they be in accordance with our desires, our changing desires, or our interests and changing interests, which are not in accordance with the Shari'ah of Allah, or will they keep changing and being altered merely according to the customs of a particular era or a particular generation? Will sovereignty, lordship and governance over the lives of people and over this earth belong to Allah, or will some matters belong to Allah and some to other people?

The command of Allah is that there is no other god besides Him. He has sent down one Shari'ah for mankind, and this Shari'ah and law is in accordance with His sovereignty. He has taken a covenant from people that they will remain upon the Shari'ah of Allah, and that this Shari'ah will remain dominant on this earth. It is the obligation of people to run their courts in accordance with this same Shari'ah, and it is also the obligation of the prophets to act in accordance with it. After the prophets, it is likewise the obligation of rulers to give their judgments in accordance with it.

The command of Allah is that in this matter there is no falsehood and no self-rule. In this matter, deviation even in the smallest of the affairs of life is intolerable. If any whole generation in any era should frame a law against it, that law has no standing. Nor does any principle of a tribe or a nation have any standing against it, unless Allah has granted permission for something.

Allah says: here the question is either one of faith and disbelief, or of Islam and jahiliyyah, or it will be Shari'ah or base desire. In this matter there is no middle position, no leniency, and no compromise. The believers are those who judge in accordance with the law of Allah, and do not deviate from it even by a mustard seed, nor alter it by a single letter. The wrongdoers (zalimun), the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun) and the disbelievers (kafirun) are those who, in this matter, deviate and do not give judgments in accordance with the law of Allah, the Shari'ah. If rulers rule in accordance with the Shari'ah of Allah, they enter the circle of faith; but if they follow some other constitution, code or law for which Allah has given no permission, then they are disbelievers, defiantly disobedient and wrongdoers. People have only two paths: either they accept the judgments issued by rulers and judges in accordance with the law of Allah, and do so in all the affairs of their lives, in which case they are believers; or if they do not adopt this path, they are not believers. There is no third path between these two. In this matter no argumentation will avail, no excuse will be accepted, and no expediency will be accepted. Allah, in any case, is the Lord of mankind, and He alone knows where the true interest of people lies. Allah legislates for the genuine welfare of people, and therefore no law or order can be better than the Shari'ah and commands of Allah. None of the servants of Allah may say, "I do not accept the Shari'ah of Allah," or that he knows the interests of people better than Allah does. If anyone says or does such a thing with his tongue or his actions, he will be considered outside the circle of faith.

This is the great issue which has been stated in this lesson in a decisive manner. Besides this, this lesson also describes the conditions of the Jews who lived around Madinah, who together with the hypocrites were plotting against Islam and devising schemes.

(Verse) "Among those who say, 'We believe,' with their mouths, while their hearts have not believed" (5:41). It also describes the circumstances in which the Noble Messenger (ﷺ) was confronting these conspiracies, and which the Jews have not ceased from since the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) until today.

Several points emerge from the wording of the Qur'an in this lesson. The first conclusion is that all the revealed religions that Allah sent down had all their judgments made in accordance with the law of Allah. Within them the entire system of life was founded upon the Shari'ah of Allah. This fact was the dividing line between Islam and disbelief, the basis of distinction between Islam and jahiliyyah, and the foundation of separation between Shari'ah and the desires of the self, in that it determines who judges by the Shari'ah and who does not. The Torah too was sent down by Allah because in it there was guidance and light.

(Verse) "By it the prophets who submitted judged for those who followed Judaism, and so did the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah, and they were witnesses to it" (5:44).

Elsewhere: "And with them is the Torah, in which is the command of Allah" (5:43). And elsewhere it is said: "And We prescribed for them in it: a life for a life" (5:45). And to Jesus, son of Mary (peace be upon him), the Gospel was given:

"Confirming what was before it of the Torah, and as guidance and instruction for the God-fearing (46). And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein" (47) (5:46–47). Then Allah sent down the Qur'an to His final Prophet:

"In truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a overseer over it" (5:48). And the Prophet of the Last Age was commanded:

"So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, turning away from the truth that has come to you" (5:48). And then it was said: "Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, they are the defiantly disobedient" (5:47). And it was commanded: "Do they then seek the judgment of jahiliyyah? And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain?" (5:50).

From these verses it is clear that there has been complete agreement among all religions on this point. Thus the boundaries of Islam are defined, and the conditions of Islam are determined, for departments and courts as well as for rulers. The essential matter is that all judgments be made in accordance with the commands of Allah, and that the common people accept these judgments, and do not run after other laws and commands abandoning the Islamic law.

Within this framework this issue acquires great importance, and the reasons for emphasising it from this angle must necessarily also be of great importance. The question is: what are these reasons? Whether we seek these reasons within these texts or throughout the verses and passages of the whole Qur'an, these reasons are entirely clear to us.

The first of these reasons is that this is in essence the question of acknowledging Allah's divinity (uluhiyyah), His lordship (rububiyyah) and His sovereignty, and that no one shares with Him in these matters. If this is not so, then the issue becomes one of denying this. This is precisely why this matter becomes a matter of faith and disbelief. It is a matter of Islam and jahiliyyah: either there will be jahiliyyah or there will be Islam.

Look at the whole Qur'an. It is a showcase, yet wherever you look it presents for observation this one truth: that Allah alone is the Creator. He alone created this entire universe, He alone created this human being, and He alone subjected to this human being the heavens and the earth and all things found between them. Creation belongs to Allah alone and He has no partner in it, whether this creation be small or great, little or much. ... That Allah is the Owner, and He is the Owner because He is the Creator. He is the Owner of the earths, the heavens, and whatever is between them and the heavens and between the two. He is the Owner of the earths and the heavens and whatever is between them: He is the sole Owner and He has no partner in it. ... Then, Allah is the Provider. No other being can provide sustenance to human beings or other living creatures, neither less nor more.

And further, Allah is the Sovereign of this universe and has authority over it, and He has authority over people as well. Because He alone is the Creator, the Owner and the Provider, and He possesses such powers that without His perfect power there can be no creation, no provision, and no benefit or harm can come. His sovereignty is over this entire universe.

Now, what is faith? Acknowledgement of the matters mentioned above is faith: that in sovereignty, ownership and lordship Allah has no partner. These attributes belong to the Divine Being alone. Islam is in reality the name of submitting oneself, and Islam is obedience to Allah within the requirements of these attributes: that the right of divinity, lordship, governance and sovereignty belongs to the Divine Being alone over this entire universe, of which man is a part. Acknowledgement of Allah's decrees of qada and qadar and acknowledgement of the laws of His Shari'ah are included in this. Indeed, acknowledgement of the Shari'ah of Allah is in fact acknowledgement of Allah's divinity, lordship, and His sovereignty and guardianship. To not submit before this Shari'ah means first of all that we are denying Allah's divinity, lordship, and His sovereignty and governance, in the sense that someone judges all the minor matters of his life according to some other Shari'ah and law. Submitting to Islam or rejecting it, whether by tongue or by action, there is no difference between the two cases. This is why this matter is one of disbelief and faith, a matter of jahiliyyah and Islam, and for this reason this verse has come:

"Whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, they are the disbelievers" (5:44). And in other verses the words defiantly disobedient and wrongdoers have come.

"And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who have certainty?" (5:50)

If someone makes such a claim, he will be neither a believer nor a Muslim. Clearly, faith and Islam cannot be combined with such claims, even if someone outwardly claims faith and Islam with his tongue.
