Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 85:

Verse 85

God knew that their hearts were sincere and their tongues truthful. They were resolved to walk the straight path, and they were ready to discharge the duty of bearing witness to the truth for this religion into which they had entered. They entered the Islamic ranks with sincerity, and they regard the discharge of this witness to the truth as a favour of God which He bestows upon whomsoever He chooses among His servants. God knew that they now wished only to follow the Islamic path and hoped that God would include them among the righteous. Since all these matters were in God's knowledge, God accepted their words and wrote for them the reward of the Hereafter. He established His testimony upon them, that these people are righteous, and this is the reward of the doers of good (muhsinun):

"So Allah rewarded them, for what they said, with Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. And that is the reward of the doers of good." (5:85)

Ihsan (excellence, the highest degrees of faith and Islam) and God Himself bears witness that these people are among the group of the muhsinun. Therefore these verses concern a specific group whose features are entirely clear, and the ruling stated about such people is:

"And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe are those who say, 'We are Christians.'" (5:82)

This is a group that, when it hears the truth, does not rebel but accepts it from the depths of its heart and openly declares that acceptance. It is a party that does not hesitate for a moment in declaring its Islam; it immediately joins the Islamic ranks. It also becomes ready to discharge all the obligations imposed by this way of life, and it becomes ready to strive for the establishment of the Islamic system of life. Moreover, it is a party whose words God confirms, announcing that they are muhsinun and stating their reward.

However, the Qur'an does not rest content with this; it adds further to the features of this group and explains who those are who hold feelings of love toward the believers. This clarification is now made by mentioning, in contrast to this group of Christians, another group of Christians whose features are that, having heard the truth and understood it, they deny it. They do not respond to it with labbayk, and they do not join those who bear witness.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 5, verse 86 (part 1 of 2):

(Verse) No. 86.

Here, "those who disbelieve" (alladhina kafaru) refers definitively to those among the Christians who hear the truth but do not accept it. Concerning Christians who hear the truth and refuse to accept it, the Qur'an here uses the word kafirin (disbelievers), so whenever Christians adopt such a stance, the application of disbelief (kufr) to them holds. In this there is no distinction between Jews and Christians, and as long as they do not accept the speech revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the true speech, there will be no difference between them and the polytheists (mushrikin) and Jews. As long as they remain deniers and do not enter Islam, this holds, because now with Allah the only religion accepted is the religion of Islam, and this theme has been repeated in several verses of the Majestic Qur'an.

"Lam yakuni alladhina kafaru min ahl al-kitab wal-mushrikina munfakkina hatta ta'tiyahumu al-bayyinah" (98:1): "Those who disbelieved from among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence."

"Inna alladhina kafaru min ahl al-kitab wal-mushrikina fi nar jahannama khalidina fiha ulaika hum sharr al-bariyyah" (98:6): "Indeed, those who disbelieved from among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. They are the worst of creatures."

"Laqad kafara alladhina qalu inna Allaha thalithu thalatha" (5:73): "Certainly they have disbelieved who say that Allah is the third of three."

"Laqad kafara alladhina qalu inna Allaha huwa al-Masihu ibnu Maryam" (5:72): "Certainly they have disbelieved who say that Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary."

"Lu'ina alladhina kafaru min Bani Isra'il 'ala lisani Dawuda wa 'Isa ibni Maryam" (5:78): "Those among the Children of Israel who adopted the path of disbelief were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary."

In short, this is a general mode of expression of the Qur'an, and this matter is known in the mind. But what is being discussed here concerns the attitude of two groups among the Christians; the real purpose is to show that the stance of two groups among the Christians regarding Islam and the people of Islam is entirely different, and therefore their outcome will also be different. For one group, who believe, there will be gardens beneath which rivers flow, and the others' outcome will be that they are people of Hell. From this discussion it becomes clear that all those who call themselves Christians are not included in the verse which says:

"Wa latajidanna aqrabahum mawaddatan lilladhina amanu" ("You will find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe"). The meaning of these verses is taken by those who read each verse in isolation. The summary is that the ruling of the verse under discussion is limited, and by it are specifically meant those who believe. The Qur'an has clearly explained these people and left no misunderstanding; it has set out both groups distinctly.

Apart from the Qur'an, many narrations have also come in explanation and confirmation of this meaning, from which it is known that the verse refers to certain specific Christians.

Qurtubi has written in his tafsir: "This verse concerns Najashi and his companions, and it was revealed when Muslims migrated to Abyssinia in the first hijrah, as Ibn Ishaq and other biographers have written. These people went out of fear and persecution by the polytheists, and they were in large numbers. Afterward, when the Prophet migrated to Madinah, these people could not come to Madinah to migrate, because wars made conditions such that they could not meet the Messenger. When the Battle of Badr took place and great leaders of the disbelievers were killed, the people of Quraysh said: 'We can take revenge on those who have gone to Abyssinia; therefore send two wise men to Najashi with instructions, and Najashi will hand these people over to you, and you will be able to kill them and avenge the people of Badr.' The people of Quraysh sent 'Amr ibn al-'As and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah with gifts. News of these reached the Messenger. He sent 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri as an envoy and gave him a letter. He met Najashi, who read the blessed letter of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then he called Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the Muhajirun, and also called his scholars and poor, and ordered Ja'far to recite the Qur'an before them. He recited Surah Maryam. These scholars and elders rose with tears flowing from their eyes. These are the people concerning whom this verse was revealed:

"Wa latajidanna aqrabahum mawaddatan lilladhina amanu alladhina qalu inna nasara" ("You will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say: We are Christians"). They recited this verse up to 'al-shahidin' (the witnesses). (This hadith was narrated by Abu Dawud from Muhammad ibn Muslimah, Ibn Wahb, Yunus, Ibn Shihab, who related from Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, beginning the hadith with the account of the first migration to Abyssinia.)

Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Ishaq that twenty persons came to the Messenger. At that time he was in Makkah or near Makkah. This was when news about him had reached Abyssinia. These people were Christians. They met the Messenger in the mosque; questions and answers took place while the people of Quraysh sat in gatherings around the Ka'bah. When their questions were finished and they had asked whatever they wished, the Messenger invited them and recited the Majestic Qur'an to them. When they heard the Qur'an, tears flowed from their eyes. They accepted his call and affirmed him. They recognised the Messenger (ﷺ) in light of the prophecies that were in their books.

When these people rose to leave, Abu Jahl and some people of Quraysh interfered. Abu Jahl said: "No one is as foolish as you. Your people sent you so that you would return and bring them information about this man, but in a few minutes of conversation you have abandoned your religion and affirmed him. I have never seen a more foolish traveller than you," or he said something similar. They said: "Peace be upon you; we do not treat you with ignorant conduct. Our deeds are ours and your deeds are yours. We do not deprive ourselves of goodness."

It is said that these people were from the people of Najran, and it is also said that these verses were revealed concerning them.

Regarding the verses "Alladhina atainahumu al-kitaba min qablihi hum bihi yu'minun ... la nabtaghi al-jahilin" (28:52–55), it is also said that Ja'far and his companions, seventy persons, came to meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). These people were wearing woollen garments. Of them, sixty-two were from Abyssinia and eight were Syrians. Among the Syrians were Bahira the monk, Idris, Ashraf, Abraha, Thamamah, Qathm, Durayd and Ayman. The Messenger (ﷺ) recited Surah Ya-Sin before them. When they heard the Qur'an they wept greatly and believed in the Messenger (ﷺ). They said: "This speech is just like that which was revealed to 'Isa (peace be upon him)." This verse was revealed concerning these people:

"Latajidanna ashadda al-nasi 'adawatan lilladhina amanu al-yahuda wal-ladhina ashraku, wa latajidanna aqrabahum mawaddatan lilladhina amanu alladhina qalu inna nasara" (5:82): "You will find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and the polytheists, and you will find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe, those who say: We are Christians."

This refers to the delegation from Abyssinia, and these people were leaders of the Christians. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said that this verse was revealed concerning them: "Alladhina atainahumu al-kitaba min qablihi hum bihi yu'minun ... ula'ika yu'tawna ajrahum marratayn" (up to the end of the verse, "they will be given their reward twice").

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said that forty of these people were from the tribe of Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b of Najran, thirty-two were from Abyssinia, and sixty-eight were Syrians. Qatadah said that this verse was revealed concerning those who adhered to the true law of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and when the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent, they believed in him. Upon this, Allah praised them.

I say that what Qatadah said is the meaning of this verse, and the context of the speech also indicates it. All the narrations mentioned above confirm it, and this meaning also agrees with other verses in this surah and with other explicit statements of the Qur'an. This meaning also accords with the stance which the Jews and Christians adopted against the people of Islam and against Islam itself. Moreover, this meaning also fits the kind of attitude they have adopted against Islam in the past 1400 years.

This surah is a unity in its tendency, atmosphere and purposes. Contradiction is impossible in the speech of Allah: "Wa law kana min 'indi ghayri Allahi lawajadu fihi ikhtilafan kathira" (4:82): "Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy." Within this surah itself there are also some judgments and verses which fully clarify the explanation of this verse.

"Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu la tattakhidhu al-yahuda wal-nasara awliya'a ba'duhum awliya'u ba'din, wa man yatawallahum minkum fa innahu minhum, inna Allaha la yahdi al-qawm al-zalimin" (5:51): "O you who believe, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies; they are allies of one another. Whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is indeed one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

"Qul ya ahl al-kitabi lastum 'ala shay'in hatta tuqimu al-Tawrata wal-Injila wa ma unzila ilaykum min rabbikum, wa la yazidanna kathiran minhum ma unzila ilayka min rabbika tughyanan wa kufran, fa la ta'sa 'ala al-qawm al-kafirin" (5:68): "Say: O People of the Book, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord. What has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief, so do not grieve over the disbelieving people."

Similarly, in Surah al-Baqarah it was said earlier:

"Wa lan tarda 'anka al-yahudu wa la al-nasara hatta tattabi'a millatahum. Qul inna huda Allahi huwa al-huda, wa la'in ittaba'ta ahwa'ahum ba'da alladhi ja'aka mina al-'ilmi, ma laka mina Allahi min waliyyin wa la nasir" (2:120): "The Jews and Christians will never be pleased with you until you follow their religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance. And if you followed their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have no protector or helper against Allah."

The history after these verses, in which Allah warned the Muslim community, confirms that both Jews and Christians never forgave the people of Islam. History has recorded the hostility of the Jews against Islam from the time Islam entered Madinah Tayyibah, and from then until today their record continues without interruption: they have been engaged in conspiracies against Islam. They have never suspended these wicked activities in any era. History has also recorded that since the clash between the Muslims and the Christians at the Battle of Yarmuk, the Christians too have continued their Crusades against Islam without cease, except for the few exceptional incidents mentioned in these verses, and except for certain Christian sects which, weary of the mischief of other Christian sects, entered the boundaries of Islam. As for the general attitude of the Christians, its true picture is seen in the Crusades. Let it be remembered that the Crusade has not ended; it continues to this day. Since the confrontation of Islam and Christianity at the field of Yarmuk, this war has continued, although apparently there is sometimes a semblance of peace.

The extent of Christian hatred and enmity towards Islam was manifested over two centuries, that is, during the famous Crusades; and this mentality is also shown by the campaign of eradication which the Christians pursued against Muslims in al-Andalus. Their colonialism and the campaign of missionary Christianity were carried out in Islamic Africa, and afterwards this colonialism and missionary Christianity were spread across the entire Islamic world.

In the war against Islam, Judaism and Christianity remained allies, although the two sects were also enemies of each other; yet in all wars against Islam they were also friends of one another. As Allah, the All-Knowing and All-Aware, said 1400 years ago: "Ba'duhum awliya'u ba'din" ("They are allies of one another"). Their friendship remained in place until they abolished the Islamic Caliphate. After that, they kept tearing out every single thread of this religion, and when they had ended the Islamic system of government, they are now bent on abolishing prayer, the foundation of Islam.

Now, in the modern age, look: the stance which the Jews adopted against Muslims, preferring the polytheists to the people of Islam, has now been proven. Now world Christianity stands behind all those idolatrous nations, provided they are fighting against Islam. Sometimes these people give support, and sometimes they directly support idolaters against Muslims in international bodies. They played exactly this role in the Kashmir issue existing between Pakistan and India.

Furthermore, these Jews and Christians cooperate with one another in uprooting all movements for the revival of Islam. They have raised up in the Muslim world so-called great leaders who, in accordance with their will and desires, are bent on eradicating Islam in their respective countries. These world powers have gathered around dwarf leaders, shouting slogans of "Long live!" This clamour has made these people into great leaders, whereas these people are extremely dwarfish in stature.

This is the summary of the record which Islamic history has written over the past fourteen hundred years, and in it the position of the Jews and Christians has been one of opposition to Islam; there is no increase or decrease in the enmity of the two. Their camps cannot be distinguished from one another, and their continuous war against the Islamic movement never diminishes. An age has passed, and no change has occurred in this situation.

This is the situation which those who understand should comprehend, and they should not run after the movements being driven by deluded people, whose aim is to melt away Islamic firmness and steadfastness. These movements derive support for the destruction of Islam from this verse, and they do so by detaching its meaning from other verses and by ignoring them, extracting the meaning that suits their purpose. In determining the meaning of this verse, these people neither look at the subject matter of the whole surah, nor benefit from the other explicit statements of the Holy Qur'an, nor do they cast a glance at Islamic history in this regard. In this way they wish to lull the consciousness of the believers to sleep, so that they become insensitive and careless in the face of these camps. Their hearts are full of malice and enmity towards Islam, and they are constantly engaged in conspiracies against the Muslim world. Through this cultural onslaught they wish to deliver their final blow to the Islamic conception of life.

What these enemy camps of Islam fear greatly is that the understanding, comprehension, consciousness and sense of the Muslims regarding the true religion should grow, even if this awareness is found among only a small number. Among those who are the worst enemies of this consciousness and awakening of the Muslims, some are deluded and have fallen into the snares of the enemies of Islam. These deluded people, despite being Muslims, are no less dangerous than the open enemies of Islam; rather, they can be more harmful to Islam and to the movement for its revival. Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most firm and upright. The Qur'an never contradicts itself. We must study the Qur'an with religious insight.

Lesson No. 53 at a Glance:
This entire lesson takes up one single issue. Although the topics are different, all of them revolve around one axis. The issue is that in the Islamic system of life, the question of legislation belongs to the Divine Being, and the right to determine the limits and bounds of the lawful and the unlawful belongs to Allah alone. It is Allah who can make decisions of permissibility and impermissibility. It is Allah who can decide that this is His command and this is His prohibition. On the basis of this fundamental principle, all matters, great and small, are equal, so the solution to all affairs of life must conform to this principle.

Whoever among mankind claims for himself the right of legislation and exercises that right is in error. According to the Islamic outlook, this right belongs to Allah alone. If someone does not acknowledge this right of Allah, he in effect challenges Allah's divinity and His sovereignty, and Allah does not approve of such encroachers. Whoever legislates according to people's customs, their terminology and their sayings, rebels against the word of Allah, and in this way he goes outside the circle of faith and the bounds of Islam, and he does not remain in the religion of Islam. All the sentences of this lesson begin with (O you who believe), such as:

(Verse) "O you who believe, do not make unlawful the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress..." (87)

(Verse) "O you who believe, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars and divining arrows are only an abomination of Satan's handiwork, so avoid it..." (90)

(Verse) "O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made known to you, would trouble you... O you who believe, upon you is your own self; no one who has strayed can harm you if you are guided... O you who believe, let there be testimony between you when death approaches a person and he makes a bequest, two just men from among you, or two others from other than you..." (5:106)

Since the subject of this lesson is the issue of legislation, the address with these words here holds great importance in this context, and a specific indication is intended in it. The aim is that this issue is connected with divinity, sovereignty, faith and religion. Believers are addressed by their attribute of faith, because it is the demand of faith that the divinity and sovereignty of Allah be acknowledged. Through this address it is intended to impress upon the minds of Muslims the first principle and lesson of Islam and religion. In this context, it is commanded that people obey Allah and the Messenger of Allah, and not turn away from obedience to Allah and the Messenger of Allah, otherwise they will face a severe punishment; whoever obeys will deserve a very great reward in the Hereafter.

After this, keeping in view the attribute of faith, a command is given: there shall be complete separation between the people of faith and the people of disbelief, because the people of disbelief do not accept the method of the people of faith. The method of the people of faith is that in matters great and small they grant the right of legislation to Allah, and do not encroach upon Allah's right of sovereignty.

(Verse) "O you who believe, upon you is your own self; no one who has strayed can harm you if you are guided. To Allah you will all return..." (5:105)

"O you who believe, look after yourselves; the straying of others cannot harm you if you are on the right path. To Allah you all return, and He will then inform you of what you used to do." The people of faith are one nation, whose religion is their own, whose Shari'ah is their own, and whose sources of Shari'ah are their own, and it does not derive law from any other source. If this nation clearly declares this position to all nations and communities, and they still go astray, there is no blame upon it; if it maintains complete separation from them and leaves them to their ignorance and misguidance, then all will return to Allah.

This is the core of this entire lesson. As for the topics within this lesson, which revolve within this circle, they are various. Now, within this general circle, we shall take up these topics in somewhat more detail.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 87–89 (part 1 of 2)

Lesson 53

Explanation of the verses 87 to 108

Verses 87 to 89

"O you who believe! The demand of your faith is that, being human beings and servants of Allah, you should not try to lay hands on the rights of Allah's divinity and sovereignty. Therefore it is not permissible for you to declare unlawful (haram) the things and acts that Allah has made lawful (halal), especially the pure things. So do not abstain from eating and drinking pure things in such a way that you make them unlawful for yourselves, because Allah created these pure things for you alone, and moreover, it is Allah alone who determines the limits of the lawful and the unlawful."

﴿O you who believe! Do not make unlawful the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾ (87) ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you as lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you believe.﴾ (88) A

"The truth is that the question of legislation is directly connected with the specific matter of sovereignty and divinity. The right of legislation is restricted to Allah's sovereignty because Allah is the owner and creator of human beings, and it is He who provides sustenance to human beings. Therefore this right belongs to Allah alone, that for His creation, out of the sustenance He has produced, He may make some things lawful and some things unlawful. This is an argument that human reason accepts with great ease. Among human beings too, only the owner of a thing has the right to deal with his property as he wishes, and whoever interferes with another's right of ownership is regarded as having committed injustice and oppression. As for those who have already believed, it is obvious that it is not expected of them that they will encroach upon the rights of Allah, because how can faith in Allah and rebellion against Him be combined in one heart?

This is the matter that these two verses present in such a clear manner that no reasonable person can engage in debate or dispute about it, because Allah does not like those who encroach. This matter establishes a general rule and principle, that all people are the servants and slaves of Allah, and conforming one's conduct to this matter is a requirement of faith. In some narrations it is reported that these two verses, and the verse that follows them, were revealed in a particular incident. That incident occurred during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but the verse is general and is not restricted to the occasion of its revelation. Yes, it is a different matter that the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) provide good assistance in understanding the Quran.

Ibn Jarir has reported that one day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting, and he reminded the people. Then he got up and left, and on that day he did not frighten them much. Those of his companions who were sitting there said: 'Why should we not begin some sayings and practices of our own? The Christians did this, so they made some things unlawful for themselves. We too should make some things unlawful for ourselves.' Some said: 'He will not eat meat and fat.' Some said: 'He will not eat during the day.' Some made women unlawful for themselves. This matter reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'How strange people are! Some make women unlawful for themselves, some make food unlawful, some make sleep unlawful. Beware, I sleep and I stand up, I fast and I break my fast, I eat and I marry women. So whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.' Upon this these verses were revealed.

﴿O you who believe! Do not make unlawful the good things that Allah has made lawful for you…﴾ In the Sahihayn (Bukhari and Muslim), a narration from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) is recorded, which also supports the narration of Ibn Jarir. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said that three persons came to the houses of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked about the worship of the Prophet (ﷺ). When they were informed about the worship of the Prophet (ﷺ), they seemed to consider those acts of worship as insufficient. They said: 'When can we reach the status of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Allah has forgiven all his past and future sins.' One said: 'As for me, I will pray all night.' Another said: 'As for me, I will fast forever and will never break the fast.' The third said: 'As for me, I will never approach women and will not marry.' When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to know of this, he came to them and asked them: 'Are you the people who said such and such? By Allah, I am the most fearful of Allah among you and the most God-conscious of you, but I fast and I also break my fast, I pray and I also sleep, and I marry women. So whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.'

Tirmidhi, with his chain of narration, has reported from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Messenger of Allah, when I eat meat, desire overcomes me and I rise for women, so I have made meat unlawful for myself.' Upon this this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe! Do not make unlawful the good things that Allah has made lawful for you…﴾

Now the verse that mentions oaths, and which comes after these two verses, also gives guidance in similar circumstances:

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is vain in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have intentionally sworn. Its expiation is feeding ten needy persons with the average of what you feed your own families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be grateful.﴾ (89) You will not be held accountable by Allah for the idle oaths that you carelessly utter, but He will certainly hold you accountable for the oaths that you swear deliberately. (The expiation for breaking such an oath is) feeding ten needy persons with the average food that you give to your own families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. And one who cannot afford this should fast for three days. This is the expiation of your oaths when you swear and break them. Guard your oaths. In this way Allah makes His commandments clear to you, so that perhaps you will be grateful.

This verse is for circumstances in which someone takes an oath against using permissible things, for example, the three persons who had sworn that they would not do such and such acts, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had forbidden them from continuing with their oath. The Quran also prevented them from making lawful and unlawful for themselves on their own authority. This is not their task. It is the task of that Allah in whom they believe. In this way it is guidance for all those situations in which someone restrains himself from a good deed by means of an oath. This is because the principle is that if someone swears not to do a good deed, he should continue with that good deed and pay the expiation for breaking the oath, the details of which are given in this verse.

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the reason for the revelation of this verse was that those who had made some foods, some clothing and marriage with women unlawful for themselves had also sworn oaths on this. When the verse ﴿Do not make unlawful the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ was revealed, they asked: 'What will become of our oaths?' Upon this this verse was revealed. The ruling is that Allah does not hold the believers accountable for idle oaths. That is, when the word of oath merely passes the tongue, but there is no firm intention from the heart. However, the command from Allah is that one should not swear by Allah on every matter without reason, because there should be some respect for the oath of Allah. The oath of Allah should have dignity, so swearing idle oaths repeatedly is also disliked. As for the true oath that is sworn deliberately, and behind which there is a firm intention to do or not to do something, it is not excused as idle. For it, expiation is obligatory, and this verse explains exactly that: ﴿The expiation for true oaths is feeding ten needy persons with the average food, or clothing them, or freeing a slave, and whoever does not have the means should fast for three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you break them.﴾

Feeding ten needy persons with average food means food of the kind that the one who swears gives to his own family. The meaning of "average" (awsat) can be both "best" (ahsan) and "middling" (mutawassit), because the word awsat is used in both senses. Both meanings can be intended by "average," because in the standard of Islam the average is itself the best.

"(Aw kiswatuhum)" means that ten needy persons should be given clothing of average quality, or a slave should be freed. Here it is not specified that the slave must be a believer. For this reason the jurists (fuqaha) have differed in opinion on this. We in Fi Zilal al-Quran do not mention the differences of the jurists in matters of fiqh. If one is unable, then he should fast for three days. This applies in the case where none of the other stated expiations can be performed. Likewise, whether these three days must be consecutive or need not be consecutive, the jurists have also differed on this, because the requirement of consecutiveness (mutatabi'at) is not specified here. In our method in Fi Zilal al-Quran, it is not possible to go into the details of fiqh. If someone is interested, he should search in the books of fiqh. All the differences in fiqh accept the principle that this expiation is imposed because the swearer has broken a firm commitment. Secondly, that oaths should not be taken lightly, because oaths are in fact a kind of covenant, and Allah's command is that contracts and covenants should be fulfilled. And if the situation is that someone swears an oath and the thing he has sworn about is a good deed, then it is obligatory upon him to break the oath and continue with the good deed. And if he has taken an oath in which he has no right, for example, to make something lawful or unlawful, then it is obligatory upon him to break that oath and pay the expiation.

Now we come to the original subject for which these verses were revealed. Viewed from the perspective of the occasions of revelation of these verses, Allah explains that the things He has declared lawful are good, and that the things He has declared unlawful, know that they are impure and filthy. Man does not have the right to adopt for himself what Allah has not adopted for him, and there are two reasons for this.

The first is that laying down the boundaries of the lawful and the unlawful is among the special rights of Allah, who is the Provider. When He is the Provider, then declaring things unlawful or lawful within that provision is also His task. If someone does not accept this right of Allah, then he is in effect encroaching upon the rights of Allah. Allah does not like this, and faith cannot be correct in this way. The second reason is that Allah has declared the good things lawful, so no one is permitted to make pure things unlawful for himself, because those things are beneficial both for that person and for the continuation of life on this earth.

The thinking and insight of man cannot reach to where the insight of the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, reaches, who has declared these good things lawful. If there were some harm in these good things, Allah would certainly have protected His servants from them. If there were some benefit in declaring them unlawful, Allah would not have made them lawful. This religion has come precisely so that goodness, welfare and betterment may be brought into effect, and so that complete harmony and balance may be established among all the powers of humanity. Islam is not heedless of any of the needs of the human nature, nor has it left any of the constructive powers of man neglected. Islam has adopted the middle path and moves along the straight way. This is why Islam fought against monasticism (rahbaniyyah), because the purpose of monasticism was the suppression of nature. It was blocking the growth of life, whereas Allah's plan was that life on this earth should flourish. Islam forbade making good things unlawful because good things are a cause of the progress of life, through which life is renewed continually in this world. Allah created this life so that it would continue without interruption, and that it would be renewed according to the system of life established by Allah. Monasticism, which declares good things unlawful, is in conflict with the scheme of the Islamic system of life. Monasticism stops humanity at a fixed point, and it creates this obstruction in the name of loftiness and elevation, whereas loftiness and grandeur are included within the system of life, which is a system in which the motivations of human nature are fully present, and which has been arranged in accordance with the knowledge of Allah.

The specific circumstances of the revelation of a verse do not confine that verse to those circumstances. The verse remains general in any case, and this generality of the verse shows that the authority to define the limits of the lawful and the unlawful in legislation also belongs to Allah alone, and this matter is not restricted to food and drink, nor is it restricted to marriage. In all matters of life, this right belongs to Allah, and to the Shariah.

We are stressing this meaning again and again because a long time has passed in which people have removed Islam from the practical current of life, although Islam's character is that it should govern the whole of life. The words halal and haram and their scope have been restricted, and now they are not taken in the meaning that the Qur'an intended. Lesson 53

Explanation of the verses 87 to 108

This is an argument that human reason accepts with great ease. Among human beings too, only the owner of a thing has the right to deal with his property as he wishes, and whoever interferes with another's right of ownership is regarded as having committed injustice and oppression. This is the matter that these two verses present in such a clear manner that no reasonable person can engage in debate or dispute about it, because Allah does not like those who encroach. This matter establishes a general rule and principle, that all people are the servants and slaves of Allah, and conforming one's conduct to this matter is a requirement of faith. In some narrations it is reported that these two verses, and the verse that follows them, were revealed in a particular incident. That incident occurred during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but the verse is general and is not restricted to the occasion of its revelation. Yes, it is a different matter that the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) provide good assistance in understanding the Quran.

Those of his companions who were sitting there said: 'Why should we not begin some sayings and practices of our own? The Christians did this, so they made some things unlawful for themselves. We too should make some things unlawful for ourselves.' Some said: 'He will not eat meat and fat.' Some said: 'He will not eat during the day.' Some made women unlawful for themselves. This matter reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'How strange people are! Some make women unlawful for themselves, some make food unlawful, some make sleep unlawful. Beware, I sleep and I stand up, I fast and I break my fast, I eat and I marry women. So whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.' Upon this these verses were revealed.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to know of this, he came to them and asked them: 'Are you the people who said such and such? However, the command from Allah is that one should not swear by Allah on every matter without reason, because there should be some respect for the oath of Allah. The oath of Allah should have dignity, so swearing idle oaths repeatedly is also disliked. As for the true oath that is sworn deliberately, and behind which there is a firm intention to do or not to do something, it is not excused as idle. Both meanings can be intended by "average," because in the standard of Islam the average is itself the best.

If there were some benefit in declaring them unlawful, Allah would not have made them lawful. This religion has come precisely so that goodness, welfare and betterment may be brought into effect, and so that complete harmony and balance may be established among all the powers of humanity. Verses 90–93

Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones and divining arrows were among the greatest marks of Jahili society, and these were habits that were very widespread within it. All of these habits were in fact a single social whole; they were interconnected and were the identifying features of Jahili society. The people of Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) consumed wine in large quantities, and in this they tried to outdo one another and took pride in it. The subject of their boastful tales and boastful poetry was often excessive wine-drinking. Alongside wine gatherings, it was also essential to slaughter animals and to serve kebabs and skewered meat with the wine. In this, both drinkers and servers took part, and in this way such gatherings had something of interest for everyone. They would perform these slaughters in the names of idols and at their shrines, and would splash the blood of these sacrifices upon the idols. Besides this, they would also slaughter certain animals in the names of their gods and soothsayers. The meat of the animals slaughtered during drinking sessions and on other occasions they would then distribute by means of arrows (divining arrows). Each person would take the portion of meat assigned by his arrow; whoever's arrow came out higher had a larger share. In this manner the meat was distributed, and in this manner the meat was distributed, until at times the person who had slaughtered the animal received nothing at all and was left in complete loss.

From these events it becomes clear that their customs and habits were interconnected and related, and these habits continued along Jahili lines. The Islamic system of life did not begin its movement by reforming these customs, because these customs and habits were founded upon certain corrupt ideological conceptions. If merely a superficial movement for the reform of customs had been started, and the root doctrinal beliefs had not been uprooted, this work would have been extremely superficial. It was by no means to be expected of Islam that it would leave the roots and limit itself to superficial matters. Islam first addressed the first knot of the human soul, namely beliefs and ideas. It first took the Jahili beliefs and conceptions, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam took their notions concerning many gods, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam exposed the corruption of their notions concerning many gods, and brought them together upon belief in the one true God. When this doctrine of Tawhid (the oneness of God) overspread their hearts and minds, they became ready to think naturally about what their true God does not like. Before this doctrinal reform, how could they have been ready to abandon their customs and rituals? They were not prepared to give up their Jahili preferred ways without doctrinal change, even though they were repeatedly admonished. The knot of human nature is in reality the knot of belief. Until this knot and problem is first resolved, no moral teaching, no program of moral refinement, and no collective reformatory scheme can succeed. Doctrine is in truth the key to human nature. Until this key is applied and human nature is opened up, access to its inner chambers and to the depths of its ways and customs will not be possible. When we open one narrow lane, several more narrow lanes will appear before us, and if we illuminate one side, ten dark sides will appear. We open one knot and ten more knots will be tied. We open one path and ten paths will be closed, and in this way we will fall into such a labyrinth that no way out will be found.

This is the reason why the Islamic system of life did not begin its reforming work with the bad customs and filthy habits of Jahiliyyah. Islam first began its work with doctrinal reform. First the demand was made that you accept the good word (the testimony of faith, the Kalimah Tayyibah). The first thirteen years in Makkah were spent in this doctrinal reform and the correction of beliefs. In those long years the aim of the Islamic movement was none other than the testimony "There is no god but Allah." During this period people were introduced to the Lord of the worlds; they were invited only to His worship, and they were called only to His sovereignty, until their souls became purified exclusively for the One Lord. Their condition became such that they began to desire for themselves what their God desired for them. When doctrinal reform reached this degree, then obligations began, acts of worship became obligatory, and now the reform of the filthy habits and customs of Jahiliyyah began; commands for changing collective practices began to be issued, economic reforms were enforced, the reform of psychological and moral conduct began, and this work started at a time when, as soon as a command came from God, the Muslims received it at once, without any hesitation or objection, because they had surrendered all authority to command and forbid to the Lord of the worlds, and had no authority of their own.

In other words, we may say that the enjoining of commands and prohibitions began after the stage at which people had bowed in complete submission. Every Muslim had surrendered everything to Allah, and acknowledged that before the commands and prohibitions of Allah he had no authority of his own, as Ustad Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi has said in his book Alam-e-Islam in the conflict between Eastern and Western outlooks, where he says:

"The great knot of disbelief and polytheism was untied. Certainly it was a great knot. With its untying, all the knots were untied. The Messenger ﷺ waged this first jihad against them, and therefore they had no further need of any jihad. For every command and every prohibition, he (ﷺ) had to make no further struggle. In this first doctrinal battle Islam was granted victory over Jahiliyyah, and after that success attended him in every battle. This happened because these people had entered fully into Islam with their hearts, their souls and their limbs. When guidance was revealed to them they did not oppose or contend with the Messenger ﷺ. Whatever decision the Messenger ﷺ made, they found no uneasiness in their hearts about it, and after the decision of the matter they had no choice or sphere of choice left for themselves. When something occurred among them in their affairs that was contrary to conscience and belief, they openly informed the Messenger ﷺ and presented themselves for punishment. When they committed a fault, the prescribed penalty was enforced upon them. When the command for the prohibition of wine came, cups full of wine were in their hands and the command of Allah intervened, and they did not bring them to their lips. Their lips remained dry and their livers thirsty. The wine jars were broken, and wine flowed through the streets of Madinah like a flood."

Yet despite this, the prohibition of wine and of the other things along with it was not a sudden matter. Before this final prohibition, the treatment of this widespread and very deep-rooted sickness was carried out with great gradualness, because the people were addicted to it, and it was for them an extremely habit-forming intoxication. Their social and economic interests were also tied up with it.

The final prohibition of wine was revealed in the third or fourth stage. In the first stage a single arrow was merely shot in the direction toward which the Islamic system was inclined. In a verse of Surah an-Nahl it was said:

"And from the fruits of the date-palm and the grapes, from which you derive intoxicant and good provision." (16:67) — "from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes, from which you obtain wine and goodly sustenance."

Here intoxicant (sakar), that is, intoxicating things, was placed in contrast with goodly provision, and by this the intended indication was that intoxicating things do not fall within the definition of goodly provision. As if intoxicating things are one thing and goodly provision is another. After that, in Surah al-Baqarah, the religious conscience of the Muslims was awakened against wine through a legal and logical argument:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219)

In this verse it was indicated that when their sin is greater, then setting aside the small benefit and abandoning them is the better course, because everything has some benefit. However, lawfulness and unlawfulness depend upon the majority; the predominance of gain or loss is looked at.

The third measure taken was that the time spent on the habit of wine-drinking was reduced, and wine-drinking was declared incompatible with the state of prayer. The following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying." (4:43) — "O you who have believed, do not approach prayer when you are in a state of intoxication until you know what you say."

Now, since the five daily prayers are mostly very close to one another, and there is not so much interval between them that someone who drinks wine would sober up again, therefore during those times the actual possibility of drinking wine no longer remained, and the scope for this act became narrow. Especially the morning wine (sabuh) and the evening wine (ghabuq), that is, the wine after Asr and after Maghrib, had their times narrowed, because in the age of Jahiliyyah wine was drunk precisely at these times. Through this scheme the Shariah broke the craving at the times of intoxication. For a Muslim this proved to be an excellent measure, because at that time it could not even be imagined that a Muslim would leave prayer and drink wine. At that time every Muslim performed his prayer at its appointed time. In this way the grip of wine was broken. After this, the fourth and final measure was taken through this verse. Now the atmosphere was ready for this final blow; people's souls were ready; so the commands came, and people believed and carried them out at once.

Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he said: "O Allah, give us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Baqarah was revealed:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited to him, and upon this he again said: "O Allah, reveal for us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer when you are intoxicated, until you know what you say." (4:43) When this verse was recited to Hadrat Umar, he again asked: "O Allah, reveal a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed:

"Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?" (5:91) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited before him, and he said: "Yes, we have desisted, we have desisted." (Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan.)

When these verses were revealed after the Battle of Uhud in the third year of the Hijrah, no other measure was needed. A crier proclaimed in Madinah: "O people, wine has been made unlawful." On hearing this, whoever had a cup in his hand broke it, whoever had a mouthful spilled it out, the wine-skins were torn open, and the wine jars were smashed, and the situation became such that it was as though people had never seen intoxication and wine at all.

Now look at the construction of the verses of the Qur'an and at the method of education which the Qur'an adopted.

"O you who believe! Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows are only an abomination, of Satan's work. So avoid it, that you may prosper. Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist? And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)."

The opening and tone is the familiar address by which people are called by their beloved title, the believers: "O you who believe." Thus the faith of the Muslims is stirred, and they are given to understand that the requirement of their faith is full obedience to the commands that are coming. After this, the manner of expression comes in a very plain and emphatic style of restriction.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 90–93 (part 2 of 3):

(Verse) "Verily, intoxicants (khamr), gambling (maysir), idolatrous altars (ansab), and divining arrows (azlam) are an abomination, of Satan's handiwork." These are filthy, Satanic deeds, and the word "good" (tayyib) cannot be applied to them. Allah has made lawful only the good things. Moreover, these are Satanic acts, and Satan is man's ancient enemy. For a believer, it is enough to know that something is Satanic: upon hearing this, he recoils from it, his whole being trembles, and he flees from it in fear.

In such circumstances, a definitive prohibition is now issued, but together with this prohibition it is also stated that by abstaining from it you will attain success in the Hereafter. This is another glimpse, through which it is shown how the Qur'an penetrates to the depths of human psychology and implants its sentiments.

(Verse) "So avoid it completely, that you may prosper." Now it is explained what Satan wishes to achieve by continuing this filth: "Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to prevent you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer." ... This is Satan's actual plan, and these are the aims which he seeks to accomplish through these impurities and immoral acts. His purpose is that enmity and hatred spread among the ranks of the Muslims, and he seeks to achieve this through wine, kebab and gambling. His second aim is to prevent the people of faith from the remembrance of God and from prayer. What greater conspiracy could there be?

These Satanic aims which the Qur'an has stated are matters which Muslims can clearly observe in their own history, although the Qur'an is true in itself and needs no historical confirmation. This matter requires no debate or investigation. We see how this Satanic plan works. Drinking destroys a person's understanding and perception; loss of flesh and blood and the agitation of emotions and inclinations are its immediate effects; and the financial loss that people suffer through gambling gives rise to deep hatred and enmity, because in gambling, the loser sees the winner carrying away his wealth as spoils of war before his very eyes, while he is defeated and stripped of his wealth. These are matters from which the arising of hatred and enmity is a natural outcome, even though drunkards and gamblers appear outwardly as friends and companions, are seen cheerful and happy in the same gathering, and are close and firm companions of one another.

As for the second evil, that these two things prevent the remembrance of Allah and prevent prayer, these are matters which need no proof. Intoxicants stupefy, and whatever stupefies is intoxicating; and the bewilderment that overtakes a person in gambling is no less than the stupor of drinking. The world of the gambler and the world of the drinker are one and the same world, and it does not go beyond wine, kebab, goblets and flagons.

When the matter reaches this point, and it is made clear what the real aims of Satan are in spreading this filth, the heart of a believer awakens and his sensitivity is heightened. He becomes ready for a decisive step, and when the question is asked, "Will you now desist from it?", there is already prepared in the heart of every believer the same answer which 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) gave: "Yes, indeed, we have desisted, we have desisted."

Now the matter moves further forward, and a final blow is struck.

(Verse) "And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)." (92) "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies only the plain delivery (of the message)." This is the principle to which all matters return: obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is Islam. Within Islam there is no room for anything other than unconditional obedience to Allah and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If anyone turns away from obedience to Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he himself will bear the responsibility for its consequences.

(Verse) "...But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies no duty other than the plain conveyance (of the message)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed the message of Allah in a most excellent manner. After this clear declaration, the full responsibility fell upon those who oppose.

This is, by indirect means, a severe threat. The body of a believer trembles, because if the believers disobey and do not obey Allah and His Messenger, then they are in effect harming only themselves. The Messenger (ﷺ) has conveyed the message and discharged his duty well, and he is free of their affair; he has washed his hands of it. Now, if they deserve punishment, the Messenger cannot avert the punishment from them, especially since they disobeyed him and did not obey him, and Allah is fully capable of punishing the rebellious and the disobedient.

This is the Islamic method of reform, which descends into the hearts of human beings, knocks at the door of hearts, and opens the closed doors of hearts. After this, there then unfold upon it the most hidden paths and ups and downs.

It is appropriate here that we give some detail about the wine which has been declared unlawful here. Imam Abu Dawud, with his chain of narration, related from Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) the narration: "Every intoxicating thing is khamr, and every intoxicant is unlawful." 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) delivered a sermon from the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in that sermon a group of the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) was present: "O people, you know the time when the prohibition of wine was revealed. Wine is made from five things: from grapes, from dates, from honey, from wheat, and from barley; and the definition of wine is: that which covers the intellect."

From these two narrations it becomes known that everything which intoxicates falls within the definition of khamr. Khamr does not mean a particular kind of intoxicant; whatever beverage intoxicates is khamr.

The disappearance of a person's consciousness through any intoxicating thing is contrary to the constant wakefulness which Islam has made obligatory for every person. Islam's policy is that a person remain awake and continually connected with Allah. Every moment he should look toward Allah. Then, in that continuous state of wakefulness, he should be engaged in the progress and growth of this world, protect this life from weakness and corruption, and safeguard his self, his wealth and his honour. He should be a guardian of the security of the Muslim community, and of the Islamic Shari'ah and the Islamic system of life, so that no one can lay hands on it, because a Muslim individual cannot remain absorbed solely in himself and his pleasures. Obligations of this kind are placed upon him, for the fulfilment of which he must remain awake at all times. Some duties are upon him from his Lord; some duties are upon him from his own self; some duties are upon him from his family; some duties are upon him from the Islamic society in which he lives. After this, some obligations also fall upon him from all of humanity, so that he may extend the Islamic call to them and teach them the path of guidance. For this reason, Islam demands of him that he remain awake always and at every moment. Moreover, even when he is benefiting from pure things, Islam demands of him that he remain awake, remain self-respecting, and not become the slave or servant of pleasures and desires; he should keep his appetites and inclinations under restraint. He should not be the slave of his desires but their master and lord. Those who seek refuge in intoxication to withdraw from this world, it is evident that such people cannot perform any of the aforementioned duties.

Then, what is the reality of plunging oneself into the state of intoxication? For a time, the drug-user separates himself from the real world, and in a sense he takes the path of escape from real life. He seeks refuge in the world of imaginings which arise in the state of intoxication and stupor. Islam declares it unlawful for a person to wander in this kind of illusory world and fanciful notions. Islam wants people to confront realities, to live amid realities, and to direct their lives according to realities; their lives should not rest merely upon illusions and imaginings. When a person faces realities, he then discovers the condition of his resolve and will. As for the method of someone who escapes from realities and dwells merely in a life of imaginings and illusions, it is a defective and sick way of living. In such a state, resolve weakens and will dissolves. Islam attaches very great importance to the human will, and its policy is that his will be free and that there be no oppressive or dominating force over him. The aforementioned Islamic policies are by themselves sufficient for declaring all intoxicating things unlawful, because they are filthy and Satanic deeds, and they produce corruption and disorder in human life.

On this matter, there is a difference among the jurists as to whether wine is impure (najis) like all impurities, or not, and whether only drinking it is unlawful. The first view, that it is impure, is the view of the majority; and the second view is that of Rabi'ah, Layth, al-Muzani (a companion of Imam al-Shafi'i) and some later Baghdadi scholars. Enough mention of this suffices for us.

When this verse was revealed, declaring wine unlawful and stating that it is impure and a Satanic act, two questions arose within the Islamic community. First, some Companions of especially pure nature and great caution raised the question: what will become of our companions who died in circumstances when they used to drink wine? Others said: what will become of those who were martyred at Uhud and had wine in their stomachs? (At that time wine was not yet unlawful.)

Those who wished to create disorder and confusion in the ranks of Islam also expressed similar apprehensions. Their aim was to spread doubts and suspicions about Islam's legislation. These people would imply that those who had died earlier had lost their faith, since they had drunk wine, which is impure and among the Satanic acts. Some of them died with this impure substance present in their stomachs. In response to both kinds of apprehensions and objections, this verse was revealed:

(Verse) "There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they are mindful (of Allah), believe, and do righteous deeds, then remain mindful and believe, then remain mindful and do good. And Allah loves the good-doers." (93)

Those who believed and began to do righteous deeds will not be taken to account for what they ate and drank before, provided that in future they remain away from those things which have been forbidden, remain steadfast upon faith, do good deeds, then refrain from what they are forbidden, and obey the command of Allah; then they maintain good conduct with God-fearing piety. Allah loves those of good character.

In this verse, the decision is that what has not been prohibited is not unlawful; that prohibition applies after the command of Allah, not before; and that prohibition does not have retrospective effect, so no punishment will be inflicted until a text has been revealed, whether this punishment is a worldly punishment or a punishment in the Hereafter, because it is the word of Allah which brings things into being. Those who died while drinking wine, or who had wine in their stomachs at a time when it was not yet forbidden, will not be held to account, because they did not use anything unlawful, nor did they commit any disobedience. They were God-fearing, abstained from sins, did righteous deeds, and hoped from Allah for a good end; they were firmly convinced that Allah knows well their intentions and knows their deeds. How can those whose circumstances are such commit the forbidden, or how can they commit disobedience?

We do not wish to enter here into the debates that the Mu'tazilah conducted concerning this ruling. The Mu'tazilah discussed whether intoxicants are impure in their very essence, or whether impurity came to them through this verse of Allah. Likewise, they discussed whether the prohibition of all prohibited things is inherent in them, or whether prohibition attaches to them because of the ruling that was revealed. This is a fruitless discussion, and the Islamic consciousness does not accept this debate at all. For when Allah declares something prohibited, it is within Allah's knowledge why He is declaring it prohibited, whether Allah specifies the cause of the prohibition or does not specify it, whether the prohibition is because the cause lies in the very nature of the prohibited thing, or the cause of prohibition lies in the person who uses it, or the thing has been declared prohibited merely for the interests of society. The knowledge of all things belongs to Allah alone. Obedience to Allah's commands is obligatory, and after the commands have come, this type of discussion yields no result. The very temperament of the Islamic system of life is realistic, so the question does not even arise: if the prohibition was because of a cause that lay in the nature of the prohibited thing, then why was that thing lawful before the prohibition? For it is possible that in Allah's knowledge there was a wisdom due to which Allah did not declare it prohibited for a period of time. Everything is within Allah's authority. This is the demand of His sovereignty. It is not the case that if a person considers something good it is good, and if he considers it bad it is bad. Sometimes a person considers something to be the cause of a ruling when it is not the cause. The respectful way before Allah is that the command be heard, accepted and implemented, whether or not one understands its cause and wisdom. Whether the cause is apparent or hidden, it is Allah who knows it, and we do not know it.

The basis of acting upon the Islamic Shariah is on the principle of the servitude and slavery of Allah. Obedience to Allah is because we are the servants of Allah, and this is Islam in the sense of submitting oneself wholly. Understanding the wisdoms of the Shariah is a stage that comes after obedience: a wise person may try, according to his own understanding, to do this in all commands and prohibitions, whether those wisdoms are stated in the texts or not, and whether human reason can comprehend them or not. For the determination of whether the Islamic Shariah is realized or not is not decided by man. It is Allah who can decide this. When Allah has commanded or forbidden, obedience becomes binding. If Allah had made human reason the final arbiter regarding the Islamic Shariah, the status of human reason would have become higher than the Shariah; in that case, what difference would remain between the status of divinity and the status of servanthood?

Now let us discuss, from the standpoint of Arabic, the construction (structure) of this verse. In this verse, taqwa is repeated three times: "Ittaqu wa amanu wa 'amilu al-salihat," that is, taqwa, faith and righteous deeds. Then "ittaqu wa amanu," taqwa and faith only. Then "ittaqu wa ahsanu," taqwa and ihsan are mentioned. Why was taqwa repeated in this manner in this expression? No commentator's explanation has been satisfying in this regard. Likewise, in the first edition of Fi Zilal al-Quran, I myself could not offer a satisfying explanation, and until now no convincing point has come to my understanding.

Among the explanations of the commentaries, the best one I have found compared to others is that of Ibn Jarir, although it is not fully satisfying. He says:

"The first taqwa means that one accepts Allah's command with fear of God, affirms it, and acts upon it with piety. The second taqwa means that one remains steadfast upon it with fear of God, and the third is the fear of God through which nearness to Allah is attained by means of ihsan and voluntary acts."

What I had said in the first edition of this book was this:

"This is an emphasis by giving further detail. In the first sentence, faith, righteous deeds and taqwa are mentioned; in the second sentence, taqwa is mentioned with faith; and in the third, taqwa and ihsan, that is, righteous deeds, are mentioned. The purpose of this emphasis is that the matter of all affairs depends upon taqwa. The meaning is that the true value of deeds arises from the inner consciousness behind them, and this inner consciousness is taqwa, which is manifested through fear of God, and because of this consciousness a person remains constantly attached to the Being of Allah. Faith in Allah, affirmation of His commands and prohibitions, and righteous deeds which are the expression of this inner belief and hidden consciousness. There is a connection between this righteous deed and this inner consciousness. All this inner consciousness and taqwa is the real object sought, and the ruling depends upon them. The ruling does not depend upon the outward forms and appearances of deeds. The point that the real basis is intention, spirit and inner consciousness is such an important and fundamental matter that it needs to be repeated again and again."

Even now I am not fully satisfied with my own statement, but no other point has come to my understanding. Wallahu al-musta'an.

The discussion continues on the subject of lawful and unlawful. The matter under discussion is hunting while in the state of ihram. The expiation for killing game, the wisdom behind why Allah has made obligatory the respect of His House, the sacred months, the offerings (hady) and the garlanded animals, and why the beginning of this surah prohibits meddling with these things, are all being addressed. At the end, a general principle and standard is mentioned for the individual Muslim and for an Islamic society: a standard by which a pure thing has greater value even if it is little, and an impure thing has no value even if it is very abundant.

This is part 1 of 3 of the commentary on verses 90–93. The text below is translated as it stands.

Verses 90–93

Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones and divining arrows were among the greatest marks of Jahili society, and these were habits that were very widespread within it. All of these habits were in fact a single social whole; they were interconnected and were the identifying features of Jahili society. The people of Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) consumed wine in large quantities, and in this they tried to outdo one another and took pride in it. The subject of their boastful tales and boastful poetry was often excessive wine-drinking. Alongside wine gatherings, it was also essential to slaughter animals and to serve kebabs and skewered meat with the wine. In this, both drinkers and servers took part, and in this way such gatherings had something of interest for everyone. They would perform these slaughters in the names of idols and at their shrines, and would splash the blood of these sacrifices upon the idols. Besides this, they would also slaughter certain animals in the names of their gods and soothsayers. The meat of the animals slaughtered during drinking sessions and on other occasions they would then distribute by means of arrows (divining arrows). Each person would take the portion of meat assigned by his arrow; whoever's arrow came out higher had a larger share. In this manner the meat was distributed, and in this manner the meat was distributed, until at times the person who had slaughtered the animal received nothing at all and was left in complete loss.

From these events it becomes clear that their customs and habits were interconnected and related, and these habits continued along Jahili lines. The Islamic system of life did not begin its movement by reforming these customs, because these customs and habits were founded upon certain corrupt ideological conceptions. If merely a superficial movement for the reform of customs had been started, and the root doctrinal beliefs had not been uprooted, this work would have been extremely superficial. It was by no means to be expected of Islam that it would leave the roots and limit itself to superficial matters. Islam first addressed the first knot of the human soul, namely beliefs and ideas. It first took the Jahili beliefs and conceptions, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam took their notions concerning many gods, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam exposed the corruption of their notions concerning many gods, and brought them together upon belief in the one true God. When this doctrine of Tawhid (the oneness of God) overspread their hearts and minds, they became ready to think naturally about what their true God does not like. Before this doctrinal reform, how could they have been ready to abandon their customs and rituals? They were not prepared to give up their Jahili preferred ways without doctrinal change, even though they were repeatedly admonished. The knot of human nature is in reality the knot of belief. Until this knot and problem is first resolved, no moral teaching, no program of moral refinement, and no collective reformatory scheme can succeed. Doctrine is in truth the key to human nature. Until this key is applied and human nature is opened up, access to its inner chambers and to the depths of its ways and customs will not be possible. When we open one narrow lane, several more narrow lanes will appear before us, and if we illuminate one side, ten dark sides will appear. We open one knot and ten more knots will be tied. We open one path and ten paths will be closed, and in this way we will fall into such a labyrinth that no way out will be found.

This is the reason why the Islamic system of life did not begin its reforming work with the bad customs and filthy habits of Jahiliyyah. Islam first began its work with doctrinal reform. First the demand was made that you accept the good word (the testimony of faith, the Kalimah Tayyibah). The first thirteen years in Makkah were spent in this doctrinal reform and the correction of beliefs. In those long years the aim of the Islamic movement was none other than the testimony "There is no god but Allah." During this period people were introduced to the Lord of the worlds; they were invited only to His worship, and they were called only to His sovereignty, until their souls became purified exclusively for the One Lord. Their condition became such that they began to desire for themselves what their God desired for them. When doctrinal reform reached this degree, then obligations began, acts of worship became obligatory, and now the reform of the filthy habits and customs of Jahiliyyah began; commands for changing collective practices began to be issued, economic reforms were enforced, the reform of psychological and moral conduct began, and this work started at a time when, as soon as a command came from God, the Muslims received it at once, without any hesitation or objection, because they had surrendered all authority to command and forbid to the Lord of the worlds, and had no authority of their own.

In other words, we may say that the enjoining of commands and prohibitions began after the stage at which people had bowed in complete submission. Every Muslim had surrendered everything to Allah, and acknowledged that before the commands and prohibitions of Allah he had no authority of his own, as Ustad Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi has said in his book Alam-e-Islam in the conflict between Eastern and Western outlooks, where he says:

"The great knot of disbelief and polytheism was untied. Certainly it was a great knot. With its untying, all the knots were untied. The Messenger ﷺ waged this first jihad against them, and therefore they had no further need of any jihad. For every command and every prohibition, he (ﷺ) had to make no further struggle. In this first doctrinal battle Islam was granted victory over Jahiliyyah, and after that success attended him in every battle. This happened because these people had entered fully into Islam with their hearts, their souls and their limbs. When guidance was revealed to them they did not oppose or contend with the Messenger ﷺ. Whatever decision the Messenger ﷺ made, they found no uneasiness in their hearts about it, and after the decision of the matter they had no choice or sphere of choice left for themselves. When something occurred among them in their affairs that was contrary to conscience and belief, they openly informed the Messenger ﷺ and presented themselves for punishment. When they committed a fault, the prescribed penalty was enforced upon them. When the command for the prohibition of wine came, cups full of wine were in their hands and the command of Allah intervened, and they did not bring them to their lips. Their lips remained dry and their livers thirsty. The wine jars were broken, and wine flowed through the streets of Madinah like a flood."

Yet despite this, the prohibition of wine and of the other things along with it was not a sudden matter. Before this final prohibition, the treatment of this widespread and very deep-rooted sickness was carried out with great gradualness, because the people were addicted to it, and it was for them an extremely habit-forming intoxication. Their social and economic interests were also tied up with it.

The final prohibition of wine was revealed in the third or fourth stage. In the first stage a single arrow was merely shot in the direction toward which the Islamic system was inclined. In a verse of Surah an-Nahl it was said:

"And from the fruits of the date-palm and the grapes, from which you derive intoxicant and good provision." (16:67) — "from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes, from which you obtain wine and goodly sustenance."

Here intoxicant (sakar), that is, intoxicating things, was placed in contrast with goodly provision, and by this the intended indication was that intoxicating things do not fall within the definition of goodly provision. As if intoxicating things are one thing and goodly provision is another. After that, in Surah al-Baqarah, the religious conscience of the Muslims was awakened against wine through a legal and logical argument:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219)

In this verse it was indicated that when their sin is greater, then setting aside the small benefit and abandoning them is the better course, because everything has some benefit. However, lawfulness and unlawfulness depend upon the majority; the predominance of gain or loss is looked at.
