The third measure taken was that the time spent on the habit of wine-drinking was reduced, and wine-drinking was declared incompatible with the state of prayer. The following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying." (4:43) — "O you who have believed, do not approach prayer when you are in a state of intoxication until you know what you say."

Now, since the five daily prayers are mostly very close to one another, and there is not so much interval between them that someone who drinks wine would sober up again, therefore during those times the actual possibility of drinking wine no longer remained, and the scope for this act became narrow. Especially the morning wine (sabuh) and the evening wine (ghabuq), that is, the wine after Asr and after Maghrib, had their times narrowed, because in the age of Jahiliyyah wine was drunk precisely at these times. Through this scheme the Shariah broke the craving at the times of intoxication. For a Muslim this proved to be an excellent measure, because at that time it could not even be imagined that a Muslim would leave prayer and drink wine. At that time every Muslim performed his prayer at its appointed time. In this way the grip of wine was broken. After this, the fourth and final measure was taken through this verse. Now the atmosphere was ready for this final blow; people's souls were ready; so the commands came, and people believed and carried them out at once.

Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he said: "O Allah, give us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Baqarah was revealed:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited to him, and upon this he again said: "O Allah, reveal for us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer when you are intoxicated, until you know what you say." (4:43) When this verse was recited to Hadrat Umar, he again asked: "O Allah, reveal a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed:

"Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?" (5:91) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited before him, and he said: "Yes, we have desisted, we have desisted." (Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan.)

When these verses were revealed after the Battle of Uhud in the third year of the Hijrah, no other measure was needed. A crier proclaimed in Madinah: "O people, wine has been made unlawful." On hearing this, whoever had a cup in his hand broke it, whoever had a mouthful spilled it out, the wine-skins were torn open, and the wine jars were smashed, and the situation became such that it was as though people had never seen intoxication and wine at all.

Now look at the construction of the verses of the Qur'an and at the method of education which the Qur'an adopted.

"O you who believe! Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows are only an abomination, of Satan's work. So avoid it, that you may prosper. Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist? And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)."

The opening and tone is the familiar address by which people are called by their beloved title, the believers: "O you who believe." Thus the faith of the Muslims is stirred, and they are given to understand that the requirement of their faith is full obedience to the commands that are coming. After this, the manner of expression comes in a very plain and emphatic style of restriction.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 90–93 (part 2 of 3):

(Verse) "Verily, intoxicants (khamr), gambling (maysir), idolatrous altars (ansab), and divining arrows (azlam) are an abomination, of Satan's handiwork." These are filthy, Satanic deeds, and the word "good" (tayyib) cannot be applied to them. Allah has made lawful only the good things. Moreover, these are Satanic acts, and Satan is man's ancient enemy. For a believer, it is enough to know that something is Satanic: upon hearing this, he recoils from it, his whole being trembles, and he flees from it in fear.

In such circumstances, a definitive prohibition is now issued, but together with this prohibition it is also stated that by abstaining from it you will attain success in the Hereafter. This is another glimpse, through which it is shown how the Qur'an penetrates to the depths of human psychology and implants its sentiments.

(Verse) "So avoid it completely, that you may prosper." Now it is explained what Satan wishes to achieve by continuing this filth: "Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to prevent you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer." ... This is Satan's actual plan, and these are the aims which he seeks to accomplish through these impurities and immoral acts. His purpose is that enmity and hatred spread among the ranks of the Muslims, and he seeks to achieve this through wine, kebab and gambling. His second aim is to prevent the people of faith from the remembrance of God and from prayer. What greater conspiracy could there be?

These Satanic aims which the Qur'an has stated are matters which Muslims can clearly observe in their own history, although the Qur'an is true in itself and needs no historical confirmation. This matter requires no debate or investigation. We see how this Satanic plan works. Drinking destroys a person's understanding and perception; loss of flesh and blood and the agitation of emotions and inclinations are its immediate effects; and the financial loss that people suffer through gambling gives rise to deep hatred and enmity, because in gambling, the loser sees the winner carrying away his wealth as spoils of war before his very eyes, while he is defeated and stripped of his wealth. These are matters from which the arising of hatred and enmity is a natural outcome, even though drunkards and gamblers appear outwardly as friends and companions, are seen cheerful and happy in the same gathering, and are close and firm companions of one another.

As for the second evil, that these two things prevent the remembrance of Allah and prevent prayer, these are matters which need no proof. Intoxicants stupefy, and whatever stupefies is intoxicating; and the bewilderment that overtakes a person in gambling is no less than the stupor of drinking. The world of the gambler and the world of the drinker are one and the same world, and it does not go beyond wine, kebab, goblets and flagons.

When the matter reaches this point, and it is made clear what the real aims of Satan are in spreading this filth, the heart of a believer awakens and his sensitivity is heightened. He becomes ready for a decisive step, and when the question is asked, "Will you now desist from it?", there is already prepared in the heart of every believer the same answer which 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) gave: "Yes, indeed, we have desisted, we have desisted."

Now the matter moves further forward, and a final blow is struck.

(Verse) "And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)." (92) "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies only the plain delivery (of the message)." This is the principle to which all matters return: obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is Islam. Within Islam there is no room for anything other than unconditional obedience to Allah and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If anyone turns away from obedience to Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he himself will bear the responsibility for its consequences.

(Verse) "...But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies no duty other than the plain conveyance (of the message)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed the message of Allah in a most excellent manner. After this clear declaration, the full responsibility fell upon those who oppose.

This is, by indirect means, a severe threat. The body of a believer trembles, because if the believers disobey and do not obey Allah and His Messenger, then they are in effect harming only themselves. The Messenger (ﷺ) has conveyed the message and discharged his duty well, and he is free of their affair; he has washed his hands of it. Now, if they deserve punishment, the Messenger cannot avert the punishment from them, especially since they disobeyed him and did not obey him, and Allah is fully capable of punishing the rebellious and the disobedient.

This is the Islamic method of reform, which descends into the hearts of human beings, knocks at the door of hearts, and opens the closed doors of hearts. After this, there then unfold upon it the most hidden paths and ups and downs.

It is appropriate here that we give some detail about the wine which has been declared unlawful here. Imam Abu Dawud, with his chain of narration, related from Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) the narration: "Every intoxicating thing is khamr, and every intoxicant is unlawful." 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) delivered a sermon from the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in that sermon a group of the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) was present: "O people, you know the time when the prohibition of wine was revealed. Wine is made from five things: from grapes, from dates, from honey, from wheat, and from barley; and the definition of wine is: that which covers the intellect."

From these two narrations it becomes known that everything which intoxicates falls within the definition of khamr. Khamr does not mean a particular kind of intoxicant; whatever beverage intoxicates is khamr.

The disappearance of a person's consciousness through any intoxicating thing is contrary to the constant wakefulness which Islam has made obligatory for every person. Islam's policy is that a person remain awake and continually connected with Allah. Every moment he should look toward Allah. Then, in that continuous state of wakefulness, he should be engaged in the progress and growth of this world, protect this life from weakness and corruption, and safeguard his self, his wealth and his honour. He should be a guardian of the security of the Muslim community, and of the Islamic Shari'ah and the Islamic system of life, so that no one can lay hands on it, because a Muslim individual cannot remain absorbed solely in himself and his pleasures. Obligations of this kind are placed upon him, for the fulfilment of which he must remain awake at all times. Some duties are upon him from his Lord; some duties are upon him from his own self; some duties are upon him from his family; some duties are upon him from the Islamic society in which he lives. After this, some obligations also fall upon him from all of humanity, so that he may extend the Islamic call to them and teach them the path of guidance. For this reason, Islam demands of him that he remain awake always and at every moment. Moreover, even when he is benefiting from pure things, Islam demands of him that he remain awake, remain self-respecting, and not become the slave or servant of pleasures and desires; he should keep his appetites and inclinations under restraint. He should not be the slave of his desires but their master and lord. Those who seek refuge in intoxication to withdraw from this world, it is evident that such people cannot perform any of the aforementioned duties.

Then, what is the reality of plunging oneself into the state of intoxication? For a time, the drug-user separates himself from the real world, and in a sense he takes the path of escape from real life. He seeks refuge in the world of imaginings which arise in the state of intoxication and stupor. Islam declares it unlawful for a person to wander in this kind of illusory world and fanciful notions. Islam wants people to confront realities, to live amid realities, and to direct their lives according to realities; their lives should not rest merely upon illusions and imaginings. When a person faces realities, he then discovers the condition of his resolve and will. As for the method of someone who escapes from realities and dwells merely in a life of imaginings and illusions, it is a defective and sick way of living. In such a state, resolve weakens and will dissolves. Islam attaches very great importance to the human will, and its policy is that his will be free and that there be no oppressive or dominating force over him. The aforementioned Islamic policies are by themselves sufficient for declaring all intoxicating things unlawful, because they are filthy and Satanic deeds, and they produce corruption and disorder in human life.

On this matter, there is a difference among the jurists as to whether wine is impure (najis) like all impurities, or not, and whether only drinking it is unlawful. The first view, that it is impure, is the view of the majority; and the second view is that of Rabi'ah, Layth, al-Muzani (a companion of Imam al-Shafi'i) and some later Baghdadi scholars. Enough mention of this suffices for us.

When this verse was revealed, declaring wine unlawful and stating that it is impure and a Satanic act, two questions arose within the Islamic community. First, some Companions of especially pure nature and great caution raised the question: what will become of our companions who died in circumstances when they used to drink wine? Others said: what will become of those who were martyred at Uhud and had wine in their stomachs? (At that time wine was not yet unlawful.)

Those who wished to create disorder and confusion in the ranks of Islam also expressed similar apprehensions. Their aim was to spread doubts and suspicions about Islam's legislation. These people would imply that those who had died earlier had lost their faith, since they had drunk wine, which is impure and among the Satanic acts. Some of them died with this impure substance present in their stomachs. In response to both kinds of apprehensions and objections, this verse was revealed:

(Verse) "There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they are mindful (of Allah), believe, and do righteous deeds, then remain mindful and believe, then remain mindful and do good. And Allah loves the good-doers." (93)

Those who believed and began to do righteous deeds will not be taken to account for what they ate and drank before, provided that in future they remain away from those things which have been forbidden, remain steadfast upon faith, do good deeds, then refrain from what they are forbidden, and obey the command of Allah; then they maintain good conduct with God-fearing piety. Allah loves those of good character.

In this verse, the decision is that what has not been prohibited is not unlawful; that prohibition applies after the command of Allah, not before; and that prohibition does not have retrospective effect, so no punishment will be inflicted until a text has been revealed, whether this punishment is a worldly punishment or a punishment in the Hereafter, because it is the word of Allah which brings things into being. Those who died while drinking wine, or who had wine in their stomachs at a time when it was not yet forbidden, will not be held to account, because they did not use anything unlawful, nor did they commit any disobedience. They were God-fearing, abstained from sins, did righteous deeds, and hoped from Allah for a good end; they were firmly convinced that Allah knows well their intentions and knows their deeds. How can those whose circumstances are such commit the forbidden, or how can they commit disobedience?

We do not wish to enter here into the debates that the Mu'tazilah conducted concerning this ruling. The Mu'tazilah discussed whether intoxicants are impure in their very essence, or whether impurity came to them through this verse of Allah. Likewise, they discussed whether the prohibition of all prohibited things is inherent in them, or whether prohibition attaches to them because of the ruling that was revealed. This is a fruitless discussion, and the Islamic consciousness does not accept this debate at all. For when Allah declares something prohibited, it is within Allah's knowledge why He is declaring it prohibited, whether Allah specifies the cause of the prohibition or does not specify it, whether the prohibition is because the cause lies in the very nature of the prohibited thing, or the cause of prohibition lies in the person who uses it, or the thing has been declared prohibited merely for the interests of society. The knowledge of all things belongs to Allah alone. Obedience to Allah's commands is obligatory, and after the commands have come, this type of discussion yields no result. The very temperament of the Islamic system of life is realistic, so the question does not even arise: if the prohibition was because of a cause that lay in the nature of the prohibited thing, then why was that thing lawful before the prohibition? For it is possible that in Allah's knowledge there was a wisdom due to which Allah did not declare it prohibited for a period of time. Everything is within Allah's authority. This is the demand of His sovereignty. It is not the case that if a person considers something good it is good, and if he considers it bad it is bad. Sometimes a person considers something to be the cause of a ruling when it is not the cause. The respectful way before Allah is that the command be heard, accepted and implemented, whether or not one understands its cause and wisdom. Whether the cause is apparent or hidden, it is Allah who knows it, and we do not know it.

The basis of acting upon the Islamic Shariah is on the principle of the servitude and slavery of Allah. Obedience to Allah is because we are the servants of Allah, and this is Islam in the sense of submitting oneself wholly. Understanding the wisdoms of the Shariah is a stage that comes after obedience: a wise person may try, according to his own understanding, to do this in all commands and prohibitions, whether those wisdoms are stated in the texts or not, and whether human reason can comprehend them or not. For the determination of whether the Islamic Shariah is realized or not is not decided by man. It is Allah who can decide this. When Allah has commanded or forbidden, obedience becomes binding. If Allah had made human reason the final arbiter regarding the Islamic Shariah, the status of human reason would have become higher than the Shariah; in that case, what difference would remain between the status of divinity and the status of servanthood?

Now let us discuss, from the standpoint of Arabic, the construction (structure) of this verse. In this verse, taqwa is repeated three times: "Ittaqu wa amanu wa 'amilu al-salihat," that is, taqwa, faith and righteous deeds. Then "ittaqu wa amanu," taqwa and faith only. Then "ittaqu wa ahsanu," taqwa and ihsan are mentioned. Why was taqwa repeated in this manner in this expression? No commentator's explanation has been satisfying in this regard. Likewise, in the first edition of Fi Zilal al-Quran, I myself could not offer a satisfying explanation, and until now no convincing point has come to my understanding.

Among the explanations of the commentaries, the best one I have found compared to others is that of Ibn Jarir, although it is not fully satisfying. He says:

"The first taqwa means that one accepts Allah's command with fear of God, affirms it, and acts upon it with piety. The second taqwa means that one remains steadfast upon it with fear of God, and the third is the fear of God through which nearness to Allah is attained by means of ihsan and voluntary acts."

What I had said in the first edition of this book was this:

"This is an emphasis by giving further detail. In the first sentence, faith, righteous deeds and taqwa are mentioned; in the second sentence, taqwa is mentioned with faith; and in the third, taqwa and ihsan, that is, righteous deeds, are mentioned. The purpose of this emphasis is that the matter of all affairs depends upon taqwa. The meaning is that the true value of deeds arises from the inner consciousness behind them, and this inner consciousness is taqwa, which is manifested through fear of God, and because of this consciousness a person remains constantly attached to the Being of Allah. Faith in Allah, affirmation of His commands and prohibitions, and righteous deeds which are the expression of this inner belief and hidden consciousness. There is a connection between this righteous deed and this inner consciousness. All this inner consciousness and taqwa is the real object sought, and the ruling depends upon them. The ruling does not depend upon the outward forms and appearances of deeds. The point that the real basis is intention, spirit and inner consciousness is such an important and fundamental matter that it needs to be repeated again and again."

Even now I am not fully satisfied with my own statement, but no other point has come to my understanding. Wallahu al-musta'an.

The discussion continues on the subject of lawful and unlawful. The matter under discussion is hunting while in the state of ihram. The expiation for killing game, the wisdom behind why Allah has made obligatory the respect of His House, the sacred months, the offerings (hady) and the garlanded animals, and why the beginning of this surah prohibits meddling with these things, are all being addressed. At the end, a general principle and standard is mentioned for the individual Muslim and for an Islamic society: a standard by which a pure thing has greater value even if it is little, and an impure thing has no value even if it is very abundant.

This is part 1 of 3 of the commentary on verses 90–93. The text below is translated as it stands.

Verses 90–93

Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones and divining arrows were among the greatest marks of Jahili society, and these were habits that were very widespread within it. All of these habits were in fact a single social whole; they were interconnected and were the identifying features of Jahili society. The people of Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) consumed wine in large quantities, and in this they tried to outdo one another and took pride in it. The subject of their boastful tales and boastful poetry was often excessive wine-drinking. Alongside wine gatherings, it was also essential to slaughter animals and to serve kebabs and skewered meat with the wine. In this, both drinkers and servers took part, and in this way such gatherings had something of interest for everyone. They would perform these slaughters in the names of idols and at their shrines, and would splash the blood of these sacrifices upon the idols. Besides this, they would also slaughter certain animals in the names of their gods and soothsayers. The meat of the animals slaughtered during drinking sessions and on other occasions they would then distribute by means of arrows (divining arrows). Each person would take the portion of meat assigned by his arrow; whoever's arrow came out higher had a larger share. In this manner the meat was distributed, and in this manner the meat was distributed, until at times the person who had slaughtered the animal received nothing at all and was left in complete loss.

From these events it becomes clear that their customs and habits were interconnected and related, and these habits continued along Jahili lines. The Islamic system of life did not begin its movement by reforming these customs, because these customs and habits were founded upon certain corrupt ideological conceptions. If merely a superficial movement for the reform of customs had been started, and the root doctrinal beliefs had not been uprooted, this work would have been extremely superficial. It was by no means to be expected of Islam that it would leave the roots and limit itself to superficial matters. Islam first addressed the first knot of the human soul, namely beliefs and ideas. It first took the Jahili beliefs and conceptions, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam took their notions concerning many gods, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam exposed the corruption of their notions concerning many gods, and brought them together upon belief in the one true God. When this doctrine of Tawhid (the oneness of God) overspread their hearts and minds, they became ready to think naturally about what their true God does not like. Before this doctrinal reform, how could they have been ready to abandon their customs and rituals? They were not prepared to give up their Jahili preferred ways without doctrinal change, even though they were repeatedly admonished. The knot of human nature is in reality the knot of belief. Until this knot and problem is first resolved, no moral teaching, no program of moral refinement, and no collective reformatory scheme can succeed. Doctrine is in truth the key to human nature. Until this key is applied and human nature is opened up, access to its inner chambers and to the depths of its ways and customs will not be possible. When we open one narrow lane, several more narrow lanes will appear before us, and if we illuminate one side, ten dark sides will appear. We open one knot and ten more knots will be tied. We open one path and ten paths will be closed, and in this way we will fall into such a labyrinth that no way out will be found.

This is the reason why the Islamic system of life did not begin its reforming work with the bad customs and filthy habits of Jahiliyyah. Islam first began its work with doctrinal reform. First the demand was made that you accept the good word (the testimony of faith, the Kalimah Tayyibah). The first thirteen years in Makkah were spent in this doctrinal reform and the correction of beliefs. In those long years the aim of the Islamic movement was none other than the testimony "There is no god but Allah." During this period people were introduced to the Lord of the worlds; they were invited only to His worship, and they were called only to His sovereignty, until their souls became purified exclusively for the One Lord. Their condition became such that they began to desire for themselves what their God desired for them. When doctrinal reform reached this degree, then obligations began, acts of worship became obligatory, and now the reform of the filthy habits and customs of Jahiliyyah began; commands for changing collective practices began to be issued, economic reforms were enforced, the reform of psychological and moral conduct began, and this work started at a time when, as soon as a command came from God, the Muslims received it at once, without any hesitation or objection, because they had surrendered all authority to command and forbid to the Lord of the worlds, and had no authority of their own.

In other words, we may say that the enjoining of commands and prohibitions began after the stage at which people had bowed in complete submission. Every Muslim had surrendered everything to Allah, and acknowledged that before the commands and prohibitions of Allah he had no authority of his own, as Ustad Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi has said in his book Alam-e-Islam in the conflict between Eastern and Western outlooks, where he says:

"The great knot of disbelief and polytheism was untied. Certainly it was a great knot. With its untying, all the knots were untied. The Messenger ﷺ waged this first jihad against them, and therefore they had no further need of any jihad. For every command and every prohibition, he (ﷺ) had to make no further struggle. In this first doctrinal battle Islam was granted victory over Jahiliyyah, and after that success attended him in every battle. This happened because these people had entered fully into Islam with their hearts, their souls and their limbs. When guidance was revealed to them they did not oppose or contend with the Messenger ﷺ. Whatever decision the Messenger ﷺ made, they found no uneasiness in their hearts about it, and after the decision of the matter they had no choice or sphere of choice left for themselves. When something occurred among them in their affairs that was contrary to conscience and belief, they openly informed the Messenger ﷺ and presented themselves for punishment. When they committed a fault, the prescribed penalty was enforced upon them. When the command for the prohibition of wine came, cups full of wine were in their hands and the command of Allah intervened, and they did not bring them to their lips. Their lips remained dry and their livers thirsty. The wine jars were broken, and wine flowed through the streets of Madinah like a flood."

Yet despite this, the prohibition of wine and of the other things along with it was not a sudden matter. Before this final prohibition, the treatment of this widespread and very deep-rooted sickness was carried out with great gradualness, because the people were addicted to it, and it was for them an extremely habit-forming intoxication. Their social and economic interests were also tied up with it.

The final prohibition of wine was revealed in the third or fourth stage. In the first stage a single arrow was merely shot in the direction toward which the Islamic system was inclined. In a verse of Surah an-Nahl it was said:

"And from the fruits of the date-palm and the grapes, from which you derive intoxicant and good provision." (16:67) — "from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes, from which you obtain wine and goodly sustenance."

Here intoxicant (sakar), that is, intoxicating things, was placed in contrast with goodly provision, and by this the intended indication was that intoxicating things do not fall within the definition of goodly provision. As if intoxicating things are one thing and goodly provision is another. After that, in Surah al-Baqarah, the religious conscience of the Muslims was awakened against wine through a legal and logical argument:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219)

In this verse it was indicated that when their sin is greater, then setting aside the small benefit and abandoning them is the better course, because everything has some benefit. However, lawfulness and unlawfulness depend upon the majority; the predominance of gain or loss is looked at.

The third measure taken was that the time spent on the habit of wine-drinking was reduced, and wine-drinking was declared incompatible with the state of prayer. The following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying." (4:43) — "O you who have believed, do not approach prayer when you are in a state of intoxication until you know what you say."

Now, since the five daily prayers are mostly very close to one another, and there is not so much interval between them that someone who drinks wine would sober up again, therefore during those times the actual possibility of drinking wine no longer remained, and the scope for this act became narrow. Especially the morning wine (sabuh) and the evening wine (ghabuq), that is, the wine after Asr and after Maghrib, had their times narrowed, because in the age of Jahiliyyah wine was drunk precisely at these times. Through this scheme the Shariah broke the craving at the times of intoxication. For a Muslim this proved to be an excellent measure, because at that time it could not even be imagined that a Muslim would leave prayer and drink wine. At that time every Muslim performed his prayer at its appointed time. In this way the grip of wine was broken. After this, the fourth and final measure was taken through this verse. Now the atmosphere was ready for this final blow; people's souls were ready; so the commands came, and people believed and carried them out at once.

Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he said: "O Allah, give us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Baqarah was revealed:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited to him, and upon this he again said: "O Allah, reveal for us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer when you are intoxicated, until you know what you say." (4:43) When this verse was recited to Hadrat Umar, he again asked: "O Allah, reveal a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed:

"Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?" (5:91) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited before him, and he said: "Yes, we have desisted, we have desisted." (Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan.)

When these verses were revealed after the Battle of Uhud in the third year of the Hijrah, no other measure was needed. A crier proclaimed in Madinah: "O people, wine has been made unlawful." On hearing this, whoever had a cup in his hand broke it, whoever had a mouthful spilled it out, the wine-skins were torn open, and the wine jars were smashed, and the situation became such that it was as though people had never seen intoxication and wine at all.

Now look at the construction of the verses of the Qur'an and at the method of education which the Qur'an adopted.

"O you who believe! Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows are only an abomination, of Satan's work. So avoid it, that you may prosper. Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist? And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)."

The opening and tone is the familiar address by which people are called by their beloved title, the believers: "O you who believe." Thus the faith of the Muslims is stirred, and they are given to understand that the requirement of their faith is full obedience to the commands that are coming. After this, the manner of expression comes in a very plain and emphatic style of restriction.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 90–93 (part 2 of 3):

(Verse) "Verily, intoxicants (khamr), gambling (maysir), idolatrous altars (ansab), and divining arrows (azlam) are an abomination, of Satan's handiwork." These are filthy, Satanic deeds, and the word "good" (tayyib) cannot be applied to them. Allah has made lawful only the good things. Moreover, these are Satanic acts, and Satan is man's ancient enemy. For a believer, it is enough to know that something is Satanic: upon hearing this, he recoils from it, his whole being trembles, and he flees from it in fear.

In such circumstances, a definitive prohibition is now issued, but together with this prohibition it is also stated that by abstaining from it you will attain success in the Hereafter. This is another glimpse, through which it is shown how the Qur'an penetrates to the depths of human psychology and implants its sentiments.

(Verse) "So avoid it completely, that you may prosper." Now it is explained what Satan wishes to achieve by continuing this filth: "Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to prevent you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer." ... This is Satan's actual plan, and these are the aims which he seeks to accomplish through these impurities and immoral acts. His purpose is that enmity and hatred spread among the ranks of the Muslims, and he seeks to achieve this through wine, kebab and gambling. His second aim is to prevent the people of faith from the remembrance of God and from prayer. What greater conspiracy could there be?

These Satanic aims which the Qur'an has stated are matters which Muslims can clearly observe in their own history, although the Qur'an is true in itself and needs no historical confirmation. This matter requires no debate or investigation. We see how this Satanic plan works. Drinking destroys a person's understanding and perception; loss of flesh and blood and the agitation of emotions and inclinations are its immediate effects; and the financial loss that people suffer through gambling gives rise to deep hatred and enmity, because in gambling, the loser sees the winner carrying away his wealth as spoils of war before his very eyes, while he is defeated and stripped of his wealth. These are matters from which the arising of hatred and enmity is a natural outcome, even though drunkards and gamblers appear outwardly as friends and companions, are seen cheerful and happy in the same gathering, and are close and firm companions of one another.

As for the second evil, that these two things prevent the remembrance of Allah and prevent prayer, these are matters which need no proof. Intoxicants stupefy, and whatever stupefies is intoxicating; and the bewilderment that overtakes a person in gambling is no less than the stupor of drinking. The world of the gambler and the world of the drinker are one and the same world, and it does not go beyond wine, kebab, goblets and flagons.

When the matter reaches this point, and it is made clear what the real aims of Satan are in spreading this filth, the heart of a believer awakens and his sensitivity is heightened. He becomes ready for a decisive step, and when the question is asked, "Will you now desist from it?", there is already prepared in the heart of every believer the same answer which 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) gave: "Yes, indeed, we have desisted, we have desisted."

Now the matter moves further forward, and a final blow is struck.

(Verse) "And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)." (92) "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies only the plain delivery (of the message)." This is the principle to which all matters return: obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is Islam. Within Islam there is no room for anything other than unconditional obedience to Allah and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If anyone turns away from obedience to Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he himself will bear the responsibility for its consequences.

(Verse) "...But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies no duty other than the plain conveyance (of the message)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed the message of Allah in a most excellent manner. After this clear declaration, the full responsibility fell upon those who oppose.

This is, by indirect means, a severe threat. The body of a believer trembles, because if the believers disobey and do not obey Allah and His Messenger, then they are in effect harming only themselves. The Messenger (ﷺ) has conveyed the message and discharged his duty well, and he is free of their affair; he has washed his hands of it. Now, if they deserve punishment, the Messenger cannot avert the punishment from them, especially since they disobeyed him and did not obey him, and Allah is fully capable of punishing the rebellious and the disobedient.

This is the Islamic method of reform, which descends into the hearts of human beings, knocks at the door of hearts, and opens the closed doors of hearts. After this, there then unfold upon it the most hidden paths and ups and downs.

It is appropriate here that we give some detail about the wine which has been declared unlawful here. Imam Abu Dawud, with his chain of narration, related from Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) the narration: "Every intoxicating thing is khamr, and every intoxicant is unlawful." 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) delivered a sermon from the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in that sermon a group of the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) was present: "O people, you know the time when the prohibition of wine was revealed. Wine is made from five things: from grapes, from dates, from honey, from wheat, and from barley; and the definition of wine is: that which covers the intellect."

From these two narrations it becomes known that everything which intoxicates falls within the definition of khamr. Khamr does not mean a particular kind of intoxicant; whatever beverage intoxicates is khamr.

The disappearance of a person's consciousness through any intoxicating thing is contrary to the constant wakefulness which Islam has made obligatory for every person. Islam's policy is that a person remain awake and continually connected with Allah. Every moment he should look toward Allah. Then, in that continuous state of wakefulness, he should be engaged in the progress and growth of this world, protect this life from weakness and corruption, and safeguard his self, his wealth and his honour. He should be a guardian of the security of the Muslim community, and of the Islamic Shari'ah and the Islamic system of life, so that no one can lay hands on it, because a Muslim individual cannot remain absorbed solely in himself and his pleasures. Obligations of this kind are placed upon him, for the fulfilment of which he must remain awake at all times. Some duties are upon him from his Lord; some duties are upon him from his own self; some duties are upon him from his family; some duties are upon him from the Islamic society in which he lives. After this, some obligations also fall upon him from all of humanity, so that he may extend the Islamic call to them and teach them the path of guidance. For this reason, Islam demands of him that he remain awake always and at every moment. Moreover, even when he is benefiting from pure things, Islam demands of him that he remain awake, remain self-respecting, and not become the slave or servant of pleasures and desires; he should keep his appetites and inclinations under restraint. He should not be the slave of his desires but their master and lord. Those who seek refuge in intoxication to withdraw from this world, it is evident that such people cannot perform any of the aforementioned duties.

Then, what is the reality of plunging oneself into the state of intoxication? For a time, the drug-user separates himself from the real world, and in a sense he takes the path of escape from real life. He seeks refuge in the world of imaginings which arise in the state of intoxication and stupor. Islam declares it unlawful for a person to wander in this kind of illusory world and fanciful notions. Islam wants people to confront realities, to live amid realities, and to direct their lives according to realities; their lives should not rest merely upon illusions and imaginings. When a person faces realities, he then discovers the condition of his resolve and will. As for the method of someone who escapes from realities and dwells merely in a life of imaginings and illusions, it is a defective and sick way of living. In such a state, resolve weakens and will dissolves. Islam attaches very great importance to the human will, and its policy is that his will be free and that there be no oppressive or dominating force over him. The aforementioned Islamic policies are by themselves sufficient for declaring all intoxicating things unlawful, because they are filthy and Satanic deeds, and they produce corruption and disorder in human life.

On this matter, there is a difference among the jurists as to whether wine is impure (najis) like all impurities, or not, and whether only drinking it is unlawful. The first view, that it is impure, is the view of the majority; and the second view is that of Rabi'ah, Layth, al-Muzani (a companion of Imam al-Shafi'i) and some later Baghdadi scholars. Enough mention of this suffices for us.

When this verse was revealed, declaring wine unlawful and stating that it is impure and a Satanic act, two questions arose within the Islamic community. First, some Companions of especially pure nature and great caution raised the question: what will become of our companions who died in circumstances when they used to drink wine? Others said: what will become of those who were martyred at Uhud and had wine in their stomachs? (At that time wine was not yet unlawful.)

Those who wished to create disorder and confusion in the ranks of Islam also expressed similar apprehensions. Their aim was to spread doubts and suspicions about Islam's legislation. These people would imply that those who had died earlier had lost their faith, since they had drunk wine, which is impure and among the Satanic acts. Some of them died with this impure substance present in their stomachs. In response to both kinds of apprehensions and objections, this verse was revealed:

(Verse) "There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they are mindful (of Allah), believe, and do righteous deeds, then remain mindful and believe, then remain mindful and do good. And Allah loves the good-doers." (93)

Those who believed and began to do righteous deeds will not be taken to account for what they ate and drank before, provided that in future they remain away from those things which have been forbidden, remain steadfast upon faith, do good deeds, then refrain from what they are forbidden, and obey the command of Allah; then they maintain good conduct with God-fearing piety. Allah loves those of good character.

In this verse, the decision is that what has not been prohibited is not unlawful; that prohibition applies after the command of Allah, not before; and that prohibition does not have retrospective effect, so no punishment will be inflicted until a text has been revealed, whether this punishment is a worldly punishment or a punishment in the Hereafter, because it is the word of Allah which brings things into being. Those who died while drinking wine, or who had wine in their stomachs at a time when it was not yet forbidden, will not be held to account, because they did not use anything unlawful, nor did they commit any disobedience. They were God-fearing, abstained from sins, did righteous deeds, and hoped from Allah for a good end; they were firmly convinced that Allah knows well their intentions and knows their deeds. How can those whose circumstances are such commit the forbidden, or how can they commit disobedience?

We do not wish to enter here into the debates that the Mu'tazilah conducted concerning this ruling. The Mu'tazilah discussed whether intoxicants are impure in their very essence, or whether impurity came to them through this verse of Allah. Likewise, they discussed whether the prohibition of all prohibited things is inherent in them, or whether prohibition attaches to them because of the ruling that was revealed. This is a fruitless discussion, and the Islamic consciousness does not accept this debate at all. For when Allah declares something prohibited, it is within Allah's knowledge why He is declaring it prohibited, whether Allah specifies the cause of the prohibition or does not specify it, whether the prohibition is because the cause lies in the very nature of the prohibited thing, or the cause of prohibition lies in the person who uses it, or the thing has been declared prohibited merely for the interests of society. The knowledge of all things belongs to Allah alone. Obedience to Allah's commands is obligatory, and after the commands have come, this type of discussion yields no result. The very temperament of the Islamic system of life is realistic, so the question does not even arise: if the prohibition was because of a cause that lay in the nature of the prohibited thing, then why was that thing lawful before the prohibition? For it is possible that in Allah's knowledge there was a wisdom due to which Allah did not declare it prohibited for a period of time. Everything is within Allah's authority. This is the demand of His sovereignty. It is not the case that if a person considers something good it is good, and if he considers it bad it is bad. Sometimes a person considers something to be the cause of a ruling when it is not the cause. The respectful way before Allah is that the command be heard, accepted and implemented, whether or not one understands its cause and wisdom. Whether the cause is apparent or hidden, it is Allah who knows it, and we do not know it.

The basis of acting upon the Islamic Shariah is on the principle of the servitude and slavery of Allah. Obedience to Allah is because we are the servants of Allah, and this is Islam in the sense of submitting oneself wholly. Understanding the wisdoms of the Shariah is a stage that comes after obedience: a wise person may try, according to his own understanding, to do this in all commands and prohibitions, whether those wisdoms are stated in the texts or not, and whether human reason can comprehend them or not. For the determination of whether the Islamic Shariah is realized or not is not decided by man. It is Allah who can decide this. When Allah has commanded or forbidden, obedience becomes binding. If Allah had made human reason the final arbiter regarding the Islamic Shariah, the status of human reason would have become higher than the Shariah; in that case, what difference would remain between the status of divinity and the status of servanthood?

Now let us discuss, from the standpoint of Arabic, the construction (structure) of this verse. In this verse, taqwa is repeated three times: "Ittaqu wa amanu wa 'amilu al-salihat," that is, taqwa, faith and righteous deeds. Then "ittaqu wa amanu," taqwa and faith only. Then "ittaqu wa ahsanu," taqwa and ihsan are mentioned. Why was taqwa repeated in this manner in this expression? No commentator's explanation has been satisfying in this regard. Likewise, in the first edition of Fi Zilal al-Quran, I myself could not offer a satisfying explanation, and until now no convincing point has come to my understanding.

Among the explanations of the commentaries, the best one I have found compared to others is that of Ibn Jarir, although it is not fully satisfying. He says:

"The first taqwa means that one accepts Allah's command with fear of God, affirms it, and acts upon it with piety. The second taqwa means that one remains steadfast upon it with fear of God, and the third is the fear of God through which nearness to Allah is attained by means of ihsan and voluntary acts."

What I had said in the first edition of this book was this:

"This is an emphasis by giving further detail. In the first sentence, faith, righteous deeds and taqwa are mentioned; in the second sentence, taqwa is mentioned with faith; and in the third, taqwa and ihsan, that is, righteous deeds, are mentioned. The purpose of this emphasis is that the matter of all affairs depends upon taqwa. The meaning is that the true value of deeds arises from the inner consciousness behind them, and this inner consciousness is taqwa, which is manifested through fear of God, and because of this consciousness a person remains constantly attached to the Being of Allah. Faith in Allah, affirmation of His commands and prohibitions, and righteous deeds which are the expression of this inner belief and hidden consciousness. There is a connection between this righteous deed and this inner consciousness. All this inner consciousness and taqwa is the real object sought, and the ruling depends upon them. The ruling does not depend upon the outward forms and appearances of deeds. The point that the real basis is intention, spirit and inner consciousness is such an important and fundamental matter that it needs to be repeated again and again."

Even now I am not fully satisfied with my own statement, but no other point has come to my understanding. Wallahu al-musta'an.

The discussion continues on the subject of lawful and unlawful. The matter under discussion is hunting while in the state of ihram. The expiation for killing game, the wisdom behind why Allah has made obligatory the respect of His House, the sacred months, the offerings (hady) and the garlanded animals, and why the beginning of this surah prohibits meddling with these things, are all being addressed. At the end, a general principle and standard is mentioned for the individual Muslim and for an Islamic society: a standard by which a pure thing has greater value even if it is little, and an impure thing has no value even if it is very abundant.

This is part 1 of 3 of the commentary on verses 90–93. The text below is translated as it stands.

Verses 90–93

Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones and divining arrows were among the greatest marks of Jahili society, and these were habits that were very widespread within it. All of these habits were in fact a single social whole; they were interconnected and were the identifying features of Jahili society. The people of Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) consumed wine in large quantities, and in this they tried to outdo one another and took pride in it. The subject of their boastful tales and boastful poetry was often excessive wine-drinking. Alongside wine gatherings, it was also essential to slaughter animals and to serve kebabs and skewered meat with the wine. In this, both drinkers and servers took part, and in this way such gatherings had something of interest for everyone. They would perform these slaughters in the names of idols and at their shrines, and would splash the blood of these sacrifices upon the idols. Besides this, they would also slaughter certain animals in the names of their gods and soothsayers. The meat of the animals slaughtered during drinking sessions and on other occasions they would then distribute by means of arrows (divining arrows). Each person would take the portion of meat assigned by his arrow; whoever's arrow came out higher had a larger share. In this manner the meat was distributed, and in this manner the meat was distributed, until at times the person who had slaughtered the animal received nothing at all and was left in complete loss.

From these events it becomes clear that their customs and habits were interconnected and related, and these habits continued along Jahili lines. The Islamic system of life did not begin its movement by reforming these customs, because these customs and habits were founded upon certain corrupt ideological conceptions. If merely a superficial movement for the reform of customs had been started, and the root doctrinal beliefs had not been uprooted, this work would have been extremely superficial. It was by no means to be expected of Islam that it would leave the roots and limit itself to superficial matters. Islam first addressed the first knot of the human soul, namely beliefs and ideas. It first took the Jahili beliefs and conceptions, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam took their notions concerning many gods, and uprooted them and cast them away. In their place it gave a pure and clean Islamic outlook on life, and it sank this conception and outlook into the depths of human nature. Islam exposed the corruption of their notions concerning many gods, and brought them together upon belief in the one true God. When this doctrine of Tawhid (the oneness of God) overspread their hearts and minds, they became ready to think naturally about what their true God does not like. Before this doctrinal reform, how could they have been ready to abandon their customs and rituals? They were not prepared to give up their Jahili preferred ways without doctrinal change, even though they were repeatedly admonished. The knot of human nature is in reality the knot of belief. Until this knot and problem is first resolved, no moral teaching, no program of moral refinement, and no collective reformatory scheme can succeed. Doctrine is in truth the key to human nature. Until this key is applied and human nature is opened up, access to its inner chambers and to the depths of its ways and customs will not be possible. When we open one narrow lane, several more narrow lanes will appear before us, and if we illuminate one side, ten dark sides will appear. We open one knot and ten more knots will be tied. We open one path and ten paths will be closed, and in this way we will fall into such a labyrinth that no way out will be found.

This is the reason why the Islamic system of life did not begin its reforming work with the bad customs and filthy habits of Jahiliyyah. Islam first began its work with doctrinal reform. First the demand was made that you accept the good word (the testimony of faith, the Kalimah Tayyibah). The first thirteen years in Makkah were spent in this doctrinal reform and the correction of beliefs. In those long years the aim of the Islamic movement was none other than the testimony "There is no god but Allah." During this period people were introduced to the Lord of the worlds; they were invited only to His worship, and they were called only to His sovereignty, until their souls became purified exclusively for the One Lord. Their condition became such that they began to desire for themselves what their God desired for them. When doctrinal reform reached this degree, then obligations began, acts of worship became obligatory, and now the reform of the filthy habits and customs of Jahiliyyah began; commands for changing collective practices began to be issued, economic reforms were enforced, the reform of psychological and moral conduct began, and this work started at a time when, as soon as a command came from God, the Muslims received it at once, without any hesitation or objection, because they had surrendered all authority to command and forbid to the Lord of the worlds, and had no authority of their own.

In other words, we may say that the enjoining of commands and prohibitions began after the stage at which people had bowed in complete submission. Every Muslim had surrendered everything to Allah, and acknowledged that before the commands and prohibitions of Allah he had no authority of his own, as Ustad Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi has said in his book Alam-e-Islam in the conflict between Eastern and Western outlooks, where he says:

"The great knot of disbelief and polytheism was untied. Certainly it was a great knot. With its untying, all the knots were untied. The Messenger ﷺ waged this first jihad against them, and therefore they had no further need of any jihad. For every command and every prohibition, he (ﷺ) had to make no further struggle. In this first doctrinal battle Islam was granted victory over Jahiliyyah, and after that success attended him in every battle. This happened because these people had entered fully into Islam with their hearts, their souls and their limbs. When guidance was revealed to them they did not oppose or contend with the Messenger ﷺ. Whatever decision the Messenger ﷺ made, they found no uneasiness in their hearts about it, and after the decision of the matter they had no choice or sphere of choice left for themselves. When something occurred among them in their affairs that was contrary to conscience and belief, they openly informed the Messenger ﷺ and presented themselves for punishment. When they committed a fault, the prescribed penalty was enforced upon them. When the command for the prohibition of wine came, cups full of wine were in their hands and the command of Allah intervened, and they did not bring them to their lips. Their lips remained dry and their livers thirsty. The wine jars were broken, and wine flowed through the streets of Madinah like a flood."

Yet despite this, the prohibition of wine and of the other things along with it was not a sudden matter. Before this final prohibition, the treatment of this widespread and very deep-rooted sickness was carried out with great gradualness, because the people were addicted to it, and it was for them an extremely habit-forming intoxication. Their social and economic interests were also tied up with it.

The final prohibition of wine was revealed in the third or fourth stage. In the first stage a single arrow was merely shot in the direction toward which the Islamic system was inclined. In a verse of Surah an-Nahl it was said:

"And from the fruits of the date-palm and the grapes, from which you derive intoxicant and good provision." (16:67) — "from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes, from which you obtain wine and goodly sustenance."

Here intoxicant (sakar), that is, intoxicating things, was placed in contrast with goodly provision, and by this the intended indication was that intoxicating things do not fall within the definition of goodly provision. As if intoxicating things are one thing and goodly provision is another. After that, in Surah al-Baqarah, the religious conscience of the Muslims was awakened against wine through a legal and logical argument:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219)

In this verse it was indicated that when their sin is greater, then setting aside the small benefit and abandoning them is the better course, because everything has some benefit. However, lawfulness and unlawfulness depend upon the majority; the predominance of gain or loss is looked at.

The third measure taken was that the time spent on the habit of wine-drinking was reduced, and wine-drinking was declared incompatible with the state of prayer. The following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying." (4:43) — "O you who have believed, do not approach prayer when you are in a state of intoxication until you know what you say."

Now, since the five daily prayers are mostly very close to one another, and there is not so much interval between them that someone who drinks wine would sober up again, therefore during those times the actual possibility of drinking wine no longer remained, and the scope for this act became narrow. Especially the morning wine (sabuh) and the evening wine (ghabuq), that is, the wine after Asr and after Maghrib, had their times narrowed, because in the age of Jahiliyyah wine was drunk precisely at these times. Through this scheme the Shariah broke the craving at the times of intoxication. For a Muslim this proved to be an excellent measure, because at that time it could not even be imagined that a Muslim would leave prayer and drink wine. At that time every Muslim performed his prayer at its appointed time. In this way the grip of wine was broken. After this, the fourth and final measure was taken through this verse. Now the atmosphere was ready for this final blow; people's souls were ready; so the commands came, and people believed and carried them out at once.

Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he said: "O Allah, give us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Baqarah was revealed:

"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." (2:219) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited to him, and upon this he again said: "O Allah, reveal for us a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah an-Nisa was revealed:

"O you who believe, do not approach prayer when you are intoxicated, until you know what you say." (4:43) When this verse was recited to Hadrat Umar, he again asked: "O Allah, reveal a sufficient and decisive statement about wine." Upon this the following verse of Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed:

"Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?" (5:91) Hadrat Umar was called and this verse was recited before him, and he said: "Yes, we have desisted, we have desisted." (Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan.)

When these verses were revealed after the Battle of Uhud in the third year of the Hijrah, no other measure was needed. A crier proclaimed in Madinah: "O people, wine has been made unlawful." On hearing this, whoever had a cup in his hand broke it, whoever had a mouthful spilled it out, the wine-skins were torn open, and the wine jars were smashed, and the situation became such that it was as though people had never seen intoxication and wine at all.

Now look at the construction of the verses of the Qur'an and at the method of education which the Qur'an adopted.

"O you who believe! Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows are only an abomination, of Satan's work. So avoid it, that you may prosper. Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist? And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)."

The opening and tone is the familiar address by which people are called by their beloved title, the believers: "O you who believe." Thus the faith of the Muslims is stirred, and they are given to understand that the requirement of their faith is full obedience to the commands that are coming. After this, the manner of expression comes in a very plain and emphatic style of restriction.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 90–93 (part 2 of 3):

(Verse) "Verily, intoxicants (khamr), gambling (maysir), idolatrous altars (ansab), and divining arrows (azlam) are an abomination, of Satan's handiwork." These are filthy, Satanic deeds, and the word "good" (tayyib) cannot be applied to them. Allah has made lawful only the good things. Moreover, these are Satanic acts, and Satan is man's ancient enemy. For a believer, it is enough to know that something is Satanic: upon hearing this, he recoils from it, his whole being trembles, and he flees from it in fear.

In such circumstances, a definitive prohibition is now issued, but together with this prohibition it is also stated that by abstaining from it you will attain success in the Hereafter. This is another glimpse, through which it is shown how the Qur'an penetrates to the depths of human psychology and implants its sentiments.

(Verse) "So avoid it completely, that you may prosper." Now it is explained what Satan wishes to achieve by continuing this filth: "Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to prevent you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer." ... This is Satan's actual plan, and these are the aims which he seeks to accomplish through these impurities and immoral acts. His purpose is that enmity and hatred spread among the ranks of the Muslims, and he seeks to achieve this through wine, kebab and gambling. His second aim is to prevent the people of faith from the remembrance of God and from prayer. What greater conspiracy could there be?

These Satanic aims which the Qur'an has stated are matters which Muslims can clearly observe in their own history, although the Qur'an is true in itself and needs no historical confirmation. This matter requires no debate or investigation. We see how this Satanic plan works. Drinking destroys a person's understanding and perception; loss of flesh and blood and the agitation of emotions and inclinations are its immediate effects; and the financial loss that people suffer through gambling gives rise to deep hatred and enmity, because in gambling, the loser sees the winner carrying away his wealth as spoils of war before his very eyes, while he is defeated and stripped of his wealth. These are matters from which the arising of hatred and enmity is a natural outcome, even though drunkards and gamblers appear outwardly as friends and companions, are seen cheerful and happy in the same gathering, and are close and firm companions of one another.

As for the second evil, that these two things prevent the remembrance of Allah and prevent prayer, these are matters which need no proof. Intoxicants stupefy, and whatever stupefies is intoxicating; and the bewilderment that overtakes a person in gambling is no less than the stupor of drinking. The world of the gambler and the world of the drinker are one and the same world, and it does not go beyond wine, kebab, goblets and flagons.

When the matter reaches this point, and it is made clear what the real aims of Satan are in spreading this filth, the heart of a believer awakens and his sensitivity is heightened. He becomes ready for a decisive step, and when the question is asked, "Will you now desist from it?", there is already prepared in the heart of every believer the same answer which 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) gave: "Yes, indeed, we have desisted, we have desisted."

Now the matter moves further forward, and a final blow is struck.

(Verse) "And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance (of the message)." (92) "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies only the plain delivery (of the message)." This is the principle to which all matters return: obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is Islam. Within Islam there is no room for anything other than unconditional obedience to Allah and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If anyone turns away from obedience to Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he himself will bear the responsibility for its consequences.

(Verse) "...But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger lies no duty other than the plain conveyance (of the message)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed the message of Allah in a most excellent manner. After this clear declaration, the full responsibility fell upon those who oppose.

This is, by indirect means, a severe threat. The body of a believer trembles, because if the believers disobey and do not obey Allah and His Messenger, then they are in effect harming only themselves. The Messenger (ﷺ) has conveyed the message and discharged his duty well, and he is free of their affair; he has washed his hands of it. Now, if they deserve punishment, the Messenger cannot avert the punishment from them, especially since they disobeyed him and did not obey him, and Allah is fully capable of punishing the rebellious and the disobedient.

This is the Islamic method of reform, which descends into the hearts of human beings, knocks at the door of hearts, and opens the closed doors of hearts. After this, there then unfold upon it the most hidden paths and ups and downs.

It is appropriate here that we give some detail about the wine which has been declared unlawful here. Imam Abu Dawud, with his chain of narration, related from Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) the narration: "Every intoxicating thing is khamr, and every intoxicant is unlawful." 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) delivered a sermon from the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in that sermon a group of the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) was present: "O people, you know the time when the prohibition of wine was revealed. Wine is made from five things: from grapes, from dates, from honey, from wheat, and from barley; and the definition of wine is: that which covers the intellect."

From these two narrations it becomes known that everything which intoxicates falls within the definition of khamr. Khamr does not mean a particular kind of intoxicant; whatever beverage intoxicates is khamr.

The disappearance of a person's consciousness through any intoxicating thing is contrary to the constant wakefulness which Islam has made obligatory for every person. Islam's policy is that a person remain awake and continually connected with Allah. Every moment he should look toward Allah. Then, in that continuous state of wakefulness, he should be engaged in the progress and growth of this world, protect this life from weakness and corruption, and safeguard his self, his wealth and his honour. He should be a guardian of the security of the Muslim community, and of the Islamic Shari'ah and the Islamic system of life, so that no one can lay hands on it, because a Muslim individual cannot remain absorbed solely in himself and his pleasures. Obligations of this kind are placed upon him, for the fulfilment of which he must remain awake at all times. Some duties are upon him from his Lord; some duties are upon him from his own self; some duties are upon him from his family; some duties are upon him from the Islamic society in which he lives. After this, some obligations also fall upon him from all of humanity, so that he may extend the Islamic call to them and teach them the path of guidance. For this reason, Islam demands of him that he remain awake always and at every moment. Moreover, even when he is benefiting from pure things, Islam demands of him that he remain awake, remain self-respecting, and not become the slave or servant of pleasures and desires; he should keep his appetites and inclinations under restraint. He should not be the slave of his desires but their master and lord. Those who seek refuge in intoxication to withdraw from this world, it is evident that such people cannot perform any of the aforementioned duties.

Then, what is the reality of plunging oneself into the state of intoxication? For a time, the drug-user separates himself from the real world, and in a sense he takes the path of escape from real life. He seeks refuge in the world of imaginings which arise in the state of intoxication and stupor. Islam declares it unlawful for a person to wander in this kind of illusory world and fanciful notions. Islam wants people to confront realities, to live amid realities, and to direct their lives according to realities; their lives should not rest merely upon illusions and imaginings. When a person faces realities, he then discovers the condition of his resolve and will. As for the method of someone who escapes from realities and dwells merely in a life of imaginings and illusions, it is a defective and sick way of living. In such a state, resolve weakens and will dissolves. Islam attaches very great importance to the human will, and its policy is that his will be free and that there be no oppressive or dominating force over him. The aforementioned Islamic policies are by themselves sufficient for declaring all intoxicating things unlawful, because they are filthy and Satanic deeds, and they produce corruption and disorder in human life.

On this matter, there is a difference among the jurists as to whether wine is impure (najis) like all impurities, or not, and whether only drinking it is unlawful. The first view, that it is impure, is the view of the majority; and the second view is that of Rabi'ah, Layth, al-Muzani (a companion of Imam al-Shafi'i) and some later Baghdadi scholars. Enough mention of this suffices for us.

When this verse was revealed, declaring wine unlawful and stating that it is impure and a Satanic act, two questions arose within the Islamic community. First, some Companions of especially pure nature and great caution raised the question: what will become of our companions who died in circumstances when they used to drink wine? Others said: what will become of those who were martyred at Uhud and had wine in their stomachs? (At that time wine was not yet unlawful.)

Those who wished to create disorder and confusion in the ranks of Islam also expressed similar apprehensions. Their aim was to spread doubts and suspicions about Islam's legislation. These people would imply that those who had died earlier had lost their faith, since they had drunk wine, which is impure and among the Satanic acts. Some of them died with this impure substance present in their stomachs. In response to both kinds of apprehensions and objections, this verse was revealed:

(Verse) "There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they are mindful (of Allah), believe, and do righteous deeds, then remain mindful and believe, then remain mindful and do good. And Allah loves the good-doers." (93)

Those who believed and began to do righteous deeds will not be taken to account for what they ate and drank before, provided that in future they remain away from those things which have been forbidden, remain steadfast upon faith, do good deeds, then refrain from what they are forbidden, and obey the command of Allah; then they maintain good conduct with God-fearing piety. Allah loves those of good character.

In this verse, the decision is that what has not been prohibited is not unlawful; that prohibition applies after the command of Allah, not before; and that prohibition does not have retrospective effect, so no punishment will be inflicted until a text has been revealed, whether this punishment is a worldly punishment or a punishment in the Hereafter, because it is the word of Allah which brings things into being. Those who died while drinking wine, or who had wine in their stomachs at a time when it was not yet forbidden, will not be held to account, because they did not use anything unlawful, nor did they commit any disobedience. They were God-fearing, abstained from sins, did righteous deeds, and hoped from Allah for a good end; they were firmly convinced that Allah knows well their intentions and knows their deeds. How can those whose circumstances are such commit the forbidden, or how can they commit disobedience?

We do not wish to enter here into the debates that the Mu'tazilah conducted concerning this ruling. The Mu'tazilah discussed whether intoxicants are impure in their very essence, or whether impurity came to them through this verse of Allah. Likewise, they discussed whether the prohibition of all prohibited things is inherent in them, or whether prohibition attaches to them because of the ruling that was revealed. This is a fruitless discussion, and the Islamic consciousness does not accept this debate at all.
