For when Allah declares something prohibited, it is within Allah's knowledge why He is declaring it prohibited, whether Allah specifies the cause of the prohibition or does not specify it, whether the prohibition is because the cause lies in the very nature of the prohibited thing, or the cause of prohibition lies in the person who uses it, or the thing has been declared prohibited merely for the interests of society. The knowledge of all things belongs to Allah alone. Obedience to Allah's commands is obligatory, and after the commands have come, this type of discussion yields no result. The very temperament of the Islamic system of life is realistic, so the question does not even arise: if the prohibition was because of a cause that lay in the nature of the prohibited thing, then why was that thing lawful before the prohibition? For it is possible that in Allah's knowledge there was a wisdom due to which Allah did not declare it prohibited for a period of time. Everything is within Allah's authority. This is the demand of His sovereignty. It is not the case that if a person considers something good it is good, and if he considers it bad it is bad. Sometimes a person considers something to be the cause of a ruling when it is not the cause. The respectful way before Allah is that the command be heard, accepted and implemented, whether or not one understands its cause and wisdom. Whether the cause is apparent or hidden, it is Allah who knows it, and we do not know it.

The basis of acting upon the Islamic Shariah is on the principle of the servitude and slavery of Allah. Obedience to Allah is because we are the servants of Allah, and this is Islam in the sense of submitting oneself wholly. Understanding the wisdoms of the Shariah is a stage that comes after obedience: a wise person may try, according to his own understanding, to do this in all commands and prohibitions, whether those wisdoms are stated in the texts or not, and whether human reason can comprehend them or not. For the determination of whether the Islamic Shariah is realized or not is not decided by man. It is Allah who can decide this. When Allah has commanded or forbidden, obedience becomes binding. If Allah had made human reason the final arbiter regarding the Islamic Shariah, the status of human reason would have become higher than the Shariah; in that case, what difference would remain between the status of divinity and the status of servanthood?

Now let us discuss, from the standpoint of Arabic, the construction (structure) of this verse. In this verse, taqwa is repeated three times: "Ittaqu wa amanu wa 'amilu al-salihat," that is, taqwa, faith and righteous deeds. Then "ittaqu wa amanu," taqwa and faith only. Then "ittaqu wa ahsanu," taqwa and ihsan are mentioned. Why was taqwa repeated in this manner in this expression? No commentator's explanation has been satisfying in this regard. Likewise, in the first edition of Fi Zilal al-Quran, I myself could not offer a satisfying explanation, and until now no convincing point has come to my understanding.

Among the explanations of the commentaries, the best one I have found compared to others is that of Ibn Jarir, although it is not fully satisfying. He says:

"The first taqwa means that one accepts Allah's command with fear of God, affirms it, and acts upon it with piety. The second taqwa means that one remains steadfast upon it with fear of God, and the third is the fear of God through which nearness to Allah is attained by means of ihsan and voluntary acts."

What I had said in the first edition of this book was this:

"This is an emphasis by giving further detail. In the first sentence, faith, righteous deeds and taqwa are mentioned; in the second sentence, taqwa is mentioned with faith; and in the third, taqwa and ihsan, that is, righteous deeds, are mentioned. The purpose of this emphasis is that the matter of all affairs depends upon taqwa. The meaning is that the true value of deeds arises from the inner consciousness behind them, and this inner consciousness is taqwa, which is manifested through fear of God, and because of this consciousness a person remains constantly attached to the Being of Allah. Faith in Allah, affirmation of His commands and prohibitions, and righteous deeds which are the expression of this inner belief and hidden consciousness. There is a connection between this righteous deed and this inner consciousness. All this inner consciousness and taqwa is the real object sought, and the ruling depends upon them. The ruling does not depend upon the outward forms and appearances of deeds. The point that the real basis is intention, spirit and inner consciousness is such an important and fundamental matter that it needs to be repeated again and again."

Even now I am not fully satisfied with my own statement, but no other point has come to my understanding. Wallahu al-musta'an.

The discussion continues on the subject of lawful and unlawful. The matter under discussion is hunting while in the state of ihram. The expiation for killing game, the wisdom behind why Allah has made obligatory the respect of His House, the sacred months, the offerings (hady) and the garlanded animals, and why the beginning of this surah prohibits meddling with these things, are all being addressed. At the end, a general principle and standard is mentioned for the individual Muslim and for an Islamic society: a standard by which a pure thing has greater value even if it is little, and an impure thing has no value even if it is very abundant.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 94 to 100:

Look back once more and read the opening verses of this surah.

"O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts. Lawful for you are the quadrupeds of the cattle, except what is recited to you, but not permitting hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills." (1)

"O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah, nor the sacred month, nor the offerings, nor the garlands, nor those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His pleasure. And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt." (2) (5:1-2)

This prohibition concerned hunting when the hunter is in the state of ihram, and this prohibition concerned the violation of the symbols of Allah's worship (sha'a'ir). The sacrificial animals, the animals bearing garlands as votive offerings, and the harassment of pilgrims were forbidden, but no worldly punishment had been prescribed for these acts. It was only said that these acts are sinful. Now, as a worldly punishment, expiation (kaffarah) is stated, so that the violator may taste the consequence of his deed. However, the forgiveness of past errors is also announced. If someone had committed these prohibited acts earlier, they are forgiven; but whoever commits them again after this announced guidance will be given a severe punishment and will not be able to escape the vengeance of Allah. The beginning of this group of verses is also made with that familiar voice.

"O you who have believed" (ya ayyuha alladhina amanu). After this address, they are told that now a trial is about to befall them, namely regarding that hunting from which they have been forbidden in the state of ihram.

"O you who have believed, Allah will certainly test you with something of the game that your hands and your lances can reach, so that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen. Then whoever transgresses after this, for him is a painful punishment." (94)

This hunting is very easy: Allah drives it toward them Himself; it is of such a kind that they can seize it even with their hands, and their spears and arrows can strike it with ease. There have been incidents in which game came right into their tents and into their homes within the Haram, and this was a trial from Allah. This is the same trial in which the Children of Israel failed, and then they could not stand on their own feet. They first insistently demanded of their prophet Musa (peace be upon him) that a day be designated for them on which engaging in economic activities would be forbidden to them. On that day they were to rest completely, pray, and not occupy themselves with any worldly or economic work. Allah designated the day of Saturday, but Allah drove game in abundance to the shores for their trial. This game would roam before their eyes, and when it was not Saturday, the game would not appear at all. Just as fish are usually hidden in water, now these poor people, seeing this constantly, could not keep their covenant with Allah. The well-known vein of the Jews throbbed; their original nature awoke. They began to make excuses and tricks with Allah. Thus they began to surround the game on Saturday, which they would hunt on later days. It was this very act of theirs upon which Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to present it before them. Allah addresses the Messenger ﷺ, saying:

"And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and did not come on the days they did not observe it. Thus We tested them because they were defiantly disobedient." (7:163)

The Ummah of Islam too was subjected to a similar trial, and it succeeded, whereas the Jews failed and were unsuccessful. And the meaning of this verse of the Holy Qur'an is this:

"You are the best nation brought forth for mankind; you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah. Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them; some of them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient." (3:110)

Countless stages came in which the Ummah of Islam succeeded in trials while the Children of Israel failed, and this was the reason why Allah removed the station of khilafah on this earth from the Children of Israel and conferred it upon the Muslim Ummah. He granted the Muslim Ummah a glory on earth that He had not granted to anyone before, because the Islamic system of life was not established in the era of any previous nation in the way it fully manifested in the era of the Muslim Ummah. But this happened in the era in which the Muslim Ummah was truly the Muslim Ummah, and in the era in which it understood that Islam is that which appears in the practical life of people and that people's lives are conducted in accordance with the Islamic Shari'ah. In that era the Muslim Ummah had the sense that this great trust had been entrusted to it and that it had been made its custodian; that the Muslim Ummah had been appointed guardian of all humanity, and its duty was to shape people's lives according to the Islamic system of life and to establish upon them this trust of Allah.

The trial in which people could hunt easily in the state of ihram, yet were prevented from hunting as a trial, is one of the trials in which this Ummah succeeded. To test this Ummah through such trials and to train it through testing was a very great and manifest mercy of Allah. From this it is known that Allah has chosen this Ummah.

Allah has also explained the wisdom of this test: "so that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen" (li ya'lama Allahu man yakhafuhu bil-ghayb). The principle placed in the conscience of a Muslim is who fears Allah in the unseen. This is an extremely firm principle upon which the edifice of the Islamic worldview stands. According to this principle, the conduct of a Muslim is determined, and this conduct conforms to the theory of khilafah on earth and the Islamic system of life.

People do not see Allah, but when they believe in Allah, Allah is present within their souls. For a human being, Allah is unseen in his conception and understanding, yet the believing heart, by believing in Him unseen, fears Allah. When this great reality, the reality of faith in the unseen, settles in a person's heart and mind, and he begins to fear Allah and becomes independent of sensory sight and sensory observation, and this believer bears witness to "There is no god but Allah" although he has not seen Allah with his own eyes, then the settling of this great reality within the human being brings about a great revolutionary change within him. His natural faculties are liberated, and the missionary spirit that Allah has deposited in his nature functions in the fullest measure; and the closer he comes to the unseen world (which has been prepared for man), the further he moves away from the world of animals; and he rises to a level that gathers the sensory within him, so that he confines himself to the material world and goes wholly into the animal sphere. This is why Allah explicitly states here the wisdom of this trial, so that the souls of the believers may strive to attain it, and Allah knows by His knowledge of the unseen who fears Him in the unseen. But Allah does not seize people in this world according to His knowledge; Allah's seizing and grasp fall only upon what actually comes to pass.

"Then whoever transgresses after this, for him is a painful punishment" (fa man i'tada ba'da dhalika falahu 'adhabun alim). Allah has informed of the trial, has made known its wisdom, and has warned that they should not fall into it, since all the means of success have been provided for them. Even now, if anyone transgresses the limits of Allah, what could be his due but a painful punishment? Beyond this, what other outcome does he deserve, since he himself chooses this punishment for himself? After this, if anyone again violates, the details of the expiation imposed upon him are given. Again, a prohibition is repeated as emphasis.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verse 95:

(Verse) "O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. Whoever among you kills it intentionally, then the compensation is an animal similar to what he killed, from the livestock, judged by two just men among you, as an offering to be brought to the Kaaba; or, as expiation, the feeding of needy people, or the equivalent of that in fasting, so that he may taste the consequence of his deed. Allah has pardoned what has passed; but whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him. Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution."

The prohibition is that any muhrim should not intentionally kill game. If, by mistake, game is killed by his hands, then he is neither sinful nor is there expiation upon him. If he hunts intentionally, then it is obligatory upon him to sacrifice an animal. And this should be of such a kind that it equals the value of the game killed; for example, for killing a deer, a young she-camel or a goat. If he kills an ostrich, he should sacrifice a cow. In the case of hunting a fox and a giraffe, a young camel; for a cat and a hare, a hare. And for an animal for which there is no domestic counterpart, he should sacrifice an animal equal in value to it.

The judgment regarding this expiation is to be made by two just Muslims. If two arbiters have decided concerning the sacrifice of an animal, the offender shall let that animal go so that it reaches the Kaaba, and there it shall be slaughtered and given to the needy. If no animal is found, the two arbiters shall then also decide concerning the feeding of the needy, and this food should be equal in value to the game, although there are jurisprudential differences about this. If he is not able even to feed the needy, the offending muhrim shall observe fasts, that is, one fast for each needy person. Now, what the value of the food for the needy will be, there are jurisprudential differences. In any case, the essential matter is that its determination will differ in every age.

The wisdom of this expiation has also been explicitly stated by the Noble Qur'an: (Verse) "(liyadhuqa wabala amrihi)", "so that he may taste the consequence of his deed." In imposing expiation there is also an aspect of punishment, because the person has violated a sanctity, and Islam is strict about it. This is why it is commanded here that what has happened has happened, and whoever does not desist in future shall face severe retribution.

(Verse) "Allah has pardoned what has passed; but whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him. Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution."

"But now, if anyone repeats this act, Allah will take retribution from him; Allah is Mighty, and has the power to take retribution."

These were the rulings concerning the hunting of land game. As for sea game, it is permissible both in the state of ihram and outside the state of ihram.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 5, verse 96:

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travellers.﴾ That is, the catch of the sea and its food have been made lawful for you: you may eat it while you are settled, and you may also make it provision for a caravan on a journey.

Sea creatures are permissible both for the one in a state of ihram (muhrim) and for the one who is not. One may hunt them and one may also preserve them. Since permission was given here for hunting and using sea creatures, the hunting of land animals was again prohibited.

﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram.﴾ Hunting land game is forbidden to you while you remain in ihram.

On what is agreed upon: it is that hunting land game is forbidden for the one in ihram. But if a non-muhrim hunts some game, is it permissible for the muhrim to eat it or not? Also, there is a difference of opinion about the meaning of "game" (shikar). Then it is another matter of disagreement whether what is meant is only those animals which are generally hunted, or whether the hunting of all animals is forbidden, whether or not they are customarily hunted, or whether this prohibition applies to all animals.

This discussion of lawful and unlawful may be concluded with the point that the basis of everything rests upon taqwa (God-consciousness). Accordingly, here too, the feelings of God-fearing and dread of God are aroused.

﴿And fear Allah, to Whom you will be gathered.﴾ (96)

Say: Be wary of disobeying that God in whose presence you will be gathered and brought to account.

The question arises: why are these restrictions placed within the Haram and upon the muhrim? In fact, this world, which is a field of struggle for people, is where Allah wishes to make the Haram a zone of peace, and this zone of peace and sanctuary are the Ka'bah and the sacred months. In this world conflict continues among people; enemies keep fighting one another, and the effort to humiliate one another never ceases. This conflict runs through all living things, and Islam provides for all of them this area of peace and this time of peace, by which fear gives way to tranquillity, war gives way to peace, and a shade of safety, serene tranquillity and security descends upon the heads of all people. The human soul continues its activities in a practical world, not merely in the ideal, but in the practical. Now it is no longer in a world of mere imaginations and dreams, which in reality weigh very heavily upon the world.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 97–100 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for the people, and the Sacred Month, and the offerings, and the garlands. That is so that you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of everything.﴾ Be warned! Allah is severe in punishment, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. The Messenger's duty is only to convey (the message), and Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.

The sanctities of the Sacred House are so extensive that within their sphere fall humans, birds, animals and creeping creatures. Even if someone reaches the boundaries of the Haram in the state of ihram, all these things remain forbidden to him. Besides this, four months have also been declared as al-ashhur al-hurum (the sacred months). In them, killing and fighting are strictly forbidden. These four months are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab. Allah had placed the reverence of these four months in the hearts of the Arabs, to such an extent that even in the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah) they used to respect these months. In these months they would not even threaten or frighten any soul. In these months they would not take blood revenge, nor would anyone expect retaliation, to the extent that a man would find the killer of his father, son or brother and yet would not cause him any harm. Thus, during this period, people would move about freely, undertake trade journeys and seek lawful sustenance. These commands of peace were also issued by Allah so that the Ka'bah might become a land of peace and security, where people's hearts would find stability and there would be no fear or restlessness. Just as the Ka'bah was a place of safety, Allah had declared these four months a period of peace. Then the bounds of this peace were further extended, and the sacrificial animal that has been sent toward the Ka'bah was also made inviolable and protected. These animals were driven during the Hajj and 'Umrah.

Accordingly, even in the Age of Ignorance these animals were not disturbed. Likewise, the one who takes refuge in the Ka'bah and places a garland of the trees of the Sacred House around his neck was also declared inviolable.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 97–100 (part 2 of 2):

Allah brought this ummah onto the stage and declared it "khayr ummah" (the best community). Allah's plan was that it should be prepared for a great task. This great task was that this ummah would bear the trust of the Islamic system upon this earth. It would establish the Islamic system of life in such a way that no ummah before it had established it in this manner. It would establish this system in people's lives in such a way that this system had never been established in this manner within any other ummah.

To achieve this great goal, it was necessary that this ummah be given such a long training as had not been given to any ummah before. The first training was that it be completely removed from the traces of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) and be lifted from the depths of jahiliyyah and raised directly to the high destination, until it stands on the highest peak of Islam. After this, this ummah should correct its concepts and ideas, and purify its habits, its consciousness and its thoughts from the traces and pollutions of jahiliyyah. After this, such resolve should be instilled in it that it accepts the truth, and then endures the trials that come as a result of that acceptance. After this, it should align its whole life according to Islamic values and standards, until it becomes a rabbani ummah (a community devoted to the Lord) and its humanity rises to the high levels of humanity. When its training has reached this point, then in its eyes good and bad will no longer be equal, even though the corrupt and impure may be abundant and dazzle the eyes and dazzle with brilliance. But when a person distinguishes between the good (tayyib) and the corrupt (khabeeth) and weighs things on the divine scale, then, despite the abundance and bulk of the corrupt, its weight is less than the good, and the pan of the good is very heavy despite its scarcity.

At this stage, this ummah becomes amin (trustworthy) and bearer of trust. It is upright and reliable. Now it is the guardian of all humanity. Now it uses Allah's scale for people and determines values with the measure of Allah. It chooses the good, and its eyes are not dazzled on seeing the corrupt. Sometimes there come occasions when this scale is extremely beneficial. In circumstances when falsehood is swollen, and a person thinks that perhaps it is progressing, the eyes see only that it is apparently powerful and abundant. A believer weighs this swollen falsehood on Allah's scale. Thus his hands are not agitated, nor are his eyes dazzled, nor is his standard spoiled. So he chooses truth against this falsehood, which has no froth and no swelling. He has no provisions or equipment around him. He is simply the truth. He is pure truth, and he has no purpose with it other than itself. On Allah's scale his weight is great, and in his own essence he is beautiful and graceful. There is a strength within his very being.

Allah trained this ummah exactly according to the Qur'anic method, and He appointed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as its qayyim (guardian) and overseer. Then it reached the level where it was to believe in the religion of Allah: not merely a psychological faith, nor a faith confined to the heart, but faith in its practical life and in all its activities upon this earth. Faith in all the agitations of life, in all desires and hopes, in all inclinations and schools of thought, in all interests and benefits, and in all the struggles of individuals and groups. In short, its faith should be such that it is faithful even in watching over this entire universe, and faithful within its great responsibilities in the boundless ocean of this life.

Allah trained this ummah through various guidances, various influences, various trials and various regulations, and made all these matters into one system in a single collective form, like a bundle, whose ultimate aims were one. That is, this ummah should prepare its beliefs and concepts, its consciousness and inclinations, its conduct and morals, and its Shariah and system in such a way that it is established upon the religion of Allah, that it is a guardian over all of humanity, and that it is Allah's right to take from His servants whatever work He wishes. Allah is sovereign in His affairs. Thus upon this earth, in this luminous form, the religion of Allah was established, shining. It was a concept that took on reality in life, and this practice was established: whenever this ummah strives for the establishment of this religion, Allah's help will be granted to it.

After this, the Muslim community is taught certain etiquettes concerning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is told that questions should not be asked about matters that the Messenger ﷺ did not mention. It may be that if you ask and the Messenger ﷺ answers, you may not like that answer, and some harm may occur, and through the answer such obligations may be imposed that it would be impossible to act upon. Or it may be that in some matter Allah had granted ease, and because of the question, hardship may come about, since Allah, out of mercy to His servants, gives them the greatest ease.

When the flames of war blaze within the conscience, their flames and smoke envelop time and space, and then all humans and animals fall within their reach. The two sanctuaries (al-Haramayn) bring about peace even in this inner battlefield. When peace and tranquillity are established within the conscience, a person who is in the state of sanctity feels reluctance even to extend his hand toward any living creature, even if that game is outside the Haram. And when peace and tranquillity are established within the conscience, a person feels reluctance to extend his hand toward any living creature. This period is a period of the training of the human self, so that it may become pure and clean, become light, rise up and connect with the higher realm (al-mala' al-a'la), and become ready to deal with the inhabitants of the higher realm.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 97–100 (part 2 of 2):

Allah brought this ummah onto the stage and declared it "khayr ummah" (the best community). Allah's plan was that it should be prepared for a great task. This great task was that this ummah would bear the trust of the Islamic system upon this earth. It would establish the Islamic system of life in such a way that no ummah before it had established it in this manner. It would establish this system in people's lives in such a way that this system had never been established in this manner within any other ummah.

To achieve this great goal, it was necessary that this ummah be given such a long training as had not been given to any ummah before. The first training was that it be completely removed from the traces of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) and be lifted from the depths of jahiliyyah and raised directly to the high destination, until it stands on the highest peak of Islam. After this, this ummah should correct its concepts and ideas, and purify its habits, its consciousness and its thoughts from the traces and pollutions of jahiliyyah. After this, such resolve should be instilled in it that it accepts the truth, and then endures the trials that come as a result of that acceptance. After this, it should align its whole life according to Islamic values and standards, until it becomes a rabbani ummah (a community devoted to the Lord) and its humanity rises to the high levels of humanity. When its training has reached this point, then in its eyes good and bad will no longer be equal, even though the corrupt and impure may be abundant and dazzle the eyes and dazzle with brilliance. But when a person distinguishes between the good (tayyib) and the corrupt (khabeeth) and weighs things on the divine scale, then, despite the abundance and bulk of the corrupt, its weight is less than the good, and the pan of the good is very heavy despite its scarcity.

At this stage, this ummah becomes amin (trustworthy) and bearer of trust. It is upright and reliable. Now it is the guardian of all humanity. Now it uses Allah's scale for people and determines values with the measure of Allah. It chooses the good, and its eyes are not dazzled on seeing the corrupt. Sometimes there come occasions when this scale is extremely beneficial. In circumstances when falsehood is swollen, and a person thinks that perhaps it is progressing, the eyes see only that it is apparently powerful and abundant. A believer weighs this swollen falsehood on Allah's scale. Thus his hands are not agitated, nor are his eyes dazzled, nor is his standard spoiled. So he chooses truth against this falsehood, which has no froth and no swelling. He has no provisions or equipment around him. He is simply the truth. He is pure truth, and he has no purpose with it other than itself. On Allah's scale his weight is great, and in his own essence he is beautiful and graceful. There is a strength within his very being.

Allah trained this ummah exactly according to the Qur'anic method, and He appointed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as its qayyim (guardian) and overseer. Then it reached the level where it was to believe in the religion of Allah: not merely a psychological faith, nor a faith confined to the heart, but faith in its practical life and in all its activities upon this earth. Faith in all the agitations of life, in all desires and hopes, in all inclinations and schools of thought, in all interests and benefits, and in all the struggles of individuals and groups. In short, its faith should be such that it is faithful even in watching over this entire universe, and faithful within its great responsibilities in the boundless ocean of this life.

Allah trained this ummah through various guidances, various influences, various trials and various regulations, and made all these matters into one system in a single collective form, like a bundle, whose ultimate aims were one. That is, this ummah should prepare its beliefs and concepts, its consciousness and inclinations, its conduct and morals, and its Shariah and system in such a way that it is established upon the religion of Allah, that it is a guardian over all of humanity, and that it is Allah's right to take from His servants whatever work He wishes. Allah is sovereign in His affairs. Thus upon this earth, in this luminous form, the religion of Allah was established, shining. It was a concept that took on reality in life, and this practice was established: whenever this ummah strives for the establishment of this religion, Allah's help will be granted to it.

After this, the Muslim community is taught certain etiquettes concerning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is told that questions should not be asked about matters that the Messenger ﷺ did not mention. It may be that if you ask and the Messenger ﷺ answers, you may not like that answer, and some harm may occur, and through the answer such obligations may be imposed that it would be impossible to act upon. Or it may be that in some matter Allah had granted ease, and because of the question, hardship may come about, since Allah, out of mercy to His servants, gives them the greatest ease.

(Verses 101–102)

Some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) many questions, and these questions concerned matters on which no command or prohibition had been revealed. They took a keen interest in the details of certain matters that the Qur'an had left in general terms, and because of that generality there was a kind of ease for people. At times they would ask about matters for which no answer was needed, since it was possible that the disclosure would not please the questioner himself, or that it would cause distress to other Muslims.

It is reported in the narrations that when the verse on the obligation of Hajj was revealed, someone asked whether Hajj had become obligatory every year. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) expressed great displeasure at this question, because the verse on Hajj was stated in general terms:

﴿And it is a duty owed to Allah by the people to make pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it.﴾

Performing Hajj once in one's lifetime was sufficient to act upon this verse. Thus, if the Messenger (ﷺ) had explained this verse as "every year," many difficulties would have arisen, whereas Allah did not consider it appropriate to place people in them.

Tirmidhi and Daraqutni narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) a hadith mursal (a report in which the Companion's link to the Prophet (ﷺ) is omitted) that when this verse was revealed, people asked, "O Messenger of Allah, every year?" He fell silent. They asked again, "Every year?" He said, "No. If I had said 'yes,' it would have become obligatory forever." Then this verse was revealed:

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you.﴾

Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O people, Hajj has been made obligatory upon you." A man stood up and asked, "Every year?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not answer his question. Then he asked again, "O Messenger of Allah, every year?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked, "Who is this questioner?" The people told him that it was so-and-so. He said, "By Allah, in whose hand is my soul, if I had said 'yes,' it would have become obligatory every year, and if it had become obligatory every year, you would not have been able to fulfil it, and if you had not been able to fulfil it, you would have become disbelievers." Then this verse was revealed:

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you.﴾

Another hadith, which Imam Muslim narrated in Sahih Muslim, is that he reports from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said on one occasion, "Ask me whatever you wish while I am standing in this place; I will inform you." A man stood up and asked, "O Messenger of Allah, where will I enter?" He (ﷺ) said, "In the Fire." Abdullah ibn Hudhafah (may Allah be pleased with him) asked, "Who is my father?" He (ﷺ) said, "Your father is Hudhafah." (Ibn Abd al-Barr writes that Abdullah ibn Hudhafah was among the early Muslims. He migrated to Abyssinia, took part in Badr, and was a man of very cheerful disposition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent him with a message to Kisra.) When this question and answer took place between him and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), namely, "Who is my father?" and he (ﷺ) said, "Hudhafah," his mother said, "I have never seen a disobedient son like you. Were you confident that I had not committed a sin like the women of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period)? Did you want to shame me before the public?" Abdullah said, "By Allah, if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had told me that I was the son of a black slave, I would still have attached my lineage to him."

Ibn Jarir narrated with his chain from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that one day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in great majesty, and his face was red. He sat upon the pulpit. A man asked, "O Messenger of Allah, where will I be?" He (ﷺ) said, "In the Fire." Another stood up and asked, "Who is my father?" He (ﷺ) said, "Your father is Hudhafah." Thereupon Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up and said, "O Messenger of Allah, we are content that Allah is our Lord, Muhammad (ﷺ) is our Prophet, and the Qur'an is our guide. O Messenger of Allah, we have only just emerged from ignorance and polytheism. Only Allah knows who our forefathers are." Then the anger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) subsided, and this verse was revealed:

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you.﴾

Mujahid narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that this verse was revealed concerning those who asked about the bahirah (a she-camel whose ear was slit and was released), the sa'ibah (a camel released freely), the wasilah (a she-camel or ewe that gave birth to females consecutively), and the ham (a stallion camel freed after a certain number of stud services). Sa'id ibn Jubair (may Allah be pleased with him) also adopted this opinion, and he said that this verse was revealed after the following verse, for that reason:

﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah or wasilah or ham.﴾ (5:103)

These narrations include all the questions about which Allah, the Exalted, forbade the believers to ask.

The purpose of the Qur'an was not merely to state beliefs and ideas, or to enforce a legal code. Rather, the aim of the Qur'an was to train a community and to bring a society into existence. The Qur'an was telling individuals that their growth and training were to be carried out upon sound moral principles. Here the Qur'an has taught the etiquette of questioning, defined the limits of debate, and indicated the method of knowledge and understanding, especially for the period in which the rain of mercy was descending and news was coming from the unseen. Wisdom required that people not ask about the details of the Shariah and that they leave the texts in their general form. Likewise, the matters of the unseen should be left as unseen, and people should desire knowledge of them only to the extent that Allah, the All-Knowing and All-Aware, grants. It is not appropriate for them to seek new texts and thereby keep placing further difficulties upon themselves. They should not ask about mere possibilities and hypothetical problems, nor pursue those unseen matters whose disclosure Allah has not made. This is because Allah knows well the power and capacity of human beings; He knows their limit of endurance. He is legislating for them according to their strength, and He discloses to them only those matters that their nature can comprehend. Some matters Allah deliberately leaves in general terms, and there is no harm for people in these matters remaining in that form. At the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, an answer might come that they would not like, or some people might not like it, and it would become a burden upon everyone.

This is why Allah, the Exalted, forbade people from asking about such matters that, if they were disclosed, would displease them. He warned them that if they did ask, an answer would come, because revelation is ongoing, and in this way the scope of obligations would widen.

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you. But if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. Allah has pardoned them.﴾

That is, do not ask about those matters that Allah has pardoned and whose imposition He has left in abeyance, because generality itself contains ease. For example, Allah has said nothing about the number of times of Hajj, or about things that Allah has not mentioned at all.

After this, Allah set before them the example of the earlier nations, namely the People of the Book, who by asking questions repeatedly narrowed the scope of their own freedom. As a result, more obligations and commands were imposed upon them, and when those commands became obligatory, they refused to comply and adopted the path of disbelief. Had they remained silent and allowed the ease that Allah had granted them to continue, there would have been no hardship upon them, and they would not have been compelled to refuse out of severity.

We have read in Surah al-Baqarah that when the Children of Israel were commanded to slaughter a cow, there were no conditions or restrictions attached to the cow; it was simply said that they should slaughter a cow. Had they slaughtered any cow, the command would have been fulfilled. Instead, they began to enumerate the attributes of the cow. They began to investigate even its colour. With every investigation and question, severity was increased upon them. Had they not made a barrage of questions, no difficulty would have arisen for them.

The same was their condition regarding the Sabbath: first they themselves demanded a day of rest, and then they refused to observe it. Because of this disposition, Allah, as a punishment, made several things unlawful for them.

It is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Leave me alone regarding what I have not commanded you. The nations that were destroyed before you were destroyed because of their excessive questioning and their disagreements with their prophets."

In Sahih Muslim, Amir ibn Sa'd narrated from his father that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The greatest criminal among Muslims against Muslims is one who asks about something that was not prohibited to the Muslims, and then, because of his questions, it becomes prohibited for them."

This set of verses and, after them, the prophetic traditions establishes a method for the acquisition of knowledge in the Islamic society. In Islam, the purpose of seeking knowledge is to learn solutions to matters that are genuinely needed, and to confine oneself to the scope of necessity. Therefore, the benefit of not being interested in the unseen is that human energies are not spent in bringing into the light matters whose reality a person has no practical need to reach. His practical life does not depend upon that reality, and it is sufficient for the human mind to believe in the unseen just as Allah, the All-Knowing and All-Aware, has stated.

When someone abandons faith and begins debating unseen realities, nothing is gained from that debate, because the human mind has not been given the power and capacity to perceive anything in the realm of the unseen. Its perception is limited to the extent that it has been told. Therefore, any effort of this kind will also be fruitless. It is another matter that such a person, groping in the dark, will exhaust himself and will himself fall into far-off misguidance.

The policy of Islam is that when a problem arises, a question should be asked about it at that time, and this is the Islamic method. Do you not see that throughout the entire Meccan period, no legal ruling was revealed whose implementation was necessary? Although rulings about certain things and individual actions continued to come, rulings requiring enforcement, such as the hudud (prescribed punishments), ta'zir (discretionary punishments), kaffarat (expiations), and qisas (retaliation), were all revealed in Medina, because an Islamic government had been established in Medina, and the enforcement of rulings is the responsibility of the government.

The early Islamic society had grasped this reality. They would not ask about a matter until it occurred, and even that question would be limited to the actual event. There was never any need for the detailed formulation of extensive legal provisions, so that questions and answers would also conform to Islam's system of training.

The practice of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was that if no dispute had arisen, he would reprimand the person who asked questions without need. Darimi, in his Musnad, and Zuhri have mentioned that when a question was put to Zayd ibn Thabit al-Ansari, he would first ask whether such an incident had occurred. If they said yes, such an incident had occurred, he would then speak according to his knowledge. And if they said the incident had not occurred, he would reply, "Let it happen, and then we will speak."

Similarly, it is reported from Ammar ibn Yasir (may Allah be pleased with him) that a question was put to him, and he asked whether such an incident had occurred. They said no, and he said, "Look, when such an incident occurs, then we will speak."

Darimi narrated with his chain from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). He said: I have not seen better people than the Companions of the Messenger of Allah. Until his death, they asked him only thirty-one questions, and all these questions are mentioned in the Qur'an, including those beginning with "They ask you" (yas'alunak):

﴿They ask you about the sacred month...﴾ ... ﴿They ask you about menstruation.﴾

And they used to ask only about that which would be beneficial to them.

Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) said: When I came to Medina, the people of Medina had no knowledge except the Book and the Sunnah. When a matter arose, the governor of Medina would gather the scholars present, and whatever they agreed upon, he would enforce. You people ask too many questions, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not approve of this.

Allamah Qurtubi, in his commentary, under this verse said: Imam Muslim narrated from Mughirah ibn Shu'bah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has forbidden you disobedience to mothers, has forbidden burying daughters alive, has forbidden withholding others' rights and demanding one's own rights, and has disliked three things: excessive idle talk, excessive questioning, and the squandering of wealth." The righteous predecessors (salaf) disliked this and considered it mere artificiality. They used to say that it does not fully fit the (actual) aspects of the matter.

If a problem actually arises, then asking about it is asking about a specific situation. But if no event has occurred, its determination is simply not possible, and whatever ruling is given about it will in practice not fit well. If we begin to answer hypothetical cases, this act would be contrary to the realism of the Shariah, and it would conflict with the method (manhaj) of Islam.

Today, an example of this is that people ask about the laws of the Shariah in countries where the purpose of establishing the Shariah is not before them. They do not seek a fatwa in order to implement some ruling of the Shariah.

The method of the Islamic Shariah is that a fatwa is sought for the sake of implementing law. If both the questioner and the one giving the answer know that they are residents of a country in which the Shariah is not being implemented, in which the sovereignty of Allah is neither acknowledged nor believed in, and in which it is not enforced in people's lives and collective affairs, in other words, in which the sovereignty of Allah is not recognized and the Most High is not obeyed, then in such circumstances what is the meaning of seeking a fatwa, and what is the benefit of the answer given by the one who answers? Both of them, in fact, are mocking the Shariah, whether they are aware of it or whether they do so unconsciously.

The truth is that this religion is a serious religion, and it came precisely in order to control people's lives. It came so that people worship and serve none but Allah. One purpose of the coming of this religion is also that the right of sovereignty and authority (hakimiyyah) of Allah, which some people have seized, be taken back from them and returned again to Allah, and that the Shariah and government of Allah be established in all affairs. It did not come so that its legal system should be merely the subject of practical discussions, nor merely so that people debate how it may be implemented. However, it is not definitively known what the question was. (Verses 101–102)

Some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) many questions, and these questions concerned matters on which no command or prohibition had been revealed. They took a keen interest in the details of certain matters that the Qur'an had left in general terms, and because of that generality there was a kind of ease for people. At times they would ask about matters for which no answer was needed, since it was possible that the disclosure would not please the questioner himself, or that it would cause distress to other Muslims.

It is reported in the narrations that when the verse on the obligation of Hajj was revealed, someone asked whether Hajj had become obligatory every year. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) expressed great displeasure at this question, because the verse on Hajj was stated in general terms:

﴿And it is a duty owed to Allah by the people to make pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it.﴾

Performing Hajj once in one's lifetime was sufficient to act upon this verse. Thus, if the Messenger (ﷺ) had explained this verse as "every year," many difficulties would have arisen, whereas Allah did not consider it appropriate to place people in them.

Tirmidhi and Daraqutni narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) a hadith mursal (a report in which the Companion's link to the Prophet (ﷺ) is omitted) that when this verse was revealed, people asked, "O Messenger of Allah, every year?" He fell silent. They asked again, "Every year?" He said, "No. If I had said 'yes,' it would have become obligatory forever." Then this verse was revealed:

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you.﴾

Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O people, Hajj has been made obligatory upon you." A man stood up and asked, "Every year?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not answer his question. Then he asked again, "O Messenger of Allah, every year?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked, "Who is this questioner?" The people told him that it was so-and-so. He said, "By Allah, in whose hand is my soul, if I had said 'yes,' it would have become obligatory every year, and if it had become obligatory every year, you would not have been able to fulfil it, and if you had not been able to fulfil it, you would have become disbelievers." ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you.﴾

He (ﷺ) said, "Your father is Hudhafah." (Ibn Abd al-Barr writes that Abdullah ibn Hudhafah was among the early Muslims. He migrated to Abyssinia, took part in Badr, and was a man of very cheerful disposition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent him with a message to Kisra.) Abdullah said, "By Allah, if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had told me that I was the son of a black slave, I would still have attached my lineage to him."

Thereupon Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up and said, "O Messenger of Allah, we are content that Allah is our Lord, Muhammad (ﷺ) is our Prophet, and the Qur'an is our guide. Then the anger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) subsided, and this verse was revealed:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 5, verse 103–104 (part 1 of 2):

(Verses) No. 103 to 104.

Human minds and hearts will either remain upon the nature on which Allah created them. They will recognise only one God, serve one Lord of the worlds, submit to His Shariah alone, and abandon all other codes and laws apart from Allah. They will abandon the lordship of all other gods and will not take their rules and regulations from any other source. This will be an extremely natural state of affairs: the servant's bond with his Lord will be intact, and his worship and his relationship with the Generous Lord will be extremely simple. Otherwise he will remain wandering in the winding, labyrinthine passages of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). Sometimes he will be an idol-worshipper and will remain lost amid layer upon layer of words. At every turn of life, a delusion and an imagination will be making him dance. Every idol of jahiliyyah will demand that he perform its rites of worship; the demand of each idol will be that he appease it. Then the rites of worship and sacrifice will also be numerous and contradictory, and an idol-worshipper's mind will have no principle. He will keep performing the rites of worship and will not understand why he is doing so. Bondage to many different and scattered lords will exhaust him and crush him, and that honour of humanity which Allah had bestowed upon man will also be lost.

When Islam came, humanity was in the latter condition. It presented the doctrine of Tawhid (the oneness of God) to the people and explained that the sovereign authority is one, and that it is the one who is obeyed. It gave the doctrine of serving only one Lord so that people might be freed from enslaving and being enslaved by one another. Through the doctrine of Tawhid, man was freed from the worship of many gods, and the human conscience was freed from the unbearable burden of delusions and superstitions.

Human understanding, perception and wisdom attained their true station and rank, and man was freed from the many and contradictory rites of worship. Then man began a jihad against idol-worship and broke and shattered all its forms. After that, it pursued it through all the ups and downs of life, and idol-worship was eradicated from every place: the depths of the heart, the methods of worship, the customs of life, the system of law and the system of government.

Among the ideas of jahiliyyah, this was a crooked notion, which the Noble Qur'an is here treating in order to set it straight, to light up that crooked path by kindling a lamp, and to kindle the lamp of the Islamic principles of thought and vision: the principles of the Shariah and the principles of the system of life.

(Verse) "Allah has not instituted any bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah or ham. But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason." (103)

"Allah has not instituted any bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah or ham. But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah, and most of them do not use their reason."

These were kinds of animals which they would leave free for their deities. They had certain special conditions, and they had derived these conditions from the layered veils of the history of thought, delusions and superstitions. What were the bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah and ham? And what was the origin and source of the delusions and superstitions prevalent among the Arabs concerning them?

The reports about their definitions differ. It would be appropriate to quote some of the reports here. Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: the bahirah is that kind of camel whose milk its owner would not use himself; it is only for the deities, and it is obvious that the property of the deities would be for the religious leaders alone. The sa'ibah is that which they would dedicate to their idols. The wasilah was a she-camel whose first offspring was female and whose second offspring was also female, meaning that the two were joined without a male being born between them. Such a she-camel they would slaughter in the name of their idols. The ham was the camel from whose progeny many offspring had been born; its number was fixed, and when it reached that number, they called it a ham because it had protected its back from further use. Now no one would ride it.

The lexicographers say: the bahirah is a she-camel whose ears they would slit. They would say, "I slit the ears of my she-camel" (bahharat udhn al-naqah bahran). Such a she-camel was also called bahurah as well as bahirah. The ears were slit up to the very end, and the word bahr (sea) is also so called because it is wide. In the view of the people of jahiliyyah, eating the flesh of the bahirah was forbidden, and it became a bahirah in this way: when she gave birth for the fifth time and the offspring was male, they would slit her ears, declare her flesh forbidden, and forbid her sacrifice and riding her. No one would prevent her from his water, and no one would prevent her from his pasture.

The sa'ibah was a she-camel that was let loose; it was also called musaybah. In the age of jahiliyyah, if someone vowed that if he returned safely from a journey or recovered from an illness, he would make this vow: he would say, "My she-camel is a sa'ibah," and in its prohibition and free grazing it would be like the bahirah. Regarding the wasilah, some lexicographers have written that if a goat had two offspring, one male and one female, the Arabs would say that this female had joined with her brother in giving birth, and they would not slaughter that goat. Some said that if the goat bore a female, it belonged to them; and if it did not bear, they would slaughter it in the name of their deities; and if male and female were born together, they would say that since these brother and sister had come together, they would not slaughter the goat. The ham was a camel whose seed produced ten offspring; about it they would say that it had protected its back, so they would not prevent it from pasture or water. (See Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas.)

Several other reports concerning the definitions of these animals have also come down, and behind them there is only this notion which we have mentioned above. For the sanctity of these animals, no lofty or reasonable cause from these reasons has come in any report. As will be clear from the above extract, all these causes were the result of idol-worship and the delusions and darkness of jahiliyyah. When decisions are made from the standpoint of delusion and dark imagination, then there is no limit to superstition and dark thinking, nor does any principle or standard remain. As a result, some religious rites come into being; sometimes these rites decrease, and sometimes they increase. This principle prevailed within the Arab jahiliyyah as well, and this same situation can occur in every age and every place. Whenever people turn away from Tawhid, they will fall prey to such imaginings, because Tawhid is the doctrine in which there is neither crookedness nor darkness. In all jahili systems the outward forms of rites and superstitions differ, but the essence is that the foundation is dark thinking, that is, taking guidance in the affairs of life from somewhere other than Allah.

Jahiliyyah is not the name of a particular age; rather, jahiliyyah is the name of a state of affairs which keeps appearing again and again, changing its colour. It comes in different forms and in different periods. Now the situation will either be such that one Allah is the sovereign, and in contrast to Him all creation is His servant and subject; all authority is for Allah; consciousness and thought are taken from Allah; intention and action are in reference to Allah; order and collective customs are according to the will of Allah; values and standards are formed from the concept of Allah; laws and regulations are enforced by Allah; and all concepts, philosophies and guidance are taken from Allah alone. Otherwise it will be jahiliyyah, in whatever colour and form: in it, a servant will be the slave of a servant, or a servant will be the slave of some creature other than Allah. This jahiliyyah will have neither limits nor regulations, because no human being can make any regulation that could be called a divine regulation and principle, since countless factors affect human reason. In every age, whenever man has attempted to give any concept or any order, he has been influenced by countless factors, and he has not been able to withstand pressure and force from various directions until he bows before the most suitable regulation.

We see that fourteen hundred years have passed since the Qur'an's statement and exposition, and whenever human reason has turned away from the doctrine of Tawhid, it has become lost in intricate paths and trapped in a maze. It has continued to adhere to many different, numerous and scattered lords. It has lost its freedom, its nobility and its power to resist. If we take only this issue under discussion, the sanctity of animals, then even today in Egypt there are dozens of superstitions, in which some animals are left free out of reverence, and these are let loose in exactly the same way that animals used to be let loose in ancient times in the names of the deities, in the names of some saints and holy people.

The matter of these rites of worship and jahiliyyah is connected with only one principle, and this principle is the starting point. From this point two roads emerge: either it will be the road of Islam, or it will be the road of jahiliyyah. The point is: whose sovereignty will prevail in people's lives? According to the Islamic Shariah, sovereignty will be Allah's, or the sovereignty of someone other than Allah will prevail, and people will be devising their own commands and methods, or they will themselves determine the rites of worship and the values and standards. In other words, we may say that divinity over people will belong to Allah, or it will belong to some other creature of Allah. Whichever of those other than Allah claims the sovereignty of Allah will simply be considered a god.

(Verse) "Allah has not instituted any bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah or ham." (5:103) "Allah has not given the status of bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah and ham to these animals." And those who obey this Shariah and law are disbelievers; these people are disbelievers because they fabricate lies against Allah. Sometimes they themselves invent a matter from their own side and then say that this is the Shariah of Allah, and sometimes they say that in our affairs we do not accept any intervention of Allah's Shariah, and along with this they also claim that we are not disobedient to Allah. (Verse) "But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason." (103)

The belief of the pagan Arabs was that they were upon the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and that this religion had been revealed by Allah to Ibrahim (peace be upon him). These people were not deniers of the Divine Being; rather, they acknowledged the existence of the Divine Being. They also acknowledged Allah's power and admitted that Allah alone disposes of affairs. Yet despite these acknowledgements, they made their own laws for themselves, and after that they believed that these laws were from Allah. This is why they became disbelievers, and this matter applies to all those who live at any time in jahiliyyah and make laws for themselves, and then suppose that these are the Shariah of Allah.

The Shariah of Allah is that which is present in the Book of Allah, which Allah revealed and the Prophet explained. It is neither ambiguous nor complicated. The Shariah of Allah does not bear that someone should invent falsehood upon the Shariah from his own side and presume that it is the Shariah or the Book of Allah, as is the custom of the followers of jahiliyyah, who themselves make a Shariah and say that it is from Allah.

This is why Allah characterises those who make such claims with kufr, and after calling them disbelievers, Allah also calls such people unreasoning, because if they were reasonable they would not fabricate lies against Allah. If they were reasonable, they would not suppose that their fabrication could succeed. After this it is shown that there is also a contradiction between their words and their deeds.

(Verse) "And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger,' they say, 'Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon.' Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?" (104)

"And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger,' they say, 'Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon.' Even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?"

The Shariah which Allah has sent down is clear. It is recorded in the form of the Noble Qur'an and the Sunnah of the Messenger. This is the criterion, and this is the unit by which the paths of Islam and jahiliyyah are separated. One is the path of faith and the other is the path of disbelief. In this world, the situation will either be that people are invited to what Allah has sent down, and they will respond to it, and in that case they will be called Muslims; or they will reject this invitation, and in that case they will be disbelievers. There is no third state between these two.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 5, verses 103–104 (part 2 of 2):

These people were such that when they were invited towards Allah and the Messenger of Allah, they would say: "The path upon which we found our forefathers is sufficient for us." They abandoned that slogan of freedom, the essence of which was: abandon the slavery of human beings and follow reason and conscience, whether this reason and conscience be their own or that of their forefathers.

After this, the Qur'an expresses wonder and regret at their position:

﴿Even though their forefathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾

The meaning of this interrogation is not that following the forefathers is forbidden because they are not intelligent, and that if they were intelligent then following the forefathers would be permissible, and in that case abandoning the commands of Allah and the Messenger of Allah would be permissible. That is not the case. Rather, in this expression of wonder, the purpose is merely to describe their actual situation, namely that their forefathers before them had accepted irrational matters. For their forefathers in turn followed their own forefathers, and those forefathers had also framed rules and regulations for themselves. And when the Divine Shariah is present, if a person follows the customs of his forefathers and grandfathers, then he is certainly devoid of reason, and is not upon guidance, no matter what he says about himself and his laws. Whereas Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware, and True, and the command of Allah is in any case this: that these people know nothing, and this is the testimony of Allah. Whoever disobeys the Shariah of Allah is ignorant, astray, and at the same time one who fabricates lies against Allah, and a disbeliever as well.

After concluding the description of the statements and actions of the disbelievers, the address now turns to those who have believed. Here they are completely separated from the disbelievers and distinguished from them. They are told what their duties and obligations are, what their position is in comparison with other people, and that they are entrusted to Allah, and their lives are not entrusted to this transient world. Nor is their aim the attainment of the worldly benefits of this world.
